classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-pl.body:
# PAL S1 U4: Printmaking Variant

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-semester-1-plan|Semester 1 Plan]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-4-graphic-design-and-the-poster|Unit 4]]

> [!important] Unit 4 may run in one of two forms
> By default, Unit 4 runs as the Graphic Design poster, with A4 as the poster. It may instead run as this printmaking variant if students ask for it. Both routes use the same Wednesdays (W16–19). Which route runs will be confirmed in class.
> On the printmaking route, these dates apply: CS4 on Wed 2026-12-16, A4 on Wed 2026-12-23, and portfolio documentation on Wed 2027-01-06. They are provisional and may shift when the school publishes the calendar.

## Overview

This variant of Unit 4 teaches printmaking with linocut instead of the graphic design poster. Over three Wednesdays you learn where printmaking comes from, transfer a design onto a block and carve it, then ink and pull an edition of prints. You log CS4, an annotated design sheet, on Wed 2026-12-16, and you sit A4, a resolved print, on Wed 2026-12-23. The final Wednesday on Wed 2027-01-06 documents your work for the semester portfolio, with the EoT portfolio due that day.

## The ideas

### Printmaking as an image culture

**Printmaking** is making an image by pressing an inked surface onto paper, so one design can be printed many times. Early prints were cheap multiples, "designed to travel." The **Ukiyo-e** prints of Japan's "floating world" are the anchor example. The guiding question is: why print instead of paint once?

- A **matrix** is the surface that holds the image: the block you carve, ink, and print from.
- **Relief vs intaglio** is the main distinction: in relief printing you print from the raised surface left after carving away the rest; in intaglio you print from lines cut into the surface. Linocut is relief.
- The history runs from Dürer to Warhol. Printmakers to know: **Dürer**, Rembrandt, Daumier, Toulouse-Lautrec, and Warhol; from Ukiyo-e, **Hiroshige** and **Hokusai**.

### Making a linocut

- **The mirror rule**: a print comes out reversed, so transfer and carve your design mirror-reversed. Say it to yourself twice before you start.
- **Safety**: always carve away from your body and hands. The tools are sharp, so carving happens only in the room, never at home.
- **Transfer** moves your design onto the block. **Carving** cuts away the areas you do not want to print. Carving is slow, so start early and choose a simple, bold design.
- **Inking and proofing**: ink the block, then pull a test proof on scrap paper before you print for real.
- **Editioning**: pull a final edition on good paper. Make several impressions, both for quality and as insurance against a spoiled pull.
- **Second color and layering** (optional): add a second color or layer using `Color Mixing Guide` sheet 1. Not required to pass.

## Day by day

- **Wed 2026-12-09 (W15).** Homework set: the three A5 drawings from `A5 Drawing Guide`. Bring finished designs to W16. Without a design you cannot start, and there is no spare session.
- **Wed 2026-12-16 (W16, S15).** Learn printmaking history and the mirror rule, take the safety briefing, transfer your design, and begin carving. CS4 is logged at the end: one annotated design sheet showing which areas print and which are cut away.
- **Wed 2026-12-23 (W17, S16).** A4 sitting. Finish carving, ink your block, pull a test proof, then print a final edition on good paper. Submit at least one resolved print.
- **Wed 2027-01-06 (W19, S17).** Pull further impressions and try a second color or layering if you are ready. Take part in the gallery walk and reflection. Document your semester portfolio; the EoT portfolio is due.

## Assessment

A4 is graded inside the BNDS scheme: Attainment 50, Course Skills 20, Learning Behaviour 10, End of Term 20. See [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS scheme]]. You get one week's notice of what A4 will be. The detailed marking criteria for A4 will be confirmed in class.

## Review

Check you can:

- Explain what printmaking is and why early prints were made as cheap multiples.
- Name the Ukiyo-e prints as the anchor example of a print culture.
- State the distinction between relief and intaglio, and say which one linocut is.
- Define the mirror rule and apply it when you transfer a design.
- State the carving safety rule.
- Transfer a design and carve a linocut block.
- Ink a block, pull a test proof, and print a final edition.
- Name printmakers such as Dürer, Hiroshige, and Warhol.

concepts/four-key-concepts.md.body:
# Four Key Concepts

The spine of CIE 9607. Everything examined in the course is an application of one of four ideas: **Language**, **Representation**, **Industry**, **Audience**. The syllabus states them once as a list and again, at length, as subject content. Candidates "should be prepared to demonstrate their knowledge and understanding of these across all components" (Syllabus 2027 p.14).

Taught as a set in [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-01-the-four-key-concepts|L01]], then rehearsed for the rest of the course.

## The syllabus definitions

| | Definition (Syllabus 2027 p.5) | Page for detail |
|---|---|---|
| **Language** | "How the media communicate meanings through their forms, codes, conventions and techniques" | [[concepts/media-language]] |
| **Representation** | "How the media construct the social world including the portrayal of ideas, individuals and groups" | [[concepts/representation]] |
| **Industry** | "How and why media texts are produced, distributed and circulated" | [[concepts/media-industry]] |
| **Audience** | "How audiences are constructed and addressed by media texts and how audiences interpret and respond to media texts" | [[concepts/media-audience]] |

The Scheme of Work reproduces these four definitions word for word and keys the whole document to them as KC1–KC4 (SoW p.4). Where a scheme-of-work row is tagged KC3, it is teaching Industry.

You will be assessed on your **direct knowledge and understanding** of the four concepts. You should be able to **describe and explain** them, **apply them to novel situations**, and **evaluate them**.

The Scheme of Work sets 90 guided learning hours, 25% of the course, for each component. The suggested teaching order is C1 → C2 → C3 → C4.

Two things about the wording are worth holding onto:

- **Audience is the only two-clause definition.** It covers both how audiences are *constructed and addressed* (the producer's side) and how they *interpret and respond* (the audience's side). The other three are single-clause. That asymmetry is the reason audience work splits into industry-facing targeting and reception-facing interpretation.
- **Industry is defined twice, differently.** The key-concepts page says "produced, distributed and **circulated**" (p.5); the subject content says "produced, distributed and **consumed**" (pp.14–15). Both are the syllabus's own words. Use whichever page you are quoting, and do not blend them.

## Where each concept is heaviest

Based on the KC tags in the Scheme of Work and the component structure in the syllabus:

| Component | Concepts tagged |
|---|---|
| C1 Foundation Portfolio | all four, applied to the candidate's own product |
| C2 Section A (unseen extract) | KC2 Representation, KC3 Industry, KC4 Audience (SoW p.13) |
| C2 Section B (contexts) | all four (SoW p.14) |
| C3 Advanced Portfolio | all four (SoW p.17) |
| C4 Section A (the three debates) | KC1 Language, KC2 Representation only (SoW pp.22, 23, 24) |
| C4 Section B (Media ecology) | all four, synoptically (SoW p.25) |

The C4 Section A tagging (Language and Representation only) is a real structural signal. The three debates are argued about how the media *speak* and *portray*, while Industry and Audience are carried by the synoptic Section B.

## What the concepts are not

They are not four separate topics to be taught in sequence and then closed. The syllabus builds them into one another. The Language content includes "how audiences respond to and interpret media language" (p.14), and the Representation content includes "how audiences respond to and interpret representations" (p.15). A lesson that teaches Language without reaching Audience is teaching half the bullet.

Cambridge also invites additions: "You may identify additional key concepts which will also enrich teaching and learning" (p.5). The course could teach, say, narrative or ideology as a fifth spine, but only these four are assessed as such.

## Capitalization trap

The syllabus capitalizes the concepts as **Language, Representation, Industry, Audience** on pp.5, 9 and 14. But C4 Section B (p.26) writes them lower case, and the portfolio skills list (p.14) uses a different noun set entirely: "media language, representation, media **industries** and **audiences**." Use the capitalized forms for the concepts and the lower-case forms for the general nouns.

concepts/case-study-method.md.body:
# Case Study Method

The 9607 course is built on case studies. In the exam you do not answer from general knowledge. You answer from institutions and texts you know in depth. This method governs Component 2 Section B and both Component 4 sections. It also shapes your portfolios.

## The syllabus definition

> "Throughout the course candidates are expected to study a wide range of linked texts, referred to as case studies. These will be used to support their responses in the examinations, and might influence their production work as well. Case studies should feature a majority of contemporary texts, although any text may be used to give historical context. **The term contemporary is used to mean a text which was first published no more than approximately five years before the examination year.**" (Syllabus 2027 p.13)

The **five-year rule** is operational, not just a turn of phrase. "Contemporary" does not mean "recent" or "within a decade." For a June 2027 AS entry, the majority of your case-study texts should date from roughly 2022 onward. You may use historical texts freely, but as *context*, not as the bulk.

For Section A TV-drama work, choose extracts that are within 5 years of when your cohort is taught, from different organizations and a mix of genres. There are two five-year clocks. Case studies date from the **examination year**. Teaching extracts date from **when your cohort is taught**.

## How many

| Requirement | Number | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Media areas studied (AS) | **at least one** | Syllabus pp.9, 17 |
| Case studies referenced in C2 Section B | **at least one** | Syllabus p.23 |
| Case study known for C2 Section B teaching | "at least one case study which is known in depth" | SoW p.14 |
| Media forms per C4 Section A debate answer | one or more | Syllabus p.26 |
| Media forms in the C4 Section B answer | **at least two** | Syllabus p.26 |
| A Level debate topics studied | **at least two of three** | Syllabus pp.9, 18 |

Each number is a **floor, not a target**. "At least one media area" does not mean "choose only one." The syllabus also requires studying "a range of media forms and media platforms" across the course (p.13). That pushes against a single-area diet.

## ⚠ "Media area" is not "media form"

Two taxonomies are easy to confuse:

- **Media areas** (Syllabus p.17): Film · Music · Print · Radio and podcasts · Video games. These are *industry study areas* for the AS contexts work. At least one is required.
- **Media forms** (Syllabus p.13): time-based audio-visual media (film, TV, radio) · print (newspapers, magazines, advertising) · video games. A three-way grouping of *medium*, with the note "There is overlap between these media forms."

Music is a media *area* but not a media *form*. So studying one media area does not by itself satisfy Component 4 Section B's "at least two media forms" requirement. Your Section B answer must span two forms, whatever your Grade 11 case study covered.

## The five media areas (Syllabus p.17)

Each carries its own required accompaniment:

- **Film**: specific studios or production companies: production, distribution, exhibition, consumption; "accompanied by a study of contemporary film distribution practices (digital cinemas, DVD, 3D, downloads and streaming, etc.)"
- **Music**: particular record labels and independent producers; "accompanied by study of wider issues around digital distribution of music"
- **Print**: contemporary newspaper and/or magazine publishing; how print "is adapting to challenges… as a result of technological changes"
- **Radio and podcasts**: production, distribution, audience consumption; "accompanied by a study of the impact of DAB and internet broadcasting… and the development of podcasting as a form"
- **Video games**: a specific game across platforms plus its reception; "accompanied by a study of the impact of next generation capabilities"

The Scheme of Work offers these as suggestions ("The case study **could include**", SoW p.14), so the list is not closed. The syllabus is the authority on what is permitted.

## Depth: what "known in depth" means

Cambridge does not define it. The from-2021 Scheme of Work gives an operational definition: the six things you must be able to demonstrate, whichever area you choose (SoW pp.14–15):

- the influence and issues of media ownership
- convergence and synergy in production, distribution, marketing and consumption
- the significance of particular technologies in production, distribution, marketing and consumption
- how these technologies have changed and how they might change in future
- local and global audiences and the differences in media consumption
- their own media consumption and production practices

If your case study can answer all six, it is deep enough. Depth also means following the same circuit in any media area: ownership and funding, production practices, distribution, marketing, audience consumption. The learning objective for each area is the interrelationship between **production decisions and consumption decisions**.

## Choose for the afterlife

Cambridge's own planning rule: "**Note also that the work for Component 2 lays the foundations for Component 4 – particularly the Media Ecology element**" (SoW p.17). **Media ecology** is synoptic. It recycles earlier work: "Examples from other components **can and should**, be drawn upon" (SoW p.26).

So you choose your Grade 11 case study twice: once for Paper 2 Section B, and once, silently, for Paper 4 Section B eighteen months later. Pick an institution that can grow across two or more media forms, or your synoptic essay starts from scratch.

At BNDS, the institution selected in [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-12-institutions-and-section-a-craft|L12]] should be chosen with the G12 [[concepts/media-ecology]] essay in view, not only for Paper 2.

classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plan.body:
# PAL S1 Unit 4: Graphic Design & the Poster

[[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|Pre A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-semester-1-plan|Semester 1 Plan]] · Unit 4 of 4 · ← [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/unit-plans/pal-s1-unit-3-collage|Unit 3: Collage]]

## What this unit does

This unit turns composition into communication. Its spine is **"Communicate · audience."** It runs over three Wednesday doubles: W16, W17, and W19. There is no class in W18, which falls in the winter break (Thu 2026-12-24 to Sun 2027-01-03).

The first session teaches what a poster must do: message, audience, and hierarchy. You test thumbnails and type. The second session is A4, the final poster, made in class by hand or digitally. The last session documents your work and closes the semester with the End-of-Term portfolio and the A5 sketchbook submission, both handed in that day.

## Two routes through the same slot

By default this unit runs as the **Poster** route, described below. It may instead run as **Printmaking** (linocut), covering the same three Wednesdays. Which route runs depends on class interest, and will be confirmed in class. A4 needs one week's notice of which form it takes. The Printmaking route has its own [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/pal-s1-u4-printmaking-variant|full variant plan]].

| | **Poster** (default) | **Printmaking** |
|---|---|---|

concepts/media-audience.md.body:
# Media Audience

**Key Concept 4.** "How audiences are constructed and addressed by media texts and how audiences interpret and respond to media texts" (Syllabus 2027 p.15).

This Key Concept has two parts: audiences as **constructed by industry**, and audiences as **active interpreters**.

## What the syllabus requires

You study (Syllabus 2027 p.15):

- how audiences are grouped and categorized by media industries, including by age, gender and social class, as well as by lifestyle and taste
- how media producers target, attract, reach, address and construct audiences
- how media industries target audiences through the content and appeal of media products and through the ways in which they are marketed, distributed and consumed
- the interrelationship between media technologies and patterns of consumption and response
- how audiences interpret the media, including how they may interpret the same texts in different ways, using a variety of theories or ideologies
- how audiences interact with the media and can be actively involved in media production
- how specialized audiences can be reached, on a local, national and global scale, through different media technologies and platforms
- how media organizations reflect the different needs of mass and specialized audiences, including through targeting
- how audiences use media in different ways, reflecting demographic factors as well as aspects of identity and culture
- the role and significance of specialized audiences, including niche and fan, to the media

## Audiences as constructed

**Categorization**: grouping audiences by age, gender, social class, lifestyle and taste.

**Mode of address**: how a text encourages a reader to recognize themselves as the addressee. The Scheme of Work defines it in the magazine section: "how is a particular audience being addressed by these elements? How is a potential reader encouraged to see her/himself as the addressee?" (SoW p.9). Magazine covers show this well, because the address is on the surface.

**Mass and specialized audiences**: the syllabus's own pairing. The Scheme of Work reaches it through the magazine pitch: "an argument, perhaps, that a niche rather than mass market exists for the publication" (SoW p.12).

**Niche and fan audiences**: named by the syllabus as significant, and reachable globally through platforms.

## Audiences as active interpreters

The syllabus requires that you understand how audiences "may interpret the same texts in different ways, using a variety of theories or ideologies" (p.15). It names no theory.

The Scheme of Work supplies one, **Stuart Hall's** ideas of encoding and decoding:

> "explore Stuart Hall's ideas of encoding and decoding when making sense of a media text" (SoW p.14)

See [[entities/stuart-hall]] for the dominant / negotiated / oppositional model. At BNDS you study these three positions. One way to see them clearly: take a text the class disagrees about, then map the actual readings onto the three positions.

## The media diary

> "**Exercise: Keep a media diary for one day – list everything you watched, listened to, played, interacted with as well as where you did it, using what technology, whether alone or in company, and for what purpose.**"

Record these dimensions over exactly one day: what, where, on what technology, alone or with others, and why.

Its purpose is forward-looking (SoW p.16): "This simple exercise starts to build the foundations for the **Media Ecology** element of **Component 4** – it starts to reveal the '**mediascape**' that we all inhabit." Diaries you keep in Grade 11 become the raw contrast material for the Grade 12 synoptic essay. Keep them.

The seven insights the diary is expected to surface (SoW p.16): media consumable anywhere on mobile technology; media on demand; limited live viewing except events and sport; social media creating a new communal live experience; news as a stream of updates rather than a fixed form, place and time; "old media" competing and integrating rather than dying; and near-universal availability via piracy.

## The attention economy

You can go beyond describing your media use and consider conceptual positions such as the **attention economy** (SoW p.16). Ask what it is and "how does it explain how I use Facebook?" Then look at "the actual economy of intellectual and artistic property," which connects to work on regulation in Component 4.

The component closes with a short question: **"What media are worth paying for? Why?"** (SoW p.16).

concepts/media-language.md.body:
# Media Language

**Key Concept 1.** "How the media communicate meanings through the use of forms, codes, conventions and techniques" (Syllabus 2027 p.14).

This is the founding claim of the course: nothing in a media text is accidental. Every element is a chosen sign that carries meaning, and audiences read those signs using shared cultural codes. [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-s1-unit-2-media-language|Unit 2]] installs this idea, and every later analysis depends on it.

## What the syllabus requires

You study (Syllabus 2027 p.14):

- the codes and conventions of media forms and products, including the processes through which media language develops as genre
- the significance of challenging and/or subverting conventions
- the ways in which media language incorporates viewpoints and ideologies
- how audiences respond to and interpret media language
- the impact of developing technologies on media language
- how combinations of media language generate meaning
- the dynamic and historically relative nature of genre

Two of these carry extra reward. **Challenging and/or subverting conventions** is marked directly: spotting a convention is the floor, explaining why a text breaks one is the ceiling. And **the dynamic and historically relative nature of genre** means you treat genre as something that shifts across decades, not as a fixed list.

## Codes and conventions

A **code** is economy. Producers lean on what you already know from other texts, and communicate character or story without spelling it out. A **convention** is a repetition that has hardened into an expectation. Following conventions reads as mainstream. Subverting them surprises or disconcerts the audience.

**Mediation** is the master idea underneath both, and the syllabus locates it in [[concepts/representation]]: media do not show the world, they go between you and it, selecting and shaping along the way.

## Signification: denotation and connotation

Meaning works in layers, a model attributed to [[entities/roland-barthes]]. What is **denoted** is what a text shows at a plain, descriptive level. What is **connotative** is what it suggests, implies, or codes. The relevant theory here is semiotics: Roland Barthes' ideas about signs, codes, and meaning.

The order matters, and the BNDS assessment design is built on it: **denotation before connotation**. CS1 in [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-01-the-four-key-concepts|L01]] is a denotation-only paragraph, because describing before interpreting is the discipline A1 later marks.

> [!note] Ideology and hegemony
> The syllabus requires "the ways in which media language incorporates viewpoints and ideologies" (p.14). One example is magazine analysis, where desire, happiness, and satisfaction are shown as tied to material consumption. The syllabus names no theorist for this.

## Cold-read exercises

Use these questions to make your reading of codes conscious:

- What do you know about the world that is not mediated? Most answers trace back to a screen, a feed, or a page.
- Identify a media text. How do you know what it is? How do you know what it is "for"?
- Film opening cold read: what can you tell about the type of film it is, what is likely to happen, and who is likely to watch it? Why?
- Magazine cover cold read: what can you tell about the type of magazine it is, what kinds of articles it contains, and who is likely to read it? Why?
- Favorite five: list your five favorite films. To what extent are they "conventional"?

You already read codes fluently. The job is to make that intuition conscious and give it names.

## For ESL learners

Vocabulary work here earns marks directly: AO1 is "using terminology appropriately" (Syllabus 2027 p.12). The magazine-term matching game is the model: match Buzz Word, Puff, Coverline, Masthead, Barcode, Anchorage Text, Superimposition, Slogan, and Unique Selling Point to features of a real cover, then justify each. Recognition first, definition second, justification third.

Full term lists: [[concepts/media-vocabulary]].

concepts/media-ecology.md.body:
# Media Ecology

Media Ecology is a compulsory A Level topic in Component 4. It is the only Component 4 topic with no choice attached. It is examined in Component 4 Section B as one 30-mark synoptic question, worth half the paper.

The 2028–30 syllabus, which is the one you sit, renames it **Changing media environments**. The content transfers. The name and the exam format do not. See [[classes/media-studies/media-studies]].

## The syllabus definition (p.19)

> "Media ecology refers to the complex environments within which media texts, producers, distributors, technologies and audiences exist. It is a way of conceiving the structure of these environments, their content, and impact on people."

## Possible areas of focus (p.19)

- audience engagement with evolving media environments
- convergence of personal communication technology and mass communication technology
- impact on society of technological change including the collection and sharing of information and data protection
- the nature of globalisation and the responses of audiences and institutions
- the changing nature of media ownership and distribution models including net neutrality
- the representation of public and private personae
- the relationships between software, hardware and audiences
- the impact of developing technologies on media language
- changing modes of reception and their impact on audiences

This is the only syllabus topic phrased as "possible areas of focus for candidates" rather than "candidates should study." The syllabus adds that these "are not exhaustive but provide examples of how candidates might adapt and apply their knowledge and understanding gained throughout the course" (p.19). So Media ecology is a compulsory topic with non-compulsory sub-content. You study something like this list, not a fixed version of it.

## What "synoptic" means here

> "Section B is synoptic, requiring candidates to **synthesise their knowledge and understanding of the key concepts of language, representation, industry and audience, studied throughout the course**. Candidates are expected to adapt and apply this knowledge and understanding to contemporary examples from **at least two media forms** in order to explore evolving media environments."

You synthesize the four key concepts, language, representation, industry, and audience, that you studied across the course. You then apply them to contemporary examples from at least two media forms. The two-media-form requirement is stated twice in the same paragraph. It is the hardest constraint in Component 4. Studying one media area at AS does not meet it, per [[concepts/case-study-method]].

Two learning objectives are unique to this topic: **synthesising** knowledge of the key concepts, and **adapting and applying** that knowledge to a variety of media environments. The syllabus also says examples "can and should" be drawn from other components, particularly those that show changes in power, technology and audience engagement.

Nothing new is taught here so much as everything already taught is re-aimed.

## What you study

The topic opens with a **media diary**: a one-day record of your own media habits. An extension looks at the attention economy and at how you use Facebook / X / BlueSky / Snapchat / Instagram. This connects to the media diary in [[concepts/media-audience]].

You compare audience behaviour across three eras:

- the **broadcast era**, to the late 1980s ("launch of Sky in the UK")
- the **early digital era**, late 1980s to early 2000s ("to the arrival of Netflix in the UK and the launch of BBC iPlayer")
- the **contemporary platform era**, 2000s onwards

Exam answers use these UK and international anchors. (In class you may map them onto Chinese media, from the CCTV-dominant broadcast era to the WeChat, Bilibili and Douyin platform era, but that stays a classroom aside.)

The topic is built around four focus areas:

1. **Audience behaviour**: engagement with evolving environments; changing modes of reception; changes to "audiences' perception of knowledge, truth and reality"; fan and "prosumer" culture.
2. **Economics of media**: ownership and distribution models; funding models; globalisation and the responses of audiences and institutions.
3. **Ethics**: platform responsibility for what is "published"; technological change including data collection and protection; public and private personae.
4. **Technological convergence**: old and new media blurring; convergence of personal and mass communication; software, hardware and audience relationships; impact on media language, codes and conventions.

Each focus area links to Section A topics. For example, Audience behaviour links to Power (audience agency versus institutional control), Postmodern Media (hyperreality and fragmented identity), and Regulation (challenges in moderating user-generated content).

Useful sources for this topic include the Nielsen Norman Group (attention economy), the Pew Research Centre, and the Ofcom Online Nation Report.

## Named theory

The syllabus names no theorists for this topic. The idea is often traced back to **Neil Postman** and **Marshall McLuhan** (see [[entities/neil-postman]], [[entities/marshall-mcluhan]]), but the current syllabus names neither and names no one in their place. The top band is still hard to reach without named theory, so your reading list for this topic comes from class.

## The connection to Grade 11

The work you do for Component 2 lays the foundations for Component 4, particularly Media Ecology. Your AS case study, your media diaries, and the industry work in [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-s1-unit-5-media-contexts|Unit 5]] are all Component 4 material.

## The marked specimen answer

A marked high answer and a marked middle answer are available for the Section B synoptic question: "Explain how changes in technology and audience behaviour have had an impact on how the media is funded" [30]. The high answer scores 27/30; the middle answer scores 17/30. Marks split AO1 18 / AO2 12, across a five-criteria rubric at 6 marks each, the same shape as elsewhere in 9607.

The high answer runs on named theory: **Hesmondhalgh** (cultural industries, horizontal and vertical integration, the big-hits logic), **Shoshana Zuboff** (surveillance capitalism), **danah boyd** (three stages of legacy-media response), **Eli Pariser** (filter bubbles), **Clay Shirky**, **David Gauntlett**, **Cory Doctorow**, and **Jaron Lanier**. The middle answer reaches for McLuhan and is not penalized for it; it loses marks for describing rather than analyzing.

What separates 27 from 17:

- The high answer is periodized: legacy advertising and licence-fee funding, then fragmentation, then subscription and surveillance models, with a concrete case anchoring each (Premier League rights costs rising 57% across five seasons). It could still make the "then versus now" comparison sharper.
- The middle answer is a list of companies: *The Guardian*, Spotify, Mr Beast. This is real material, but it treats funding through a business lens and ignores political, social and cultural factors. Here funding is a media-environment question, not a business one.
- AI is live material in this topic: SAG-AFTRA, training-data rights, audience backlash to AI imagery, and Netflix using AI in production.

concepts/media-industry.md.body:
# Media Industry

**Key Concept 3:** "How and why media texts are produced, distributed and consumed" (Syllabus 2027 p.15). This is the knowledge base of **Component 2 Section B**. It also leads into [[concepts/media-ecology]] two years later.

This is not abstract economics. The exam wants you to know at least one institution in depth, and to use it to illustrate general processes. See [[concepts/case-study-method]].

## What the syllabus requires

You study (Syllabus 2027 p.15):

- how processes of production, distribution and consumption shape media products
- processes of production, distribution and consumption by organisations, groups and individuals in a global context
- the specialised and institutionalised nature of media production, distribution and consumption
- the relationship between technological change and media production, distribution and consumption
- the significance of patterns of ownership and control, including conglomerate ownership, vertical integration and diversification
- the significance of economic factors, including commercial and not-for-profit public funding, to media industries and their products
- how media organisations maintain varieties of audiences locally, nationally and globally, including marketing
- the regulatory framework of contemporary media and the impact of technological change on media regulation
- the impact of convergent media platforms on media production, distribution and consumption

The AS contexts list (Syllabus 2027 p.17) adds ownership and funding issues, cross-media convergence and synergy, recent technologies at every level, and "the ways in which the candidates' own experiences of media consumption illustrate wider patterns and trends in audience behaviour." This last point connects to the media-diary exercise in [[concepts/media-audience]].

## The key concepts

**Vertical integration:** one company owning production, distribution and exhibition. For example, companies "such as Sony Pictures, still maintain a significant presence through practices of vertical integration," with "huge investment in technology and talent, and vast distribution networks."

**Conglomeration and synergy:** look at "Disney's acquisition of Pixar, Marvel, Lucasfilm and Marvel and consider synergies between films, TV, theme parks, merchandise, games and so on." **Synergy** is "the process through which a series of media products derived from the same text is promoted in and through each other."

**Convergence:** "the coming together of media technologies so that the boundaries blur. Usually this refers to technologies of distribution and reception (e.g. TV and the internet)."

Conglomeration continues in the digital era. For example, Spotify's acquisition of podcast companies. Cheap tools did not stop consolidation.

## Two key exercises

### The pre-digital scenario

> "**Exercise: Imagine in the pre-digital/internet era if you wanted to be a film director how would you go about it?**"

This surfaces production, distribution, exhibition and consumption without naming them first:

- "The need for production technologies – what was required and available? What would it cost? Who would pay?"
- "If you managed to make it, what would you need to do to make it available? How would copies get made? How would it get into cinemas? Why would cinemas show it? How would people know it was there?"
- "How would people see your film? What would their experience of watching it be?"

Historical work is useful because it highlights key differences in the contemporary situation. Every constraint the scenario reveals shows what digital changed. The same historical contrast drives [[concepts/media-ecology]] in Grade 12.

### Follow the money

> "**Exercise: Choose a media company. Find out its connections with other media companies – either as a property or an owner. Why do you think these connections exist? Who benefits? How?**"

Worked example: in video games, **Ninja Theory** is interesting. Its history with, and eventual acquisition by, **Microsoft** shows how particular software (games) can help sell particular hardware (**Xbox**).

## The democratization debate

A key critical debate about the industry. Explore the claim that traditional media power has been reduced because of:

- affordable and accessible technology
- distribution channels open to all (for example Vimeo and YouTube)
- widespread high-speed broadband enabling home streaming

Then push back: "how genuinely 'democratic' is this: To what extent do the products of 'amateurs' have the status of those of 'professionals'?" And: "at ground level, how are large companies continuing to grow, to conglomerate and to create synergies between different divisions?"

This amateur/professional question is the natural bridge to [[concepts/power-and-the-media]].

concepts/media-regulation.md.body:
# Media Regulation

Media Regulation is one of the three **A Level Media debates** topics. You study at least two of the three (Syllabus 2027 pp. 9, 18). It is examined in Component 4 Section A as one 15-mark essay, "referring to one or more media forms" (p. 26).

Syllabus framing: "Media regulation considers issues of morality and decency, accuracy of content and media ownership" (p. 18).

The core question: **who should control what media can say and show, and does control actually work?**

## What candidates must study (Syllabus 2027 p. 18)

- the nature of contemporary and historical media regulation
- the arguments for and against specific forms of media regulation
- the effectiveness of regulatory practices, including the ability to impose or recommend sanctions
- the wider social issues relating to media regulation
- the roles of different regulatory bodies in relation to ownership, morality and accuracy
- the legal and ethical frameworks within which media producers and distributors must operate

Note the second point: **arguments for and against**. This topic is assessed as a two-sided argument, not a description of a regulatory system. If you explain how regulation works but never argue about whether it should exist, you answer the wrong question.

## Sub-topics (SoW p. 23, suggested)

"Regulation could include: taste and decency · illegality and incitement to crime · ownership and pluralism · intellectual property and piracy · public service and responsibilities to the nation."

The internet complicates all of them: "The debates about internet regulation are particularly pertinent and action is problematic because of its lack of central organisation and the fact that it is an international medium, so does not fall under a particular jurisdiction" (SoW p. 23).

## Activity bank

Regulation can also focus on **misinformation** alongside intellectual property, ownership and piracy. Activities include:

- **Regulatory authority comparison:** compare two regulatory organizations for legal authority, enforcement powers, sanctions, criticisms, and "challenges in the digital era". You choose which two.
- **Regulation in context:** for key regulatory developments, map trigger, technological context, reactive or proactive, and intended and unintended outcomes.
- **Regulatory sanctions case study:** breach, speed of response, severity, impact, public trust.
- **Ideological debate:** argue assigned positions (free market, public service, critical theory) on "The media should be strictly regulated to protect society".
- **Regulatory gap mapping:** streaming, social media, influencer marketing, UGC; jurisdiction issues and "platform vs publisher responsibility".
- **Global regulation comparison:** "Is national regulation still effective in a globalised media industry?"
- **Question planning workshop:** command words, argument strands, counter-argument, peer-assessed against AO1/AO2.

## ⚠ Cambridge's sensitivity advice

This is the only topic in the Scheme of Work that carries a handling caveat:

> "It is preferable to study regulation in your country/region. However, **this may not always be possible because of the sensitivity of the subject.** If this is the case, and you still wish to explore this topic, it is suggested that you encourage learners to research **the UK model**. There is plenty of material available on the Internet to facilitate this approach. **Alternatively, an approach to regulation could be taken which focuses on intellectual property, ownership, piracy or misinformation – issues of morality are only one dimension.**" (SoW p. 22)

And on the historical timeline activity: "(Once again, this needs to be handled sensitively according to the political situation of the country/region where the material is being delivered.)" (SoW p. 22)

Cambridge allows three routes: study your own region (preferred); substitute the UK model; or reframe onto intellectual property, ownership, piracy and misinformation rather than morality and press freedom.

At BNDS, the workable path is the third route, or the UK model studied comparatively. This is the alternative Cambridge names in its own document. The two debates currently studied are [[concepts/postmodern-media]] and [[concepts/power-and-the-media]], with regulation as the alternative.

## Suggested teaching activities (SoW pp. 22–23)

- **Opening discussion:** "How is Media regulated where you live? / Has Media always been regulated in this way? / What effect does Media regulation have on consumption? / Are there different ways of regulating the Media? / How do other countries/regions regulate their Media?"
- **Historical timeline:** groups take different decades of the 20th and 21st centuries and different media (TV, Film, Print, Radio, Online), research developments in regulation during their period, and present. Findings combine into "a visual timeline of the historical context of regulation."
- **Comparative research:** regulation in other countries, "especially the UK and the USA," compared with your own.
- **Independent case studies**, then shared "in preparation for responding to an unseen question about media regulation."

## No named theorists or bodies

The syllabus names no theorist, no theory, and no regulatory body for this topic. The activities say "learners select two regulatory organisations" and leave the choice open. No BBFC, no IPSO, no NRTA. Ofcom appears only as a resource link elsewhere in the SoW ("Ofcom – Media Ownership Rules" under the Power topic; "Ofcom – Online Nation Report" under Changing media environments). Any regulator, framework or thinker you use in this topic is your own choice.

## The 2028 specimen answer

A marked high and middle answer are available for **"Evaluate the reasons for and against stricter media regulation" [15]**, the exact Section A regulation question shape. High scores **13/15** (AO1 8/9, AO2 5/6); middle scores **8/15** (AO1 5/9, AO2 3/6).

The syllabus names nobody, but the high answer is built on named theory throughout: **Stanley Cohen's moral panic** worked through all five stages, **Martin Barker** on the *Ill Effects* lineage of censorship, **David Buckingham**, **Sonia Livingstone** critiquing **Jonathan Haidt**, and **Gramsci** on spontaneous consent. The examiner credits exactly this: the response "synthesises theory very well and goes above and beyond the usual theory references." The middle answer reaches for Uses and Gratifications and the hypodermic model as an add-on, and is marked down for that bolted-on quality.

So Cambridge does not prescribe thinkers, but the standard it rewards needs them. Your named-theory choices are the difference between the middle and top bands.

Two more things the examiner asks for that the syllabus does not say out loud:

- **Use contemporary regulatory events, not the canon.** The high answer runs on the UK Online Safety Act, age verification and VPN circumvention, and platform moderation. The common-error list opens with "candidates should be focused on contemporary material and examples." This matches the [[concepts/case-study-method|five-year rule]].
- **Argue both sides.** The high answer loses two marks for having no paragraph making the case for stricter regulation. The examiner names freedom of speech versus the right not to be harmed as the missing move. Build this into your own answers.

⚠ The specimen's examples are UK-centric and politically live: the Online Safety Act, Molly Russell, TikTok/Oracle, a 2025 political killing. Given the sensitivity advice above, use the structure of the high answer with substituted regional examples rather than the whole booklet.

concepts/narrative.md.body:
# Narrative

At AS, narrative is mostly about **expectation**: how an opening plants enigmas, establishes roles, and sets a trajectory. It is not a separate key concept. It sits inside [[concepts/media-language]] and appears in both the C1 film-opening brief and Component 2 Section A.

## What Cambridge says

Cambridge says little about narrative, and it helps to know how little.

The syllabus mentions narrative twice: media language "develops as genre", and genre is "dynamic and historically relative" (p.14). At A Level it adds "the relationship between postmodernism and narrative" (p.18).

The Component 2 guidance also mentions narrative twice: openings "set up some **narrative expectations**", and it points to [[entities/roland-barthes]] and "narrative codes".

No narrative-structure model is named in any Cambridge document. There is no Todorov, no Propp, no Lévi-Strauss, no three-act structure, no equilibrium/disequilibrium. Barthes' codes are the only narrative apparatus Cambridge offers. The C1 film brief names "Roland Barthes' 5 Narrative Codes", though the codes themselves are never listed.

The narrative-analysis work comes without theory. There is a narrative-mapping task: linear vs non-linear sequencing, flashbacks, parallel plotlines, cliffhanger placement. There is an ellipsis and time-construction task: "How does editing construct narrative clarity or confusion?" Structure is taught through editing, and the models come from class.

## Where it does appear: enigma

The strongest narrative content in the Cambridge sources is the **enigma**, and it comes through production rather than theory.

For C1 story groundwork you "should be able to explain what sort of film this is; who the main character is; what the central conflict is likely to be; the questions or enigmas that the opening creates, that is, what information is given? What is withheld? What clues are provided?"

The C1 research prompts ask: "how does the film establish an enigma from the outset?"

So enigma is examined twice: as something to analyze in real openings, and as something to construct in your own opening. That double duty makes it the highest-value narrative idea in the AS year.

## The BNDS layer

The Semester 1 scheme teaches a fuller narrative toolkit than Cambridge provides, across two lessons.

[[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-05-narrative-and-the-planning-lock|L05]] teaches **Todorov's equilibrium** and then **Propp's character functions**, each on a single day. You apply them straight to your own C1 plans: where is the disturbance in your opening? You should be able to map characters by function rather than identity, and name where Propp strains.

[[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-06-a1-timed-media-language-analysis|L06]] puts Propp and Todorov under load on real texts: Propp on a trailer, Todorov across an episode. You hunt for where the theory strains, because strain is what a top-band answer discusses. Each day ends by logging where the theory failed to fit and why that is analytically interesting.

Propp and Todorov are not prescribed by Cambridge. The syllabus requires "key theories of media studies" (p.13) without naming any, and Cambridge states it does "not prioritise one theory or approach over another" (p.18). Know that you are using a chosen framework, not a required one. Examiners credit the application, not the name.

Since no model is prescribed, the mark cannot come from reciting one. It comes from showing where a model illuminates a text and where it does not.

## What to watch

The syllabus lists "the significance of challenging and/or subverting conventions" (p.14), but its own teaching support does not cover it, and the word "subvert" does not appear there. Narrative subversion is one place where the BNDS material builds from scratch.

concepts/postmodern-media.md.body:
# Postmodern Media

Postmodern Media is one of the three **A Level Media debates** topics (Syllabus 2027 pp.9, 18). It is one of the two topics BNDS has chosen, alongside [[concepts/power-and-the-media]]. The final choice will be confirmed in class.

The core question: **is the distinction between reality and representation collapsing, and does it matter?**

## The syllabus framing (p.18)

> "Postmodernism can be characterised by modes such as pastiche, parody, intertextuality, self-referentiality and a conscious engagement with other texts. **We do not prioritise one theory or approach over another, and candidates are encouraged to explore a range of approaches and perspectives, across a range of media forms.**"

That second sentence is the syllabus's clearest statement about the role of theory in 9607.

## What candidates must study (Syllabus 2027 p.18)

- the different versions of postmodernism (historical period, style, theoretical approach)
- the arguments for and against understanding some forms of media as postmodern
- the ways postmodern media texts can challenge traditional relationships between texts and audiences
- the relationship between postmodernism and popular culture
- the ways media audiences and industries operate differently in a postmodern world
- the relationship between postmodernism and narrative

Exam questions focus on the last five.

**Arguments for and against understanding some forms of media as postmodern** does real work here. You can argue that postmodernism is an unhelpful lens, as long as you argue it with evidence.

## The concept is unstable

> "Postmodernism is notoriously tricky to pin down… it can refer to **a general condition of contemporary life** in which representations, reality, surfaces and styles are chaotically intermingled, or it can refer to **specific modes of communication** which are arch, self-referential and knowing (irony is often referred to as exemplary of the postmodern mode)." (SoW p.23)

That two-way split, condition versus textual mode, is a good essay structure in itself.

## The two named thinkers

**[[entities/guy-debord]]** (SoW p.23): *The Society of the Spectacle* (1967), "a critique of media-saturated capitalist culture… still relevant in diagnosing aspects of the postmodern condition."

**[[entities/fredric-jameson]]** (SoW pp.23–24) "diagnoses the postmodern condition as characterised by":

- "An ahistorical mode (lacking a sense of the past – history becomes another set of signifiers which can be played with)."
- "A lack of distinction between 'high' and 'low' culture."
- "Surfaces – increasingly there is no time for depth – politics becomes soundbites, protests become slogans, the world is a collection of images."
- "Affectlessness – the predominant mode of irony and 'knowingness' leaves little room for real emotion, but short, sharp intense emotional responses are elicited through surface representations of things of which people have no first-hand experience, e.g.: Brexit, the death of Diana, refugees."
- "Technologies of reproduction and recirculation, e.g.: all social media."

Each of these five converts directly into an essay paragraph with a contemporary example.

## How you study this topic

- **Conceptual framework comparison**: postmodernism as historical period vs stylistic mode vs theoretical approach, tabulated with media examples.
- **Textual feature analysis**: pastiche, parody, intertextuality, self-referentiality, and genre hybridity identified in one chosen text.
- **Structured critical debate**: "Contemporary media is fundamentally postmodern" vs "Postmodernism is an overused or outdated concept."
- **Narrative deconstruction**: linear vs postmodern structure: non-linearity, fragmentation, ambiguity, open endings.
- **Text/audience relationships**: participatory culture, fan remixing, and meme circulation, and whether this increases or commodifies audience power.
- **Intertextuality mapping**: a network diagram of references, borrowings, and parodies, and whether intertextuality supports commercial strategies.
- **Essay planning workshop**: command word, analytical strands, counterarguments.

Resources include the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and a **Jean Baudrillard** entry (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy).

## Classroom activities

- **Foraging exercise**: you gather online definitions and discussions of postmodernism independently, then the class tests and secures them together. There are plenty of definitions and discussions online, so independent research is the efficient route.
- Test **pastiche, intertextuality and parody** against real media texts as characteristics emerge.
- Identify "what sorts of repertoires of knowledge and experience are necessary in order to make sense of certain media texts, and how they might function '**dialogically**' – that is, say one thing, but invoke other meanings through referencing or quoting from something else."
- Identify "ways in which belief in certain kinds of reality can be less important than belief in media representations of that reality."
- Watch a TV news story. Ask what features it has of "The Society of the Spectacle".
- Read up on the difference between pastiche and parody, then find contemporary examples of each.

You already live in postmodern media: memes, remixes, franchise self-reference. Start from your own examples, then add the names.

## Technique note

> "As always, **anchoring the arguments in specific texts or phenomena is key** to demonstrating a sophisticated understanding of the concept and how it might be useful in making sense of contemporary media." (SoW p.24)

concepts/media-vocabulary.md.body:
# Media Vocabulary

This is Cambridge's glossary of media terms, taken from the six appendices of the Scheme of Work (pp. 27–35). It has 56 terms, and every one is defined. Use it as the reference for the glossary you keep from week one.

Some definitions below read oddly. That is Cambridge's wording, not a mistake. The odd ones are flagged at the bottom of this page.

For how these terms fit together, see [[concepts/technical-elements]] and [[concepts/media-language]].

## Appendix 1: Introductory media language (SoW p.27)

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Media forms** | Different types of media products, such as films, TV programmes, magazines, radio programmes. |
| **Media platforms** | A term which has arisen to account for the various convergent combinations of old and new media, for example, Amazon, Netflix and iPlayer are internet platforms for distributing and exhibiting TV and film. A platform is a technological space in which media can be consumed. |
| **Synergy** | The process through which a series of media products derived from the same text is promoted in and through each other. |
| **Representation** | The processes (and end results) by which reality is subject to selection, exaggeration and repetition, so that certain representations (often of subordinated groups and associated places) become typical and taken for granted. Also used, more neutrally, to refer to aesthetic representation. |
| **Mise-en-scène** | The visual information in a scene or shot, such as, setting, lighting, colour, shape, costume, make-up, expression, movement, symmetry. Mise-en-scène tends to refer to the content of a shot, but this will be inflected by the shot-type. |
| **Media franchise** | The capacity to extend the life of characters, settings or trademarks by producing further products, usually in popular genres such as super-hero or action. |
| **Iconography** | Icons are particular signs that are powerfully associated with something else, such as religious icons. By extension, in media, icons are signs we associate with particular genres (e.g. technology for sci-fi, saloon doors for westerns). |
| **Intertextuality** | Within a text, visual or audio references are made to other texts. It is expected that audiences will recognise such references, although more obscure references will require different repertoires of experience in the audience |
| **Genre** | A term of classification which groups media texts of a particular kind together – usually particular kinds of film or TV narrative, but styles, stars and production companies may all be used to make generic distinctions between texts |
| **Convergence** | The coming together of media technologies so that the boundaries blur. Usually this refers to technologies of distribution and reception (e.g. TV and the internet). |

## Appendix 2: Camera shots and angles (SoW pp.28–31)

| Shot type | Description |
|---|---|
| **Extreme long / Establishing** | Used to set the scene or as an establishing shot, often outside. This shot can be taken from as far away as a quarter of a mile. |
| **Master** | This shot, like the Establishing Shot also sets up the scene through showing key signifiers, however, whilst the Establishing Shot leans towards showing the setting and location, the Master Shot contains the main characters for the length of the shot. |
| **Long** | This shot shows images in 'life size' in the context of the distance between the cinema screen and the image: for example, the height of a child might appear to be 3-4 feet. Usually this contains a full body shot. |
| **Medium / mid** | A shot that shows a character from the waist up. An alternative to this shot is a two shot (includes two people) and a three shot (includes three people). |
| **Over the shoulder** | This shot is taken from 'over the shoulder' of a character and is often used to make the audience feel as though they are actually included in the conversation/action. It is a form of point of view (POV) shot. |
| **Point of view (POV)** | This shot is taken from the view of the person looking/speaking. POV may be literal (as in this image) or it may be implied when, for example, a character looks off-screen and we then see what they are looking at. |
| **Close up** | This shot shows a part of something, for example, someone's face and is used to draw attention to the thing / person or emotions. |
| **Extreme close up** | This shot is even closer than the last one, and creates an image larger than the eye would usually see. |
| **Wide** | A shot in which an actor might appear very small against the landscape as the image as a whole gives a much wider view than the individual. |
| **Aerial** | A shot taken from a high viewpoint, as though it is taken from a drone showing a bird's eye view. |
| **High angle** | A shot that is taken from above a character / setting to create a sense of empowerment for the character with Point of View, as it diminishes the figure in the frame. |
| **Low angle** | A shot taken from a low angle, this helps to reinforce intimidation or disempowerment for the character with Point of View, as it creates an overwhelming perspective. |
| **Canted angle / Dutch angle** | This is a shot taken with a tilted horizon, often used to signify imbalance or uncertainty, but sometimes for aesthetic effect. |

## Appendix 3: Camera movements (SoW p.32)

| Movement | Description |
|---|---|
| **Pan** | A camera movement along a horizontal axis, with the camera body turning to the left or right on a stationary tripod. |
| **Tilt** | A camera movement along a vertical axis, with the camera body turning up or down on a stationary tripod. |
| **Track** | Any shot in which the camera body moves forwards, backwards or laterally. This may be on a wheeled support ('dolly'), or hand-held, possibly with a stabilisation device such as Steadicam. |
| **Dolly** | A camera support with wheels to facilitate tracking shots. The dolly may move on tracks, or freely on a smooth surface – hence 'dolly shot'. |
| **Crane** | A crane shot involves the camera being mounted on a crane or jib. It enables a wide, high perspective to be achieved, and large-scale tracking shots to be accomplished. |
| **Steadicam** | Steadicam is the brand name for a particular kind of camera stabilisation device, which has become a generic term for any similar device. It enables smooth hand-held tracking shots, which would otherwise be shaky. |
| **Hand-held** | Hand-held camera work, without the use of Steadicam, is characteristically 'unpolished'; it may involve slight movement, usually used to signify an immediacy and realism, or very erratic movement to communicate peril and excitement. |
| **Zoom** | Unlike a tracking shot, where the camera body moves in or out, a zoom shot is achieved by increasing (zoom in) or decreasing (zoom out) the magnification of the object with the camera's lens. |
| **Reverse zoom** | The reverse zoom is a combination of a tracking shot and a zoom shot: the camera tracks towards the subject while zooming out at the same rate. The subject (usually a character) maintains the same position and size in the frame, while the background shifts around them – often used to signify a turning point in the character's story. A similar effect is achieved by tracking backwards while zooming in. |

## Appendix 4: Sound vocabulary (SoW p.33)

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Diegetic sound** | Sound which has its source in the scene, or 'world of the film' (even if it is applied in post-production). A test for diegetic sound is: would the characters be able to hear this? |
| **Non-diegetic sound** | Sound which does not have its source within the world of the film, for example, mood music, voice-over addressed to the audience. |
| **Foley** | Sound effects produced to enhance the realism of actions in the scene, for example, footsteps, the clink of ice in a glass, the sound of a kiss. Foley effects are always produced in post-production and are always diegetic. |
| **Harmony** | A term which refers to simultaneous or consecutive musical notes which (according to convention) sound pleasant. In film and TV harmonious music may suggest that all is well in the world. |
| **Dissonance** | The opposite of harmony: simultaneous or consecutive musical notes which (according to convention) sound harsh or unpleasant. In film and TV dissonant music is likely to suggest that something is wrong, or about to go wrong in the world. |
| **Pitch** | The frequency of a sound. High pitched dissonant strings will magnify the effect of aggression (as in Psycho, for example). Low pitches may sound ominous. |
| **Rhythm** | A recurring beat forming a pattern. Rhythms may be rapid or slow, regular or irregular, producing different emotional effects in the viewer/listener. |
| **Room tone** | A recording of the sound at the location of a shoot – may be used as part of the soundscape to provide depth and atmosphere. |
| **Soundscape** | A collection of background sounds which reinforce the realism of a scene – these may be augmented in post-production with, for example, library sound effects, such as crowd murmer. This might also be described as 'atmosphere'. |
| **Soundbed** | In film and TV this may be used interchangeably with 'soundscape', but in audio work it usually refers to music played low in the mix in order to create mood or atmosphere. |

## Appendix 5: Website terminology (SoW p.34)

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Web banner** | This is the title or header on a webpage and is the equivalent to a masthead in a newspaper, or a magazine title. It is used to attract the audience and can be used to indicate the genre of the music through the font selection. |
| **Navigational features** | These are the buttons that help you move around the website. They are clearly displayed on a web page and often change appearance when you hover over them. |
| **Multimedia features** | This term refers to the use of images, video, text and audio on a website. These features add variation, information and entertainment. |
| **Advertisements** | Many websites advertise products closely linked or connected to the main focus, this is often a good way of increasing revenue from hits on the interconnected websites. |
| **Web links** | When links connect you to elsewhere on the website this is referred to as 'internal links' whereas links to another website are called 'external links' |
| **Interactive elements** | These enable users to take part and contribute to the website and could be in the form of quizzes, games, surveys, discussion forums or an opportunity to give feedback or comments about something. |

Under the 2028–30 spec, C3's third medium is a **website home page**, so this appendix matters. See [[classes/media-studies/media-studies]].

## Appendix 6: Magazine terminology (SoW p.35)

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Masthead** | The name of the magazine, in its typical font, on the cover. |
| **Selling line** | The short description of the 'identity' of the magazine under the masthead. |
| **Main image** | The image which fills the cover – a model, celebrity, animal, artefact. |
| **Coverlines** | 'Teasers' for the contents of the magazine on the cover. |
| **Typography/font** | The shape, style, size and colour of the letters used. |
| **Drop cap** | The enlarged initial letter of the first word of an article – an aesthetic feature which is designed to engage the reader. |
| **Pull quotes** | Enlarged quotes from an article – these may be included in coverlines, but are also used in the body of the article to break up the page and to attract the attention of the reader. |
| **Byline** | The name of the writer of the article, usually found at the beginning. Simply, it is the 'line' which tells you who the article is by. |

The Coursework Handbook's matching activity (CWH p.11) uses a partly different set of terms: Buzz Word, Puff, Coverline, Masthead, Barcode, Anchorage Text, Superimposition, Slogan, Unique Selling Point. Puff, buzz word, barcode, anchorage text and USP are not in this appendix. Both lists are Cambridge's, so know both.

## Source oddities

Some entries read oddly. The wording is Cambridge's own:

- **"High angle"** (Appendix 2) reads against the usual convention. Cambridge writes that it creates "empowerment for the character with Point of View," which only makes sense if read as empowering the viewer, not the subject.
- **"Web banner"** (Appendix 5) mentions "the genre of the music," a leftover from a music-website example.
- **"crowd murmer"** (Appendix 4, Soundscape) is a misspelling in the original.
- **"Selling line"** and **"Web links"** end without final punctuation in the source. Punctuation is supplied here; the wording is untouched.

concepts/power-and-the-media.md.body:
# Power and the Media

Power and the Media is one of the three **A Level Media debates** topics (Syllabus 2027 pp.9, 18). It is one of two topics chosen for BNDS, alongside [[concepts/postmodern-media]]. The choice will be confirmed in class.

Syllabus framing: "Power and the media considers issues surrounding access to the media, identity, representation, ideology and democracy" (p.18).

The core question: **who gets to speak, who gets spoken for, and whose version of the world wins?**

## What you must study (Syllabus 2027 p.18)

- the relationships between media texts, their producers, distributors and audiences
- the mediation of national, regional, individual and group identities
- the dynamic nature of power relationships within and between audiences and the media
- the power of rhetoric in the media
- the construction and reception of campaigning and marketing messages
- the way access to the media may be limited or controlled, including the democratic distribution of voices

The last five of these are listed as the key areas in the examination.

⚠ Unlike the other two debates, this topic has no "arguments for and against" bullet. You analyze how power operates, rather than argue whether it should.

## Three kinds of power

The topic points to a useful taxonomy:

> "This could be **the power to represent, to speak for a particular group**, or the power to **acquire independent companies in order to benefit from their brand and market share**. It could also be the growing **power of individuals to produce and distribute their own material**, to create their own brands and to make an impact on political discourse via social media."

So there are three kinds: **representational power**, **corporate power**, and **distributed individual power**. A strong essay usually sets at least two of them against each other.

## Dominant ideology

> "although there may now be an enormous quantity of voices in the public sphere, there is still a sense that some voices are more powerful than others, some representations are more potent than others, and that **when media messages are aligned with dominant ideologies they are particularly powerful**."

This connects straight back to [[concepts/representation]]: the systematic reinforcement of values across many texts is the mechanism by which representation becomes power.

## The named thinker

**[[entities/slavoj-zizek]]** is the only theorist Cambridge names in this topic. Media ownership is one factor: outlets can be directly influenced by their owners, or can self-censor. But more significant is what Žižek calls the media's **'Standard Operating Procedure'**:

> "its reproduction of ideological 'truths' about which voices count for more than others, its reduction of complex conflicts to spectacle, and the general reinforcing of 'common sense'."

Also consider how much has changed since then in the representation of different ethnicities in media productions, and analyze how and why change has happened in different degrees.

## Counter-power

People can also reject or subvert media messages. One strategy is **détournement**: reworking existing texts so their meaning turns against itself. It is linked to [[entities/guy-debord]] and the Situationists. Other strategies include producing your own texts or running social media campaigns. Cambridge's example is a Guardian piece on young Brixton activists who recreated film posters with Black leads.

## Activities and resources

One activity fits each syllabus bullet:

- **Media power flow analysis**: producers → distributors → platforms → audiences; gatekeeping and concentration.
- **Mediation of identity**: national, regional, group, and individual.
- **Audience power dynamics**: activism, backlash, and fan campaigns; whether participatory culture increases or commodifies audience power.
- **Rhetorical strategy analysis**: framing, emotive language, and binary oppositions.
- **Campaign analysis**: mode of address, ideological positioning, and oppositional readings.
- **Access mapping**: ownership concentration, economic barriers, **platform algorithms**, and cultural gatekeeping.
- A synoptic debate on the motion "Media power remains concentrated in the hands of institutions rather than audiences."

Resources: Media Reform Coalition, Ofcom media-ownership rules, Pew, and the Reuters Institute Digital News Report.

## Suggested exercises

1. "Find two or three news stories about refugees/asylum seekers. How are they represented? What rhetoric is used? How is the reader positioned in relation to the refugees?"
2. "What kinds of representations of women can you find in advertising? How 'powerful' are they?"

## What the syllabus does not name

The topic names only Žižek. The terms "public sphere," "dominant ideologies," and "common sense" all appear as vocabulary with no named originator. These thinkers and ideas are relevant but not named by the syllabus: **Gramsci**, **hegemony**, **Stuart Hall**, **Habermas**, **Herman & Chomsky**, the **propaganda model**, **Curran & Seaton**, and **Foucault**.

## The specimen answer

A marked high answer and middle answer respond to the question: **"'Now that everyone has a voice in the media, everyone has equal power to influence.' How far do you agree? [15]"**. The high answer scores **12/15** (AO1 7/9, AO2 5/6); the middle answer scores **7/15** (AO1 4/9, AO2 3/6).

The high-band answer uses the very names the topic withholds. It names **Gramsci** and **hegemony**, **Chomsky's *Manufacturing Consent*** and the **Overton Window**, and **Curran & Seaton's *Power Without Responsibility***; the examiner's AO2 breakdown credits "theories of Hegemony and dominant ideology." It also uses **Clay Shirky** for technological determinism, **Evgeny Morozov** against him, **Mark Fisher** on political economy, and **David Buckingham** on social media reproducing offline class advantage.

The two answers separate on structure, not knowledge:

- The middle answer is all illustration: BLM, the Arab Spring, Joe Rogan, and the 2024 US election. The examiner calls the Arab Spring "old" and "quite badly outdated" (15 years), and marks the answer down for describing influencers instead of addressing *everyone*. Not answering the actual question is the failure.
- The high answer argues by counter-evidence. It concedes the democratization case, then dismantles it with shadow-banning research, ownership consolidation, and reach economics. The two marks it misses are for never asking whether a digital voice can actually *change* anything, and for ignoring cost and accessibility barriers.
- The examiner is explicit about case studies: "a collection of associated texts, linked thematically," known well enough to include how they were made, distributed, and consumed. See [[concepts/case-study-method]].

concepts/production-craft.md.body:
# Production Craft

AO3 is the practical part of the course. **AO3 is 40% of the whole A Level and sits entirely inside the two portfolios** (Syllabus 2027 p.12). Production weeks carry the most marks.

Both Cambridge documents set out the same method: you build skills through **short, discrete, self-contained exercises before the assessed production begins**, not through one large project. A phone camera is enough for all of them (SoW p.9).

## Camera exercises (SoW p.9)

"A series of short, self-contained exercises with camera (or even phone) can combine technical elements with story elements."

- "a slow tilt up to reveal character and create suspense"
- "an establishing shot to set the scene"
- "a close-up (CU) to indicate significance (or extreme close-up if particularly significant)"
- "a canted angle / Dutch tilt to indicate dissonance"
- "simulation of point of view (POV)"

There is also a shoot-from-a-storyboard drill: "some frames of an existing, or pre-prepared, storyboard can be provided and learners asked to shoot from it. The results can be presented and critiqued in class."

Each exercise pairs a **technique** with a **meaning**. None of them is "practise a close-up."

## Editing exercises (SoW pp.9–10)

Start small: "These exercises can be developed into editing short sequences, just two or three shots to begin with."

- "someone looking off-screen followed by the object they are looking at"
- "shot / reverse shot for a conversation between two people (which is also an opportunity to highlight the 180-degree rule)"
- "a cut from an exterior establishing shot to an interior, suggesting spatial continuity"
- "cross-cutting between two different actions in order to suggest a connection"

## Sound exercises (SoW p.10)

- **Foley:** "incidental sound effects which are created artificially to enhance the drama, but which are diegetic… e.g. footsteps, gunshots, punches and kisses"
- Post-production voice: "Voices (breathing, gasping, for example) may also be added in post-production"
- Non-diegetic demonstration: you present short edited sequences and the class discusses the effect of different music choices
- **Re-cut trailers:** "the impact on perception of genre is clear." This is the fastest way to prove that editing and music construct genre.

## Print and campaign craft (SoW pp.11–12)

- Photograph for a new music magazine cover, then present it with a rationale: "they should experiment with various angles, poses and post-production treatments"
- Devise a title for a new magazine and discuss "the connotations of the title"
- Given a title, devise a strapline, with rationale
- Devise coverlines, then draft the opening paragraphs of those articles

The Coursework Handbook adds the layout drills (CWH pp.11–12): the terminology matching game, box-mapping where text falls on a page, and a **mood board** for "house style, use of colours, formatting of page numbers, fonts and images."

**House style** is the print equivalent of continuity. It is a mark-bearing requirement: "in the case of the magazine option, present a clear house style" (CWH p.7), and it appears on the peer-feedback form.

## Story before shooting

Even for a two-minute product, the Scheme of Work insists on story groundwork (SoW p.10):

> "it's worth doing some basic work on story along with genre – learners should be able to explain what sort of film this is; who the main character is; what the central conflict is likely to be; the questions or enigmas that the opening creates – that is, what information is given? What is withheld? What clues are provided?"

The Coursework Handbook gives the build order for storyboarding (CWH p.12): "plan the narrative, then the mise en scene/generic conventions, then the camera shots, sound, movement and finally the transitions."

Use the planning table it describes: rows for *Elements / Symbolic codes / Technical codes / Genre / Mise-en-scène / Transition* against each sequence, "a useful way to encourage learners to avoid a narrative approach and engage with the media strategies required at this level" (CWH p.12). It is the clearest picture either document gives of what a good planning document looks like.

## The research-to-production rule

The load-bearing sentence (CWH p.12):

> "The production plan should draw on the research stage and should evidence decision-making based on media techniques, codes and conventions that have been identified."

Paired with: "Creative choices should be based on research, and evidenced and justified in the blog" (CWH p.7). If you challenge conventions, "they **must** justify and document it in both their blog, and their creative critical reflection work" (CWH p.12).

**Every production decision should be traceable to something you researched.** That is what criterion 4 of the mark scheme rewards.

## Peer review

The Coursework Handbook supplies a six-prompt feedback form for screening drafts (CWH p.13), including "What might stop this product being viewed as a professional product for publication?" and "If you were to re-edit this product what would your top three priorities be?"

Reserve time for the re-edit: "two or three hours should enable learners to re-film a sequence after feedback and complete a reasonable level of editing before submitting" (CWH p.13). This is advice, not a rule, but losing the re-edit window costs marks in criteria 2 and 3.

## Two rules that constrain the room
