- **Acting is not assessed.** "As acting is not a skill that is assessed in media studies… groups may use personnel external to the group to appear in their productions in photos, video or audio. **The ability of candidates to direct actors is part of the assessment**" (Syllabus 2027 p.30). You may cast anyone. You are marked on direction, not performance.
- **Teachers must not design the product.** "while you should not offer suggestions for production, you might consider recommending relevant materials to facilitate this critical engagement" (CWH p.8). Your teacher recommends sources, never solutions.

## Originality

For C1 (Syllabus 2027 p.21): all images and text original, sound "predominantly original", music from an acknowledged source permitted. For C3 (p.24): "Images and video should be original material only. Sound should be predominantly original."

Neither document specifies **how** music must be acknowledged. There is no format, placement, or credit rule.

Generative AI: "Cambridge International has a policy on the use of generative AI by candidates in coursework. The inappropriate use of AI should be treated as a form of plagiarism" (Syllabus 2027 p.30). Under the 2028–30 spec, AI images become permitted with documented prompts and justification, see [[classes/media-studies/media-studies]].

concepts/process-evidence-and-reflection.body:
# Process Evidence and Reflection

This page explains how you prove you made your coursework product, and what you say about it afterward. Two of the five C1 marking criteria attach directly to this evidence. A weak evidence layer often caps an otherwise strong product.

> [!note] Which spec applies to you
> G11 sits the 2027 spec: a blog plus a creative critical reflection. G12 sits the 2028–30 spec: a slide portfolio plus a roughly 2000-word evaluative essay. Everything below describes the 2027 regime unless marked. For the crossover, see [[classes/media-studies/media-studies]].

## The blog (2027 spec)

You set up and maintain your own blog, from the start of research: "Learners should set up and maintain a blog outlining the creative processes… The blog should be **set up at the outset of the research stage** and should be **maintained regularly**." In a group, each member keeps a separate blog: "All learners are required to maintain **separate blogs**… These should include details of their individual role within the group task."

### What must be in it

- the process of research, planning and production
- refinement, changes or edits and reflections on key moments
- all individual contributions to group tasks
- evidence of any preliminary exercises
- the final finished product, clearly labeled
- the creative critical reflection, clearly labelled

You must also cover the key areas: **forms and conventions, production contexts, the role of technologies, audiences and representations**.

The process your blog should narrate runs: set up the blog, decide groupings and select the brief, research codes and conventions, storyboard, cast, script, write recce reports and risk assessments, carry out production, reflect and edit, then evaluate in light of the contemporary media landscape.

### Dating and freezing

Update your blog regularly to keep "a **continuous narrative of the production process**." There is no minimum post count or frequency. "Regularly" is as specific as Cambridge gets.

The freeze rule is hard: "**Blogs must be accessible online for the duration of the moderation period. During this period no changes may be made to the portfolios**." Your center presents one hub URL linking every candidate's blog, recorded on the Individual Candidate Record Card.

This is why the BNDS rule is: post dated the day it happens, never backfilled. A blog assembled afterward cannot show a continuous narrative, and you cannot fix it after submission.

### Why a thin blog caps a good product

Research and planning is criterion 4 of the five C1 criteria, and the mark scheme judges the blog, the product, and the reflection together at every level. Level 5 requires research "drawn on to inform the production and explored in the creative critical reflection." Level 2 describes a blog that "may make reference to the research but may not fully engage with it." A strong product with a thin blog cannot reach the top band, because the evidence for the top band lives in the blog.

## Group work

Groups are a maximum of **four** candidates, with "clearly defined roles."

Form the group by skill set, not friendship: "**Each learner in the group should adopt an area of expertise. This does not necessarily mean that they are the only person to work on this element, but that they lead on that part of the production.**" Roles like director, technical, creative, and editor are examples, not a required set.

Authentication is tighter for groups: "Sufficient work must be carried out under **direct supervision** to enable you to authenticate the coursework marks, with confidence. This is particularly important if the production work is carried out as a group." Your teacher comments on your own contribution on the record card.

For the magazine option under the 2027 spec, each group member produces **a unique edition in the same house style**, with "a minimum of four images per candidate."

## The creative critical reflection (C1, 2027 spec)

The creative critical reflection is individual, in a digital format of your choice: "any digital format, such as director commentaries, a presentation with voiceover, podcasts or screencasts." You may use a **different format for each question**.

### The four compulsory questions

1. "How does your product use or challenge conventions and how does it represent social groups or issues?"
2. "How does your product engage with audiences and how would it be distributed as a real media text?"
3. "How did your production skills develop throughout this project?"
4. "How did you integrate technologies – software, hardware and online – in this project?"

Note the shape: Q1 is Language plus Representation, Q2 is Audience plus Industry, Q3 and Q4 are AO3 process. The four questions are the [[concepts/four-key-concepts]] wearing a different hat.

The reflection must also state "the role they adopted if working as part of a group" and "draw on evidence from the research, production and editing stages." It sits **before the final post** in the blog.

### The failure mode Cambridge names

> "there is often a tendency for learners to provide a **blow by blow account** of the production process instead of a genuinely critical evaluation of the final work and how it was developed. One way round this is to ensure that there is a **focus on critical incidents and turning points**"

The prompts that produce turning points: "What were the breakthroughs in developing a story opening? How were particular technical challenges overcome? What new understanding was gained at key points in the process? **Is the final product successful? According to what criteria?**"

That last question is the one most students never answer, and it is where AO2 marks live.

There is **no word count or duration** for the C1 reflection. The 1000–1500 word figure belongs to C3, not C1.

## The C3 critical reflection (2027 spec)

This is "An evaluative essay of around 1000–1500 words," individual "even if learners had collaborated in the creation of their products," guided by four compulsory questions:

1. "How do your products represent social groups or issues?"
2. "How do the elements of your production work together to create a sense of 'branding'?"
3. "How do your products engage with the audience?"
4. "How did your research inform your products and the way they use or challenge conventions?"

Note: the syllabus gives two figures for this essay. Its assessment overview says "around 1000 words," while the detail section says "around 1000–1500 words." Your teacher will confirm which applies in class.

## How it is marked (C1, 2027 spec)

Five criteria, 10 marks each, 50 total:

| Criterion | AO |
|---|---|
| Analyse and evaluate own work | **AO2** (10 marks) |
| Use of media language | AO3 |
| Use of technical skills | AO3 |
| Research, planning and application of key concepts | AO3 |
| Creative Critical Reflection skills | AO3 |

**AO3 Practical Application = 40 marks; AO2 Evaluation = 10 marks.**

Evidence per objective: AO2 is evidenced **solely** by the reflection. AO3 is evidenced by the blog, the finished product, and, at AS only, the reflection as well. So the reflection feeds both objectives at AS. Marking is best-fit against generic grids, with part marks rounded up.

**AO1 is not assessed in the C1 grid at all.** It is taught at this component, but not marked here.

## What changes for G12 (2028–30 spec)

Under the 2028–30 syllabus, the evidence moves from an online blog to a **dated chronological slide portfolio** on Submit for Assessment. The reflection becomes a single **roughly 2000-word evaluative essay**. The coursework AO split changes from AO2 20 / AO3 80 to **AO1 20 / AO2 20 / AO3 60**. C3's third medium becomes a **website home page**. The C1 magazine task becomes **individual only**.

The habits carry over: dated evidence, decisions traceable to research, turning points over blow-by-blow. The format does not. Do not carry blog-shaped assumptions into a slide portfolio.

## A worked C1 exemplar: Candidate A, Level 3

Cambridge publishes a complete Foundation Portfolio Film exemplar on the School Support Hub, openly accessible, marked and commented: **Candidate A**, a **secure Level 3** across most objectives. Fourteen blog pages, five preliminary and nine final-production, ending in the Critical Reflection and Final Draft. It is from the 2021/2027 regime, so it fits G11's C1 and says nothing about G12's slide portfolio.

The examiner's diagnosis inverts the warning above. Candidate A's blog was not thin, and its posts were properly dated and showed progression. It capped at Level 3 because the volume sat in the wrong place: far too much preliminary material and not enough assessed material focused on the set brief, with some preliminary work not relevant to the final outcome at all.

So there are two ways the evidence layer caps a good product, not one:

| Failure | Looks like | Guard |
|---|---|---|
| Thin blog | few posts, backfilled, research not carried into the product | the dating rule, already taught |
| **Misweighted blog** | plenty of posts, but the mass sits in preliminary work and off-brief material | **audit the ratio, not just the count** |

The product itself was the strongest element and pulled the grade up. A good film opening does not rescue a misweighted portfolio any more than it rescues a thin one.

### What Cambridge wanted in planning

Planning was the named shortfall: adequate but too narrow. The examiner lists the expected range: **recce reports, casting sessions, scripting and screenplay production, test shots (especially for any effects used), storyboarding, risk assessments.**

Five of these six already appear in the process chain above. **Test shots for effects is the addition:** cheap to run, easy to evidence, and missing from the chain.

### What capped the reflection

Two things, both fixable in teaching rather than in production:

1. **One digital application, used throughout.** The syllabus lets you use a different format per question, and the examiner explicitly wanted a wider creative range of applications. Answering all four questions in one tool leaves AO3 marks on the table for no production reason.
2. **The four questions were answered, but thinly.** The examiner's point is that short responses do not let you demonstrate your understanding of the production process. The diagnosis is **descriptive rather than analytical**.

For more, see [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-07-reading-systematically-toward-the-blog-midpoint|L07]] (the mid-point audit) and [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-10-the-creative-critical-reflection|L10]] (the reflection build). Use it as calibration for [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-a3-c1-portfolio|A3]].

## Candidate B: the top of the range, and the one mark it dropped

The same Hub page publishes a second portfolio: **Candidate B**, film brief, marked at the **top of Level 5** across most objectives. Research is called sophisticated with detailed evidence throughout the blog, the product is entirely convincing as a film opening, and the moderator calls it an excellent example of what is expected at this level.

Its planning is the direct answer to Candidate A's shortfall. Where A's planning needed a wider range of tasks, B's is listed as **recce reports, casting information, scripting and storyboarding**: four of the six artefact types Cambridge names. The gap between a Level 3 and a Level 5 portfolio here is not talent. It is which planning documents exist.

### Both exemplars lose the same mark, in the same place

Candidate B drops below top band on exactly one strand: **AO3iv, the reflection strand**, placed at the top of the band below. The reason is the same one the moderator gave for Candidate A: digital creative tools used to limited effect, **only one application employed**.

Two published exemplars, one at Level 3 and one at the top of Level 5, and both are held back by the same avoidable choice. This is the cheapest credit in Component 1:

| | Candidate A (Level 3) | Candidate B (top of Level 5) |
|---|---|---|
| Product | strongest element, pulled the grade up | entirely convincing |
| Research and planning | too narrow; preliminary-heavy | sophisticated; recce, casting, scripting, storyboards |
| Preliminary relevance | far too much, some off-brief | some material not directly connected |
| **Reflection applications** | **one** | **one** |
| Reflection outcome | thin answers, capped | **the only strand below top band** |

The consequence is blunt: you can do everything else at the top of the range and still lose the strand, and the fix costs a single afternoon. Treat the format spread as a requirement, not a suggestion. See [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-10-the-creative-critical-reflection|L10]].

concepts/representation.md.body:
# Representation

**Key Concept 2.** "How the media construct the social world, the portrayal of ideas, individuals and groups" (Syllabus 2027 p.14).

This is the concept that turns description into argument. Component 2 Section A never asks you to list techniques. It asks how the extract *constructs* a person, group, event or place, and to what effect.

## The chain

The syllabus's own logic, compressed from the p.14 bullets:

**reality → selection and combination → mediation → a version**

Producers choose what is shown and how it is combined. Repeated choices harden into typicality. Typicality carries values. Values reinforced across many texts become ideology, and ideology positions audiences.

The Scheme of Work's glossary makes the hardening explicit (SoW p.27):

> "The processes (and end results) by which reality is subject to selection, exaggeration and repetition, so that certain representations (often of subordinated groups and associated places) become typical and taken for granted."

## What the syllabus requires

You study (Syllabus 2027 p.14):

- the ways in which events, issues, individuals and social groups are represented through processes of selection and combination
- the ways in which, through representation, versions of reality are mediated
- the processes which lead media producers to make choices about how to represent events, issues, individuals and social groups
- the effect of social and cultural context on representations
- how and why particular social groups, in a national and global context, may be under-represented or misrepresented
- how representations convey values, attitudes and beliefs about the world and how these may be systematically reinforced across a wide range of media
- how audiences respond to and interpret representations in the media
- the effect of historical context on representations
- how representations may invoke discourses and ideologies, and position audiences
- how interpretations of representations reflect social, cultural and historical circumstances

This is the longest content list of the four key concepts. It is the only one that names **under-representation** and **misrepresentation** as objects of study in their own right.

Many bullets are about **context and change**: social, cultural, historical, national and global. Representation is not a fixed set of stereotypes. It shifts with who is making it, when, and for whom. That is why you study theories of the gaze across decades, not as settled fact.

## How it enters the exam

Component 2 Section A fuses representation with [[concepts/technical-elements]]: candidates "discuss… how the following technical elements create specific representations of individuals/groups/events/places, and help to articulate specific messages and values that have social significance" (Syllabus 2027 p.16).

So the exam question is always some version of: **how is this person, group or place constructed, and to what effect?** If you name techniques without reaching representation, you have answered half the question.

The reassembly stage of [[concepts/the-viewing-protocol]] is where you practice this handoff: "How are particular representations of individuals, groups, events and places constructed through the technical elements identified?" (SoW p.14).

## Ways to practice

- **Compare the coverage** (SoW p.24): "Find two or three news stories about refugees/asylum seekers. How are they represented? What rhetoric is used? How is the reader positioned in relation to the refugees?" Look at what is selected, what is omitted, and how the reader is positioned. This connects to the [[concepts/power-and-the-media]] debate.
- **Magazine representation grid** (SoW p.9): "To what extent does the image conform to conventional ways of portraying men, women and celebrities? How are ethnic, cultural and subcultural dimensions emphasised or not?"
- **Advertising and power** (SoW p.25): "What kinds of representations of women can you find in advertising? How 'powerful' are they?"
- **Stills annotation.** Annotate frames with technical terms plus the representation each choice constructs.

## Theories of representation

The 2028 Scheme of Work names theorists you can use for this concept:

> "candidates need to develop the habit of applying knowledge of technical elements to better understand the representation of **class, age, gender, ethnicity**… candidates need to learn the concept of Representation - best done with reference to theories of representation where there is a variety of student-friendly materials available - such as **Hall, Van Zoonen, hooks, Gilroy, Alvarado**." (2028 SoW, C2 Section A)

[[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-09-the-gaze|L09]] teaches **Liesbet van Zoonen**, **bell hooks**, and **Laura Mulvey**. Van Zoonen and hooks appear in the Cambridge-suggested list. Mulvey is a BNDS addition, named in no Cambridge document. The ideas covered include **the gaze**, gender as performance, the three looks, and the oppositional gaze. [[entities/paul-gilroy]] and [[entities/manuel-alvarado]] are named by Cambridge and extend the ethnicity strand.

The 2028 SoW also names the **axes of representation** for Section A analysis: class, age, gender, ethnicity. Some texts use stereotypical representations of these groups. Other texts consciously seek to challenge stereotypes. The exercise bank runs each technical element through those axes:

- **Camera:** "Who is shot from a high/low angle? Who gets the close-ups?"
- **Sound:** "How does vocal performance construct representation of class / age / gender / ethnicity?"
- **Mise-en-scène:** "Who occupies the foreground? Who is marginalised spatially?"

concepts/technical-elements.md.body:
# Technical Elements

This is the most concretely examinable content in 9607: the four-part toolkit for reading moving image. You drill it all year. It is tested directly in **Component 2 Section A**, and it doubles as the vocabulary of production.

The syllabus frames it as a means, not an end (Syllabus 2027 p.16):

> "Candidates should study a range of texts so that they can discuss, in response to the question, how the following technical elements create specific representations of individuals/groups/events/places, and help to articulate specific messages and values that have social significance."

**Naming alone earns little.** The mark is in technique → meaning → representation. This is the single most repeated correction in the whole course.

The Section A support is built around this chain. It reproduces the syllabus element lists inside its teaching rows, and the lists below are unchanged. It then supplies a large per-element exercise bank: shot-type identification drills, freeze-frame deconstruction, camera power mind maps ("Who is shot from a high/low angle? Who gets the close-ups?"), re-shoot planning, sound audit tables, dialogue-and-power micro-analysis, foley and contrapuntal-sound workshops, mise-en-scène audits, genre deconstruction, editing timeline breakdowns, paper-based re-edits, flashback construction, plus quick retrieval games (shot bingo, "define diegetic in 10 seconds," correct-the-flawed-analysis). Every exercise routes technique through representation of **class, age, gender, ethnicity**: the technique → meaning → representation chain in practice. The named representation theorists are covered in [[concepts/representation]].

## The four elements, per the syllabus (p.16)

### Camera: shots, angle, movement, composition

- **shots**: establishing, master, close-up, mid-shot, long, wide, two-shot, aerial, point-of-view, over-the-shoulder, "and variations of these"
- **angle**: high, low, canted
- **movement**: pan, tilt, track, dolly, crane, steadicam, hand-held, zoom, reverse zoom
- **composition**: framing, rule of thirds, depth of field (deep and shallow focus), focus pulls

Learn these as meaning pairs, not as a list: low angle grants power, canted angle signals dissonance, shallow focus isolates, hand-held destabilizes.

### Sound

- diegetic and non-diegetic, synchronous/asynchronous, sound effects, sound motif, sound bridge, dialogue, voiceover, mode of address / direct address, sound mixing, sound perspective
- **soundtrack**: score, incidental music, themes and stings, ambient sound

Sound is often neglected, so it is worth targeted work (SoW p.13): "Sound is often neglected, so it is worth doing some targeted work on this, in particularly helping learners to develop a vocabulary of sound terminology, e.g. harmony, dissonance, discordance, sound bed, rhythm, crescendo, pitch, timbre." *(sic, "in particularly" is the source's own slip.)*

Because it is neglected across the candidature, sound is the cheapest way for a script to stand out.

### Mise-en-scène

- **production design**: location, studio, set design, costume and make-up, properties
- lighting, colour design

⚠ Note what is *not* here: **acting and performance are not listed under mise-en-scène**, and the syllabus states separately that "acting is not a skill that is assessed in media studies" (p.30). Body language and expression are also absent from the syllabus bullet, though the Scheme of Work's own glossary includes "expression, movement, symmetry" in its mise-en-scène definition (SoW p.27).

If you read English as a second language, this is the highest-yield element: costume, lighting and colour are visible, nameable, and rich in connotation.

### Editing

"This includes transition of image and sound – continuity and non-continuity systems."

- **cutting**: shot/reverse shot, eyeline match, graphic match, action match, jump cut, crosscutting, parallel editing, cutaway, insert
- **other transitions**: dissolve, fade-in, fade-out, wipe, superimposition, long take, short take, slow motion, ellipsis and expansion of time, post-production, visual effects

⚠ **Long take, short take and slow motion are filed under Editing**, not camera. They are routinely misfiled.

Editing is invisible until you make it visible, which is exactly what the cut-counting exercise in [[concepts/the-viewing-protocol]] is for.

## How it is examined

Component 2 Section A: an unseen extract "from a TV drama and will last for a maximum of five minutes. It will be played four times. The screening time will last a total of 30 minutes, including note-taking" (Syllabus 2027 p.23). Then 45 minutes of writing, 25 marks.

The syllabus's coverage caveat is worth knowing (p.23):

> "It is acknowledged that not every one of the technical areas will feature in equal measure in any given extract and other areas may also be credited where appropriate… We do not expect each aspect to be covered in the same degree of detail, but as appropriate to the genre and extract provided and to the discussion of the extract's representation."

So your script does not need to hit all four elements evenly. It needs to hit what the extract actually does, and tie each observation to representation.

## The analytical paragraph frame

The expected output shape (SoW p.14): technique named → terminology → meaning created → link to representation → link to the question.

This frame is the direct rehearsal for A1 and A4 in [[classes/media-studies/assessments/9607-s1-assessments|the S1 register]], and it is what CS4, CS6 and CS8 practise.

## Spec note

The 2027 spec screens the extract from **DVD, four times**. Under the 2028–30 syllabus the exam is digital and the extract is embedded in the platform: see [[classes/media-studies/media-studies]] for the straddle. The technical vocabulary transfers unchanged. The **format practice does not**.

entities/bell-hooks.md.body:
# bell hooks

Named in the 2028 Scheme of Work as a representation theorist. She styled her name in lowercase, surname only.

## What Cambridge attributes to her

> "candidates need to learn the concept of Representation - best done with reference to theories of representation where there is a variety of student-friendly materials available - such as **Hall, Van Zoonen, hooks, Gilroy, Alvarado**." (2028 SoW, C2 Section A camera row)

Cambridge names hooks but does not attach a work or a concept to her, not even the **oppositional gaze**, which is what a media-studies course reaches for when it reaches for hooks.

## BNDS usage

You meet hooks in [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-09-the-gaze|L09]], on the Friday single. The lesson teaches the **oppositional gaze**: the act of looking as refusal and rereading, by someone "who the text never expected to be looking." It closes the gaze arc and feeds CS6. Homework is a 300–400-word hooks extract in an accessible gloss, in English with Chinese support.

entities/bill-nichols.md.body:
# Bill Nichols

Bill Nichols is named for **documentary modes** in the Component 3 documentary brief. The reference points to Nichols' six modes of documentary.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "It would also be useful to introduce the notion of documentary modes, using the work of **Bill Nichols**" (SoW p.20)

The Scheme of Work links to an outside article on "Nichols' 6 modes of documentary." It does not name or list the modes. The attribution is a pointer, not content.

## When it becomes relevant

This matters only if you take the **documentary package** for [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-course-map|Component 3]]. Cambridge lets a centre limit the choice: "you may decide to offer only one of the Set Briefs outlined in the syllabus, or you may decide to give learners free choice" (SoW p.17).

You may not be offered the documentary brief. The promotion briefs, music and film, fit a five-period week better than documentary or short film, which need much more shooting and editing time. Which briefs run will be confirmed in class.

If the documentary brief does run, the modes are needed. The pitch-feedback prompts ask "What mode would be most appropriate" (SoW p.20), so you cannot pitch without them.

## Where Nichols would sit

Cambridge suggests these documentary research questions (SoW p.20): "What different kinds of documentaries are there? / What is the purpose of a documentary? / What is the audience for documentary?" A modes framework answers exactly these questions. You can also reach the same material by sorting a published documentary list: "What different categories of documentary are listed here? What stories get told? Whose stories get told?" This is an empirical route into the material without leading with the theory.

entities/fredric-jameson.md.body:
# Fredric Jameson

Fredric Jameson is the theorist Cambridge develops most fully in the Scheme of Work. Cambridge gives him a full analytical framework, not just a name and a link.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

"Similarly, and more recently, **Fredric Jameson** diagnoses the postmodern condition as characterised by:" (SoW pp.23–24)

| Symptom | Cambridge's wording |
|---|---|
| **Ahistorical mode** | "lacking a sense of the past – history becomes another set of signifiers which can be played with" |
| **Collapse of high/low** | "A lack of distinction between 'high' and 'low' culture" |
| **Surfaces** | "increasingly there is no time for depth – politics becomes soundbites, protests become slogans, the world is a collection of images" |
| **Affectlessness** | "the predominant mode of irony and 'knowingness' leaves little room for real emotion, but short, sharp intense emotional responses are elicited through surface representations of things of which people have no first-hand experience, e.g.: Brexit, the death of Diana, refugees" |
| **Technologies of reproduction and recirculation** | "e.g.: all social media" |

## Why this list is worth learning

It is the most usable analytical tool in Component 4. Each symptom becomes an essay paragraph: name the symptom, supply a contemporary text, show the symptom operating, then judge whether the diagnosis holds.

The list is also complete enough to argue against. The syllabus asks for "the arguments for and against understanding some forms of media as postmodern" (Syllabus 2027 p.18). A five-point checklist is exactly what you need to show where a text does not fit.

## Relation to Debord

Cambridge places the two theorists in order: [[entities/guy-debord]] first (1967, spectacle), then "similarly, and more recently, Fredric Jameson." The implied argument is continuity: a diagnosis of image-saturated culture, restated for a later moment. Cambridge does not develop the comparison. You can.

concepts/the-viewing-protocol.md.body:
# The Viewing Protocol

The **Viewing Protocol** is the course's core analytical method. Use it from week one: break an extract into its component parts by isolating one element at a time, then reassemble them.

The point of this is to reach insights into how a TV drama extract produces particular meanings.

## The four passes

You watch the same short extract several times. Each pass isolates one element.

| Pass | What runs | What you focus on |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Full extract, ~5 min | Nothing yet: no response is required |
| 2 | Sound down | Mise-en-scène |
| 3 | Sound still off | Camera: shots, angles, movement, composition |
| 4 | Screen covered or blanked | Sound |

For the sound pass, work through these prompts:

- What do we hear?
- Is it diegetic or non-diegetic?
- What mood is created?
- How could the music be described?
- To whom are the voices addressed?

## The editing pass

Editing gets its own move, because it is the element you cannot see. Count out loud, or tap, whenever there is a visual transition. This simple exercise makes something potentially "invisible" become visible.

Then ask:

- Is it a cut or a mix/dissolve?
- What is the effect of this?
- What visual elements are brought together?
- Does it create continuity? Contrast?
- Does it reveal something about character?
- Does it develop the story?

## The reassembly

The protocol is not finished until the parts go back together. Finally, bring all these elements together:

- What is the function of this opening?
- How does it set up the beginning of a story?
- How does it establish character, mood and setting?
- What kinds of competence does it require of the audience?
- How are particular representations of individuals, groups, events and places constructed through the technical elements identified?

The last question turns description into exam marks. It is where the protocol hands off to [[concepts/representation]].

## Choosing the extract

- Openings of first episodes usually work well, because they establish setting, tone, and character, and set up some narrative expectations.
- A range of examples helps, including ones that have previously featured in examinations, such as **The Handmaid's Tale**. Building expertise in what to look for and how to say it is an iterative process.

Using past exam extracts makes the practice authentic and matches you to the real difficulty level.

## Output

This work is formative. You practice the analytical process, possibly in groups and then present your findings, and/or individually in a short-form essay. Group analysis presented, then individual short-form writing: frequent and low stakes.

## Why it is worth the ritual

1. It is direct rehearsal for **Component 2 Section A**, where the extract is screened four times. Four screenings is the exam's own version of this protocol. If you have practiced element-isolation, you know what to do with each pass.
2. It rescues sound, the element most often neglected. A dedicated screen-covered pass is the only reliable way to make yourself hear.
3. It continues from C1: the approaches and terminology are the same as your analytical work for the Foundation Portfolio. The same protocol serves research for the portfolio and analysis for the exam.

entities/liesbet-van-zoonen.md.body:
# Liesbet van Zoonen

**Liesbet van Zoonen** is a representation theorist. Her work in feminist media theory is the standard media-studies reference for the gender strand of **Representation**.

## What Cambridge attributes to her

> "candidates need to learn the concept of Representation - best done with reference to theories of representation where there is a variety of student-friendly materials available - such as **Hall, Van Zoonen, hooks, Gilroy, Alvarado**." (2028 SoW, C2 Section A camera row)

This clause is about representation of class, age, gender, and ethnicity. Van Zoonen is the reference for the gender strand.

## BNDS usage

In [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-09-the-gaze|L09]] you study **gender as performance**, worked on two advertisements, before Mulvey's three looks are stated precisely.

entities/guy-debord.md.body:
# Guy Debord

Named in the Scheme of Work for **The Society of the Spectacle**, as an anchor for the [[concepts/postmodern-media]] debate.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "**Guy Debord's 1967 work The Society of the Spectacle** is a critique of media-saturated capitalist culture is still relevant in diagnosing aspects of the postmodern condition" (SoW p.23)

In short: Debord wrote a 1967 critique of media-saturated capitalist culture. Cambridge treats it as still useful for diagnosing the postmodern condition.

## Where he is used

The Scheme of Work sets one exercise (SoW p.24):

> "**Exercise:** Watch a TV news story. What features does it have of 'The Society of the Spectacle'?"

This task asks you to turn an abstract diagnosis into observable features of a real text. Anchoring your arguments in specific texts or phenomena is what marks a sophisticated answer.

## Spectacle and détournement

**détournement** appears in [[concepts/power-and-the-media]] as a strategy of resistance (SoW p.25). Cambridge names it but credits no one.

Both ideas come from the same tradition: Debord and the Situationists. The tradition supplies both the diagnosis, the spectacle, and the counter-move, détournement. Linking them is a genuine synthesis you can make in a strong answer.

entities/manuel-alvarado.md.body:
# Manuel Alvarado

**Manuel Alvarado** is a theorist of representation named in the 2028 Scheme of Work.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "candidates need to learn the concept of Representation - best done with reference to theories of representation where there is a variety of student-friendly materials available - such as **Hall, Van Zoonen, hooks, Gilroy, Alvarado**." (2028 SoW, C2 Section A camera row)

The clause concerns representation of "class, age, gender, ethnicity." Alvarado is the standard A Level media-studies reference for racial-stereotype categories, usually taught alongside Hall and Gilroy.

## Status in the course

**Not currently taught at BNDS.** Like [[entities/paul-gilroy]], he is a possible way to deepen the ethnicity strand of [[concepts/representation]] in the G12 year.

entities/paul-gilroy.md.body:
# Paul Gilroy

Paul Gilroy is a representation theorist named in the 2028 Scheme of Work.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "candidates need to learn the concept of Representation - best done with reference to theories of representation where there is a variety of student-friendly materials available - such as **Hall, Van Zoonen, hooks, Gilroy, Alvarado**." (2028 SoW, C2 Section A camera row)

This is all Cambridge says about him. The clause is about the representation of "class, age, gender, ethnicity." Gilroy is the standard A Level media-studies reference for the ethnicity strand, alongside Hall, hooks and Alvarado.

## Status in the course

Gilroy is not currently taught at BNDS. The S1 representation block ([[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-s1-unit-4-representation|U4]]) uses Hall, van Zoonen, Mulvey and hooks. He may be taught in the G12 year, where the class, age, gender and ethnicity axes recur across both exam components.

entities/roland-barthes.md.body:
> **Taught in two courses, for two arguments.** Everything below is Media Studies (9607), where Barthes anchors semiotics and the narrative codes. For the [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]], where he gives a one-sentence statement of [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]], skip to [the last section](#in-the-oxbridge-discussion-group).

Barthes is the most-used theorist in 9607. The from-2021 Scheme of Work names only two theorists for the AS year: Barthes and [[entities/stuart-hall]].

## What Cambridge attributes to him

Two distinct contributions, in two places.

**Semiotics: signs, codes and meaning.** Named as the theory hook for C1 research on both briefs: "Relevant theory: semiotics – **Roland Barthes'** ideas about signs, codes and meaning" (SoW p.8 for film, p.9 for magazine).

**Narrative codes and signification.** In the Component 2 textual-analysis material (SoW p.14):

> "This work does not need to be densely theoretical, but there is an opportunity to use some of **Roland Barthes'** narrative codes to provide some explanatory depth… as well as notions of signification – what is **denoted** at a descriptive level, and what is suggested, implied or coded at a **connotative** level"

Cambridge lists Barthes here as optional explanatory depth, not required content.

## Where he earns his place in the course

- **[[concepts/media-language]]**: **denotation** and **connotation** is the ladder the whole of Unit 2 climbs. The denotation-before-connotation discipline is built into CS1 in [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-01-the-four-key-concepts|L01]] and marked in A1.
- **[[concepts/narrative]]**: the **enigma code** gives narrative analysis explanatory depth without heavy theory. It connects to the C1 film-opening research question "how does the film establish an enigma from the outset?" (CWH p.11).
- **C1 research**: signs and codes are the vocabulary you use to annotate real openings and covers.

## BNDS usage

Taught across [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-02-semiotics-how-images-mean|L02]] and [[classes/media-studies/lesson-plans/9607-s1-lesson-03-sign-types-and-codes|L03]] as the semiotics spine of Unit 2.

## In the Oxbridge Discussion Group

A different Barthes, and a smaller one: a single sentence, delivered once.

### The claim in one line

Ideology works best when it presents itself as **nature** rather than as a position. So the most ideological text is the one that appears to have no author.

### The quote

> The author who disappears behind the text is the most ideological author of all.

### How that course uses him

Barthes arrives at the end of [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]], to name what you have already built out of maps and video-game boundaries. He is the cleanest statement of [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]] in a single sentence. The examples come first: the line is compressed enough to memorize without understanding if it arrives too early.

### The connection between the two courses

Both are the same claim about signification in different registers. 9607 teaches denotation and connotation as a method for reading a text. Oxbridge takes the political consequence: a text that hides its own authorship is doing the most ideological work, and never touches the semiotic apparatus at all. A student in both rooms would not obviously recognize him as the same figure.

entities/marshall-mcluhan.md.body:
# Marshall McLuhan

Marshall McLuhan is named, with [[entities/neil-postman]], as an origin of [[concepts/media-ecology]].

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "The notion of media ecology can be traced back to **Neil Postman** and **Marshall McLuhan**, but its contemporary relevance is clearly driven by the saturation of all aspects of contemporary existence with media and media technologies." (SoW p.25)

That is the full attribution. Cambridge credits no idea, book, or coinage to him. There is no "the medium is the message", no global village, and no hot and cool media.

## Media ecology in the course

Media ecology is a compulsory 30-mark synoptic paper. It is half of Component 4. The syllabus defines it as "the complex environments within which media texts, producers, distributors, technologies and audiences exist" (Syllabus 2027 p.19).

**The ecology metaphor** is the idea behind the name: media are environments we live inside, not tools we pick up.

entities/neil-postman.md.body:
# Neil Postman

Named, with [[entities/marshall-mcluhan]], as the origin of [[concepts/media-ecology]].

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "The notion of media ecology can be traced back to **Neil Postman** and **Marshall McLuhan**, but its contemporary relevance is clearly driven by the saturation of all aspects of contemporary existence with media and media technologies." (SoW p.25)

Cambridge names him as an origin of media ecology. It credits him with no specific idea, work, or argument.

## What is left standing

Cambridge gives media ecology as a **method** rather than a theory (SoW pp.25–26):

- historical contrast: "What did the media landscape look like before 1990?" set against your own media diary
- a premise: contemporary life is saturated with media and "mediatised"
- a temporal orientation: "contrasting the present with the past, and analysing the present in order to develop ideas about the future"

The before/after contrast does most of the analytical work. The exam rewards "informed, imaginative analysis" (SoW p.26) grounded in contemporary evidence. The syllabus also requires you to "use key theories of media studies" (Syllabus 2027 p.13).

This is Grade 12, Semester 4 content. See [[concepts/media-ecology]] and [[classes/media-studies/unit-plans/9607-course-map|the course map]].

entities/stuart-hall.md.body:
# Stuart Hall

Stuart Hall is a media theorist. You study him for two ideas: **encoding and decoding**, and **representation**.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

**Encoding and decoding** is Hall's model of how you make sense of a media text. The producer encodes a message; you decode it, and you may not read it the way the producer intended. This is offered as an Extension activity, with a video to explore.

**Representation** is the second idea. Hall is one of the named theories of representation you can use, alongside Van Zoonen, hooks, Gilroy, and Alvarado. His work here covers stereotyping and the racialized regime of representation.

## Why he matters here

The syllabus asks you to understand:

> "how audiences interpret the media, including how they may interpret the same texts in different ways, using a variety of theories or ideologies" (Syllabus 2027 p.15)

Hall's model is one answer to that. His three reading positions are **dominant** (you accept the intended message), **negotiated** (you partly accept it, partly resist), and **oppositional** (you reject it and read against it). Treat these three positions as course-standard knowledge.

## Its status in the course

Encoding and decoding is an Extension activity: extra content for stronger learners, not core AS material. It is still the cleanest bridge from thinking of the audience as a target to thinking of the audience as an interpreter. It feeds forward into [[concepts/power-and-the-media]], where the question of whose reading counts becomes the topic itself.

## The teaching move

Take one text the class disagrees about. Map the actual readings onto the three positions: dominant, negotiated, oppositional. Your own argument becomes the evidence, and a disagreement turns into exam-usable analysis.

entities/slavoj-zizek.md.body:
# Slavoj Žižek

The only theorist Cambridge names in the [[concepts/power-and-the-media]] debate.

The 2028 Scheme of Work keeps the Standard Operating Procedure passage below and adds one line: "In the years since the publication of this article, it is now also worth considering how much has changed in terms of increased representation of different ethnicities in media productions - and also analyse how and why degrees of change have occurred." Treat the diagnosis as something to test, not as settled fact.

## What Cambridge attributes to him

> "Media ownership will be one factor to consider, and there are examples of media outlets being directly influenced, or self-censoring, because of their owners, but more significant will be what **Slavoj Žižek** calls the media's **'Standard Operating Procedure'** – its reproduction of ideological 'truths' about which voices count for more than others, its reduction of complex conflicts to spectacle, and the general reinforcing of 'common sense'." (SoW p.25)

Three mechanisms, all usable as analytical categories:

1. reproduction of ideological "truths" about whose voice counts
2. reduction of complex conflicts to spectacle
3. general reinforcement of "common sense"

## Why Cambridge reaches for him here

The sentence structure is the argument. Ownership and self-censorship are the obvious answers to where media power lives, and Cambridge says something else is "more significant." The point is that power operates **without anyone issuing an instruction**, through the ordinary, unremarkable procedures by which stories get told.

For your essay, this is the move from a conspiratorial reading (owners dictate content) to a structural one (procedures reproduce common sense). The structural reading is far more defensible and much harder to argue against.

## Connection to spectacle

"Reduction of complex conflicts to spectacle" links directly to [[entities/guy-debord]] in the [[concepts/postmodern-media]] topic. It is the same concept, and it carries weight in two of the three debates. Cambridge does not flag the overlap. If you study Postmodern Media and Power together, you learn spectacle once and use it in both.

shared/bnds-ai-policy.md.body:
# BNDS AI Policy

School-wide, from the **A-Level Student Guide 2025-26 §VI** (pp.22–24), inside the Academic Honesty Policy. It applies to every course.

The policy does not simply permit or ban AI. It defines **six graded levels**, and each assignment declares which level applies.

## The six levels (Guide pp.23–24)

| Level | Name | What is allowed |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | Human-Only Work | You produce everything without AI help. No disclosure required |
| **1** | AI for Ideation | AI only to clarify the task, surface key terms, or map existing knowledge. Not to generate fresh concepts. You still do your own brainstorming. Typical: definitions, locating foundational references, checking feasibility, keyword lists for literature searches |
| **2** | AI for Structuring | Level 1, plus AI organizes material: outlines, templates, flowcharts. No full paragraphs, code blocks, calculations or images generated |
| **3** | AI for Refinement | Levels 1–2, plus AI edits or polishes a human draft: grammar, style, citation format, code linting. Keep a before-and-after or tracked-changes file showing what was accepted |
| **4** | AI Co-Creation | Levels 1–3, plus you and AI share the work. Substantial parts AI-generated or transformed, then shaped by you. Track who did what and cite the model and version |
| **5** | AI-Generated for Review | Levels 1–4, plus the whole piece is AI-produced, submitted only so humans can critique or annotate it. Label it "AI-generated". Grading focuses on your analysis, not the AI text |

> *"Always check assignment AI Level"* (Guide p.23). Some assignments ban AI entirely: the handbook names exams and personal reflections. Others actively encourage it.

## Attribution requirements (Guide p.22)

Whenever you use AI, you must:

1. **Cite the tool**, for example "Generated with assistance from [AI Tool Name]"
2. **Explain how you used it**, for example "Used for brainstorming but all analysis is my own"
3. **Cite the prompt** you used

Instructors may also require a disclaimer or a reflection on AI use.

## Permitted and prohibited (Guide p.22)

**Permitted:** assisting learning (brainstorming, clarifying concepts, summarizing readings, generating practice questions); enhancing productivity (grammar checks, citation formatting, organizing research); encouraging creativity (AI output as a *starting point* for original work, with attribution); developing digital literacy.

**Prohibited:** submitting AI-generated work as your own without citation or permission; using AI to replace independent analysis, original thought or personal reflection unless explicitly allowed; spreading unverified AI content. You "must verify AI-generated content for accuracy."

Misuse follows the Academic Honesty Policy: resubmission, grade penalties, or disciplinary action (Guide p.23).

## The Art & Design worked example (Guide p.24)

The handbook's only subject-specific illustration is for Art & Design:

- **Level 1:** AI summarizes Bauhaus color theory so you can plan palette experiments
- **Level 2:** AI offers a clean portfolio layout grid (page order, caption placeholders, margins) that you fill with original work
- **Level 3:** AI polishes the grammar of an artist statement and reorganizes paragraphs for flow
- **Level 4:** Midjourney, Stable Diffusion or similar generates an image that you then collage, annotate and contextualize, detailing the AI's role in the process

## ⚠ Where school policy meets exam-board policy

These are separate rules, and the exam board is the stricter authority on assessed work. You must satisfy both.

| | Position |
|---|---|
| **BNDS** | Six levels; Level 4 co-creation explicitly permitted, including generated images in Art & Design, with attribution |
| **Cambridge 9479 (2028-30)** | AI-generated images permitted **only** with the candidate's own role demonstrated and justified — see [[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design]] |
| **Cambridge 9607 (2027)** | *"Cambridge International has a policy on the use of generative AI by candidates in coursework. The inappropriate use of AI should be treated as a form of plagiarism"* (Syllabus 2027 p.30). The 2027 spec does not otherwise address AI; the 2028-30 spec permits it with documented prompts and justification |

**The practical rule for coursework:** BNDS Level 4 may be allowed for classroom tasks, but anything going to Cambridge as assessed coursework is governed by the syllabus for the exam year. Where they differ, the syllabus wins. The handbook's own attribution requirements (cite the tool, explain the use, cite the prompt) are exactly what the 2028-30 Art & Design spec asks for, so satisfying BNDS properly also satisfies Cambridge.

⚠ This is the **2025-26** edition of the handbook. The AI policy may change in later editions, so check the current edition before relying on the level definitions.

shared/bnds-assessment-framework.md.body:
# BNDS Assessment Framework

This is the school-wide grading scheme from the **BNDS A-Level Student Guide 2025-26**. Every course uses it. This page is the single reference, so course pages do not restate it.

This is the current edition. Its rules stay valid except where they touch syllabus specifics, which change per subject and per exam year. Treat the framework, curving, notice, retake, and AI rules as live. Check anything syllabus-shaped against your syllabus.

## Grade composition

| Category | Weight | Definition (per handbook) |
|---|---|---|
| **Attainment** | **50%** | Major, summative. Syllabus content only, sat under exam conditions, curved to CIE past-paper data. Should give a reliable Forecast Grade. Project completions and portfolio milestones count. |
| **Course Skills** | **20%** | Minor, formative. Skills and content relevant to the syllabus. Flexible format: quizzes, drafts, practice tasks, homework. |
| **Learning Behaviour** | **10%** | Glossary upkeep, blog punctuality, screening and feedback participation, case-study contributions, correcting work, submitting on time. |
| **End of Term Exam** | **20%** | Summative, on previously covered content, sat in the school exam window (S1 2026-27: Mon 2027-01-11 – Mon 2027-01-18). |

## Notice rule

You get **at least one week's notice** before an Attainment (Guide p.13). For non-attainment assessments you get **72 hours**.

## Standing rules

- **4–6 attainments per semester.** None fall in the first two teaching weeks.
- **Attainment dropping.** One grade may be dropped per semester, late in the semester, but only if the class has at least 6 attainment grades in MB, and you have missed none, have no plagiarism or cheating record, no unexcused absences, are always on time, and attend all required grade and programme meetings (Guide p.12). All four courses here run four attainments, so no student in any of them is eligible. This is a result of course design, not of your conduct.
- **One grade per week** is posted on MB for each subject (Guide p.12). Learning Behaviour postings fill weeks with no CS task or attainment.
- **Marking is returned within 5 working days** (Guide p.12).
- **Homework is capped at 30 minutes per subject per day** (Guide p.13). Break homework is about 3–4 hours per ten-day holiday.
- **Extensions** must be requested at least 24 hours before the deadline (Guide p.13).
- **Absence from an assessment** means you must contact the subject teacher 24 hours before the due time, and illness needs a doctor's note. ⚠ *"If no communication is made with the subject teacher in advance you may be given 0, even if this is due to illness"* (Guide p.8).
- **Late-work cutoff:** *"three weeks before the last school day of the semester"* (Guide p.13). For S1 this date falls inside the winter break, so the exact cutoff will be confirmed. See [[calendar|school academic calendar]].
- **Assessment content:** only what has been taught and practised. *"You should have seen similar content or formats beforehand,"* though "the context in which the knowledge or skills are applied may be novel" (Guide p.9).
- Every formative (CS) task next to an attainment is **direct practice for it**.
- **Seniors get a reduced assessment load** in the week before the 1 November and 1 December university deadlines (Guide p.13).

## Curving and grade boundaries

Attainments are **not recorded as raw marks** (Guide pp.11–12):

- They are curved against **CIE past-paper data**, "allowing for where students are on their learning trajectory."
- Curves are more generous in G10 and stricter in G11 and later in the year. This applies to [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design|PAL]], the G10 course here.
- Grades "reflect your learning trajectory, not what you would score on a CIE exam today."
- Past-paper grade thresholds are "the best starting point" for setting boundaries.
- **Moderation** is required where an attainment runs across multiple classes taught by different teachers. The Head of Department checks large between-class differences and may adjust curves or boundaries.
- *"You will always be told how grade boundaries and curves are decided."*

An attainment "should make a reliable **Forecast Grade**" (Guide p.11).

## Grade conversion (Guide p.11)

| CIE scale | A-Level grade | BNDS GPA |
|---|---|---|
| 90–100 | A* | 4.3 |
| 80–89 | A | 4.0 |
| 70–79 | B | 3.5 |
| 60–69 | C | 3.0 |
| 50–59 | D | 2.5 |
| 40–49 | E | 2.0 |
| below 40 | U | 0 |

**Failing is below 50%** (Guide p.15). A grade **at or below 70%** triggers the **Academic Concern Steps**: your advisor and the A-Level Director are informed, and support measures follow (Guide p.13).

## Retake policy (Guide §IV, pp.15–16)

You get one opportunity to retake a failed course, in the holiday after the semester, with 2–3 teacher meetings for support. The work is "just as challenging" and similar in quantity to the original. The grading policy is explained before finals and cannot be changed once agreed. You must sign an academic-honesty declaration. Plagiarism means immediate failure with no resubmission.

**A passed retake earns the equivalent of a D**, not the grade you actually achieved. A failed retake leaves the original grade standing. Under force majeure, more than 50% completion plus written, parent-signed evidence can pass. Without evidence, you fail.

Graduating seniors get only **two weeks** for a retake, because their Summer Holiday starts early.

## How the four courses satisfy it (S1 2026-27)

| Course | Attainments | CS layer | LB layer | End of Term |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design\|A Level Art & Design]] | A1–A4 (portfolio milestones) | CS1–CS10 | Learning Behaviour | the Final: a teacher-marked assessment of the portfolio so far against Cambridge criteria |
| [[classes/media-studies/media-studies\|Media Studies]] | A1–A4 | CS1–CS9 + HW1–2 | LB1–LB7 | full Component 2 paper in the exam window |
| [[classes/art-appreciation/art-appreciation\|Art Appreciation]] | A1–A4 | CS1–CS5 | LB1–LB9 | retrospective sat in class Tue 2027-01-05, submitted online |
| [[classes/pre-a-level-art-design/pre-a-level-art-design\|Pre A Level]] | A1–A4 | CS1–CS4 + HW1 | weekly sketchbook posting | semester portfolio on 2027-01-06 (to be confirmed in class) |

**Codes:** the wiki calls attainments **A1–A4** in every course. Your course register may use different codes, such as MA1–MA4 or M1–M4. These are the same assessments.

classes/a-level-art-design/9479-departme.body:
# 9479 Department Handbook

This is the Art & Design handbook you are given for the 9479 course. It runs to 208 pages and was written and designed by Doğan Arslanoğlu.

It covers the visual elements, the principles of design, the three components, the assessment objectives with checklists, the four disciplines, theme selection, artist studies, the Personal Study, and about 87 pages of portfolio samples.

## The handbook uses old-syllabus numbers

> [!important] Use the syllabus numbers, not the handbook's
> The handbook was written for an older version of the 9479 specification. Many of its numbers are out of date. Do not act on the numbers below. Use the current 2028-30 syllabus instead.

| Feature | Handbook says | Current syllabus |
|---|---|---|
| C1 name | "Component 1: Coursework" | Component 1: Portfolio (coursework is still an OK informal name) |
| C1 mark | single mark out of 100 | 60/60/75-mark grids |
| C2 supervised test | 15 hours | use the current syllabus |
| C2 submission | three sheets of A2, photographed and mounted | all-digital submission |
| C1 submission | five sheets of A2 | use the current syllabus |
| C3 submission | eight sheets of A2 | use the current syllabus |
| C3 written analysis | 1000–1500 words | 2000–2500 words ← use this |
| C3 mark | out of 100, "weighted to 200" | use the current syllabus |
| AOs | AO1 Record, AO2 Explore, AO3 Develop, AO4 Present | new per-component splits |

Every hard number you could act on, such as sheet counts, hours, word counts and mark totals, comes from the previous specification. The [[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design|course page]] also warns you never to take numbers from the older support documents. This handbook is one of them. Its prose, structure and teaching content are fine. It is the numbers that are wrong.

## Where the handbook contradicts itself

1. **Personal Study word count.** Pages 36 and 104 say 1000–1500 words. Pages 114–115 say an essay of 2000–3000 words that "should not exceed 3000 words." Use the current syllabus figure: 2000–2500 words. Pages 114–118 were adapted from a different exam board and do not describe this course, so ignore their rules, including the claim on p.111 that a missing bibliography means you "would automatically fail the whole unit."

2. **Tint.** Page 18 has it right: **tone** means adding darker shades, and **tint** means adding white. The p.19 glossary wrongly says "tint, another word for shade." Use the page 18 definitions.

3. **Assessment Objective names.** The handbook uses three different names for the assessment objectives. Use the set on page 39: **Record**, **Explore**, **Develop**, **Present**.

## What is in it

### Visual Elements (pp.7–23)

Six elements, each with a definition and a full-page plate: **Line** (Fred Sandback), **Shape** (Escher, *Sky and Water II*), **Space** (Doug Wheeler), **Tone** (Wolfgang Mattheuer), **Color** (pp.18–21, with a CMYK note and six example plates), **Texture**.

Form is not covered in this chapter. The fullest vocabulary for the elements is at p.81, in the Artist Studies chapter, which adds Form and gives adjective banks for all six. For example, Texture: "flat, raised, smooth, rough, coarse, shiny, glossy, reflective, scratched, matt, satin, frosted, visible, smooth, blended, impasto, washes, glazes, stippled, splattered, bold, timid, lively, layered."

### Principles of Design (pp.24–30)

- **p.25 "How to Read Images"**: the four-stage method, **Description**, **Formal Analysis**, **Interpretation**, **Judgement**, over a grid of 15 paired opposites for visual communication: balanced/unstable, gestural/technical, sharp/diffuse, symmetry/asymmetry, active/still, distorted/realistic, solitary/juxtaposed, flatness/depth, transparent/opaque, regular/irregular, subtle/amplified, vivid/neutral, unified/fragmented, ordered/loose, light/dark.
- **p.26 "17 Key Principles of Design"**: Alignment, Hierarchy, Contrast, Repetition, Proximity, Balance, Color, Space, Emphasis, Proportion, Rhythm, Pattern, Movement, Variety, Unity, Lines, Shapes.
- **pp.27–30**: worked demonstrations of eight: Emphasis (focal point), Hierarchy, Scale/Proportion (size, ratio, divisions), Contrast (in shape, color, scale, layout), Repetition, Unity & Variety, Balance (symmetrical, asymmetrical).

### The four disciplines (pp.48–57)

**Fine Art** (painting, drawing, sculpture, photography, printmaking, mixed media, assemblage) · **Graphic Communication** (illustration, printmaking, packaging, branding, advertising, signage, typography) · **Three-Dimensional Design** (sculpture, ceramics, product, architecture, interior, environmental, set design, jewellery) · **Textiles and Fashion** (fashion design/illustration, costume, constructed textiles, screen printing, batik, digital-printed textiles, surface pattern).

You may focus on one discipline or combine several. Two distinctions:

- **Fine Art** responds to "a theme" only. The other three respond to "a theme or brief."
- **Three-Dimensional Design** also requires you to consider "the setting in which the final outcome will be situated, e.g. interior/exterior, urban/rural" (p.55).

### Themes (pp.66–72)

Guidance on choosing a theme. It is not a list of past Cambridge themes; the handbook does not contain one. It gives nine qualities of an appropriate theme (personal relevance, breadth and depth, creativity and originality, flexibility, researchability, visual and conceptual interest, educational value, relevance to the assessment objectives, engagement with broader issues), then a seven-step selection guide, then the assignment: complete a theme selection form for at least four possible themes, each with related artists and possible artworks, then choose one and justify it. Submit it by the end of the week. This is Component 1 work.

### Assessment Objectives (pp.38–47)

The four AOs are on p.39 with bullet guidance, then a two-page overview and checklist for each. The checklists are usable: AO1's runs seven questions, from "collected images to show your inspiration and stimuli?" to "clearly linked all of your work to your starting point?"

Take the assessment objectives and all rubrics from the 2028-30 syllabus, not from this handbook. The handbook's AO checklists (pp.41–47) are still useful as scaffolding, as long as the objectives they hang from come from the syllabus.

### Personal Study (pp.104–118)

Three study types (p.105), which you can combine: **Technical** (media, surfaces, tools, techniques), **Stylistic** (signs, symbols, metaphor, meaning, figurative and formal elements), **Contextual** (art and society, social/historical/cultural contexts, theories of art).

Keep the integration rule (p.105) in mind: "the study will form the starting point of your practical coursework. The two must link together and inform each other i.e. they are not separate elements but dependent on each other. Your success depends on this point."

Use 2000–2500 words for this study, and ignore the word counts and rules on pp.114–118.

### Portfolio samples (pp.119–205)

About 87 pages of sample work, captioned "Final Outcome" or "SAMPLE 1 / Component 1."

## Practical notes

- The AI examples in [[shared/bnds-ai-policy|the school AI policy]] are Art & Design examples. Its attribution requirements match what the 2028-30 syllabus asks for on AI-generated images.
