- Build and resolve composition 2 with **equal effort**, to the same standard as composition 1.
- Explain why a fair comparison needs two finished compositions, not one finished and one sketched.
- Draft your research paper sections as **integrated writing**, real prose built from your own material and tied to the visual work.

# 9479 S2 Lesson 12: Critique and Targeted Tests

[[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design|A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/unit-plans/9479-s2-unit-4-development|Unit 4]] · Lesson 12 of 15 · ← [[classes/a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/9479-s2-lesson-11-composition-2-and-paper-drafts|Lesson 11]] | [[classes/a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/9479-s2-lesson-13-evaluation-draft-1-and-a3|Lesson 13]] →

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sessions | 5 days (S13) |
| Dates | Mon 2027-05-17 → Fri 2027-05-21 |
| AO focus | AO3 Develop |
| Deliverable | Both compositions critiqued against the intention; the critique acted on; targeted tests on what is unresolved; the final direction chosen with the rejection written out |
| Graded | **CS8** (targeted tests + critique response) Fri 2027-05-21 — sketchbook. **A3** (development + paper draft 1, AO3) sits Fri 2027-05-28 |
| Homework | ≤30 min: write evaluation notes toward A3 and consolidate the paper draft, ahead of [[classes/a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/9479-s2-lesson-13-evaluation-draft-1-and-a3\|Lesson 13]] |

## Overview

This week you decide which of your two resolved compositions becomes the mid-point piece, and why. You critique both against your intention, act on what you hear, run targeted tests on what is still unresolved, and choose the final direction. You produce **CS8**, the targeted tests plus your critique response, due Fri 2027-05-21 in your sketchbook. The written rejection of the composition you drop is part of this work. It feeds A3, the development milestone and paper draft 1, which you sit Fri 2027-05-28.

## The ideas

### Critique against the intention

A **structured critique** judges each composition against your stated intention, not against the effort you put in. The question is whether each piece does what the investigation set out to do. Hours spent do not count. Fit to intention does.

A critique only counts when you act on it. A critique you nod at and ignore is worthless. The mark is in the **critique response**: you change something in the work because of what the critique told you.

### Targeted tests

**Targeted tests** are surgical tests on named problems. You test only what is still unresolved, the specific passages the critique flagged. This is not a fresh round of exploration. You read the test results back into your decision and note what they settle.

### Choosing is development

Choosing the final direction is development in its own right. You pick which composition carries into the mid-point piece, and you **write the rejection**: why not the other one. A choice you can justify earns AO3. A choice by default does not. A reasoned "not this one" earns AO3 as much as the piece you keep.

- **Thu 05-20.** Finish the tests and read the results into your decision.
- **Fri 05-21.** Choose which composition carries into the mid-point piece and write out the rejection. Submit **CS8**, the targeted tests and your critique response. Homework (≤30 min): write evaluation notes toward A3 and consolidate the paper draft, ahead of Lesson 13.

- Act on a critique by changing the work in response to it.
- Run targeted tests on only what is still unresolved.
- Choose the final direction and write out the rejection as AO3 development.

## Overview

This week you narrow and deepen. In the studio you carry two candidate compositions forward and develop both to the same standard, so your later choice is fair. Alongside the studio, you reopen the research paper as draft 2: structure first, then argument, with your summer reading woven in. ## The ideas

### Two candidates carried forward

**Carrying two candidates forward** means you develop two compositions, not one. Keep two, because a single idea cannot be compared. With only one, there is nothing to judge it against. Develop both to the same standard so neither wins by neglect of the other. When you finally choose, write down the rejection: record which candidate you drop and why. Because both reach a judgeable standard, the comparison in the Lesson 04 critique stays honest.

### Research paper draft 2

**Research paper draft 2** is built structure first. Set out the sections and decide what each one must prove before you write the prose. Argument comes before prose.

Your summer reading appears **woven into the argument, not as summary**. Use each source as evidence inside your argument. Do not add a book report at the back.

The research paper has no coursework sitting of its own. Its written thread runs through CS3 here and continues in the Unit 5 final-text sessions toward A3.

- **Thu 09-16.** Research paper draft 2 opens. Structure first: the sections and what each must prove. Argument before prose.
- **Fri 09-17.** Draft 2 sections continue, with the summer reading woven into the argument. CS3 marks the sections drafted. Homework (≤30 min): outline the next draft-2 section, the argument, not the prose.

## Review

- Explain why you carry two candidates forward and why a single idea cannot be compared.
- Develop two candidate compositions to the same standard.
- Write down the rejection when you choose one candidate.

- Weave your summer reading into the argument as evidence, not as summary.

## Overview

This lesson closes the second pass at development and brings you to your first graded milestone of the semester. Monday to Wednesday, you finish your evaluation and close the named gaps in your work, then check your pages honestly against the AO3 band descriptors. On Thursday you sit **A1**, the development milestone, marked against AO3. On Friday you turn the marker's response into three specific actions for Unit 5. ## The ideas

### The self-check against AO3

The **self-check against the AO3 band descriptors** means applying the AO3 band descriptors honestly to your own pages and asking where your work actually sits. Use it to find the specific gaps in your development, then close those named gaps. This is targeted repair, not a general polish.

### A1: the development milestone

**A1** is the **development milestone**. You submit your outcome-candidate compositions, targeted tests, evaluation, Stage 6 page, and **research paper draft 2**. It is marked against AO3.

AO3 reads development as **tested, rejected, decided**: it wants to see what you tried, what you set aside, and what you chose. Your submission should show that trail, not just a finished-looking result.

A1 feeds your mid-term grade (around Thu 2027-10-28) at the two-week minimum. A2 next week informs your comments, not the grade. The milestone is a gate, not a pause: Unit 5 opens straight into building your final outcomes.

You sit A1 on Thursday. This keeps it clear of Fridays, which can collide with Foreign Culture Days. If a collision does land, the feedback slips, never the assessment.

## The ideas

### Sequencing so it reads to a stranger

**Sequencing** is the order in which your investigation is read: where it starts, where it turns, and where it lands. The work must **read in order without you in the room**. Sequence is an AO4 mark, not a formality. If a stranger stalls on a page, the sequence has a gap to fix.

### Documentation verified page by page

**Documentation** is the record of your work: every page photographed, labeled, and legible. Verify it now so the record survives without you. Checking it page by page this week means the submission QC later is a check, not a scramble.

### Integrating the bibliography

The **bibliography** is your list of sources. Integrate it into the body of the work, where each source did its work, not parked at the back. A detached bibliography cost AO1 marks in the 90/100 C3 exemplar. Where the sequence exposes a gap, repair it before the critique.

This week is the dress rehearsal for your submission and for any interview. You present and defend your whole investigation, the process, the research, and the outcomes, in a viva-style critique. ## Overview

This lesson closes exploration and carries it into development. You study a second artist and answer them in your own work. You make a **bridge piece** that moves your study into development, and you run a **scale trial** at the supervised-test dimensions to expose problems now. You lay out exploration pages that reason rather than display swatches. On Tue 03-21 you sit **CS5**, which checks your artist pages and bridge piece. ## The ideas

### A different angle on the same question

Artist 2 gives you **a different angle on the same question**. You use a second artist to look at the same question from a new direction, not to repeat the first artist. Citation without response earns nothing. **The response is the evidence**: for both artists, you must answer them in your work, not just cite them. ### The bridge piece

The **bridge piece** is the hinge from exploration into development. It takes what you found in study and moves it into development work. It is what CS5 checks alongside your artist pages.

### The scale trial

The **scale trial** is a trial run at the exact dimensions the supervised test will use. You work at the test scale on purpose. This surfaces problems now, while you still have time to fix them, rather than in the test room. What breaks in the trial is what you learn from.

### Exploration pages that reason

Your exploration pages should reason, not display swatches. Show why you chose these media for this question. A swatch chart shows what you tried; a page that reasons shows why you tried it.

# Oxbridge W03: Can Measurement Reach the Thing Itself?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2: The Gap]] · Week 3 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|← W02]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is the gap between us and the world a problem with our instruments, or a condition of being an observer at all? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | **None.** "This session runs entirely on examples students already possess" |
| Carried out | A tree falls in a forest with no one there. Does it make a sound? |

## Overview

This lesson asks whether the distance between you and the world comes from your instruments or from being an observer at all. It uses examples you already have, so there is no reading. You build the argument yourself, then commit to a position: is the gap a fact about instruments, or a fact about reality? You leave with one question to answer for next week. Your position and your answer both feed [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]], which opens by polling them.

## The ideas

### Measurement and disturbance

**The gap** ([[concepts/the-gap]]) is the distance between an observer and the world being observed. The lesson asks what causes it: your tools, or the act of observing.

**Measurement disturbance** is the way an instrument changes the thing it measures. A thermometer placed in a glass of water changes the temperature of the water. In the double slit experiment, observing which slit a particle passes through changes the result.

You might answer that this is trivial: you calculate the disturbance and subtract it. But to calculate it you need another measurement, which also disturbs. This is a **regress**: the correction never terminates, because each correcting measurement needs correcting too.

You might answer that disturbance only matters at very small scales. Then the question is whether the gap is a fact about reality or only a fact about **magnitude**. And you might answer that better instruments will one day close the gap. That is the position the whole lesson tests.

### The gap in language

Now move the same problem into language. You say the water is cold. I say it is cool. Which of us is wrong? Some words cannot be translated between languages. That may mean the thing they name is harder to reach, not that it does not exist. So which gap is wider: between the word "cold" and the actual temperature, or between the thermometer reading and the actual temperature?

Language is not trying to be precise in the way a measurement is, so it is not failing when it is vague. That can make language better suited to some things than measurement. And **numbers are also a language**: a measurement is a representation too.

The point both examples reach: both language and measurement involve a gap. Science narrows the gap. Nothing closes it. Narrowing is not the same as arriving, and you cannot describe a state with no gap without using a representation.

### From instruments to reality

The final move is to choose: is the gap a fact about our instruments, or a fact about reality? Saying "about reality" is already a step into the **ontological turn** ([[concepts/the-ontological-turn]]), the shift from asking how we know the world to asking what the world is.

## Day by day

- **This week.** In one 45-minute session you work from the thermometer and double slit examples to the language examples, then commit to a position on whether the gap is about instruments or about reality. Homework: bring an answer to the closing question, "A tree falls in a forest with no one there. Does it make a sound?" [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] opens by polling it.

## Review

Check you can:

- Build an argument from examples you already have, without leaning on a reading.
- Explain **measurement disturbance** using the thermometer and the double slit experiment.
- Explain why correcting for a disturbance leads to a **regress** that does not terminate.
- Compare the gap in language with the gap in measurement, and say why science narrows the gap but nothing closes it.
- Say whether the gap is an instrument problem or a condition of observing, and name what stepping toward "reality" has to do with the **ontological turn**.
- Name what an instrument changes by measuring.

# Oxbridge W02: Do Images Represent Reality or Produce It?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1: The Image]] · Week 2 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|← W01]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is the quality of an image a technical fact or a political one? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | [[entities/hito-steyerl\|Steyerl]], "In Defense of the Poor Image", e-flux |
| Prepared | The single sentence in Steyerl students found **most arguable**, ready to say which and why |
| Bring | Two versions of one image: high resolution, and badly compressed / screen-recorded / re-uploaded |
| Carried out | A thermometer measures temperature. Does it show you the temperature, or change it? |

## Overview

This lesson asks whether the quality of an image is a technical fact or a political one. You read Steyerl's "In Defense of the Poor Image" and work from two versions of one image, a sharp one and a degraded one, to test what "more real" means. What you produce is a single committed sentence, with one reason, on whether images show us the world or make the world showable. The closing question about a thermometer hands you straight into [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]].

## The ideas

### The poor image

The **poor image** is Hito Steyerl's term for a low-resolution image that has been copied, compressed, screenshotted, and re-uploaded many times. It is blurry and cheap because it has traveled. The high-resolution image is clean because it was kept and controlled. So resolution is not only physics. It is a marker of value, of institutional access, and of who is permitted to circulate an image. As Steyerl puts it: the poor image is degraded because it moved; the high-resolution image is pristine because it was kept.

You can measure compression, and that stays true. The harder point is why those measurable properties line up so neatly with ownership and access. If an image loses quality every time it is shared, then high quality also tells you how little an image was shared.

Steyerl argues the poor image carries defiance and appropriation as well as conformism and exploitation. It can be both at once. Be careful with the easy version of this: a poor image may be cheaper to distribute without being more democratic. Those are not the same claim.

The idea reaches past digital files. It also covers reproduction in general: prints, copies, textbook plates, museum lighting. A screenshot of a painting raises the same question as a compressed photograph.

### Representing reality or producing it

The second idea is a distinction to hold without collapsing. An image can **represent** an event, showing something that happened. Or it can **produce** the event as a public thing, making it showable and shared in the first place. If an event is never photographed, in what sense did it happen publicly? The task is to keep both possibilities open rather than reduce one to the other.

### Back to neutral perception

W01 asked whether perception can be trained toward neutrality. Now push it: if a neutral image were possible, what would it look like, and who could afford it? Image quality has a cost, so neutrality has a price. This is why [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]] matters here.

As a closing aside, a thermometer measures temperature but may also change it. Hold that question. It looks like a different subject in W03. It is not.

## Day by day

- **This session (45 minutes).** Both versions of one image go up, and you write in silence on which is "more real". You work through what "more real" means, then Steyerl's reversal that resolution marks access and circulation, then the distinction between representing an event and producing it as public. You close by committing to one sentence, with one reason, on whether images show the world or make it showable. Before class, read Steyerl, pick the sentence you find most arguable, and bring your two versions of one image.

## Review

Check you can:

- Argue whether the quality of an image is a technical fact or a political one.
- Use Steyerl's **poor image** to make a case an opponent has to answer.
- Explain why resolution marks value, institutional access, and circulation, not only physics.
- Hold the distinction between **representing** reality and **producing** it without collapsing one into the other.

## Links

[[entities/hito-steyerl]] · [[concepts/the-poor-image]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]]

# Oxbridge Assessment — none

## Why the page exists at all

This course is not graded. There is no register and no marks. If you came here from one of the other four courses looking for one, this is the answer.

## What replaces marking

Nothing is measured. But the sessions still hold a standard for what a good contribution looks like, and it is named aloud in the room:

1. **Commitment.** Do you take a position rather than survey positions?
2. **Pressure.** Do you name the strongest objection to your own case?
3. **Precision.** Is the claim narrow enough to be wrong?
4. **Movement.** Does the argument arrive somewhere it did not start?

Ungraded, these four do their best work as **spoken feedback in the commit movement**. "That is a survey, not a position" is a sentence you can act on right away, which a grade is not. They map onto the three interview moves: commitment is take a position quickly, pressure is absorb the push, and movement is what the mock debrief measures. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]].

## The claim that survives without the essays

The course tests its central claim in speaking, not writing: fourteen commit movements, in which neutrality is the one banned position.

## Where the hedging repair went

The writing existed to fix one failure mode: **hedging**. That repair now lives in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]], a pure pressure workshop with paired push practice and a four-line spine built in the room, no essay attached. It also runs in every session's commit movement.

The old writing prompts are now discussion questions in [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank|the question bank]].

# Oxbridge W01: Is Perception Ever Neutral?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1: The Image]] · Week 1 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is seeing something we do, or something that happens to us? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | [[entities/john-berger\|Berger]], *Ways of Seeing*, ch. 1, first six pages (BBC episode as second entry point) |
| Bring | **One image no student will recognize**, plus one uncomfortable fact about it, withheld |
| Carried out | If seeing is never neutral, what is a photograph evidence of? |

## Overview

This lesson asks whether perception is ever neutral. You look at an image you do not recognize, then separate what you see from what you know and what you assume. Later you learn a fact about the image and look again. By the end you take a side in one sentence: is perception ever neutral? That single-sentence position is what you produce, and it feeds into Week 2, which asks whether images represent reality or produce it. You also carry out one open question: if seeing is never neutral, what is a photograph evidence of?

## The ideas

### Seeing, knowing, assuming

An image can be described in three different ways. What you **see** is what is in front of you. What you **know** is the fact or context you bring to it. What you **assume** is what you fill in without checking. When two people look at the same image and report different things, the difference is rarely eyesight. It usually comes from what each person already knows or expects. This is why "we noticed different parts" needs a further question: why those parts.

### Berger's claim

**Berger's claim**, from *Ways of Seeing*, is that the way we see things is affected by what we know or what we believe. Berger also holds that we never look at one thing alone: we look at the relation between things and ourselves. Test this on a photograph of a stranger. When you learn the title, date, context, and one uncomfortable fact about an image, the picture does not change, but your experience of it does. That raises the hard question: if the picture is the thing that produces an experience, and the experience changed, in what sense is it the same picture? And can you unlearn something in order to see freshly?

### Two positions on neutrality

There are two positions to expect when you take a side.

The **trained eye** position says perception is shaped, but training can make it better, more accurate, more neutral. The challenge to it: better according to what standard?

The **no exit** position says there is no neutral place to be trained toward. The challenge to it: if no view is better than another, why study anything?

## Day by day

- **Week 1 session (45 minutes).** Read Berger's first six pages before class, or use the BBC episode as a second way in. In class you view an unfamiliar image in silence, then write what you see, what you know, and whether knowing changed the seeing. You compare descriptions, learn the fact about the image, look again, and finish by stating in one sentence whether perception is ever neutral. Your answer is kept, because Week 2 builds on it.

## Review

Check you can:

- Separate what you **see** from what you **know** from what you **assume** on an unfamiliar image.
- Explain why seeing might be something that happens to you rather than something you do.
- State **Berger's claim**: the way we see things is affected by what we know or what we believe.
- Take a side on whether perception is ever neutral, and say what the **trained eye** and **no exit** positions each claim.
- Carry out the question: if seeing is never neutral, what is a photograph evidence of?

# Oxbridge W04: Is There a Reality Behind Appearances?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2: The Gap]] · Week 4 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|← W03]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Last week asked how well we can know things. This week asks what kind of things there are to know |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | [[entities/plato\|Plato]], Allegory of the Cave, *Republic* VII — clean modern translation, ≈ two pages |
| Bring | A Renaissance perspective construction |
| Carried out | Is the gap a loss, a liberation, or just the condition? **Bring a case** |

## Overview

Last week you asked how well we can know things. This week you ask what kinds of things there are to know. You read Plato's Allegory of the Cave and look at a Renaissance perspective construction to test whether there is a reality behind appearances. What you produce is a case to bring to Week 5, where the question becomes whether the gap is a loss, a liberation, or just the condition. Bring a case, not a position.

## The ideas

### From knowing to being

**Epistemology** asks how well we know things. **Ontology** asks what kinds of things there are. Moving from the first question to the second is the **ontological turn** [[concepts/the-ontological-turn]].

Take the question: a tree falls in a forest with no one there, does it make a sound? One answer: the vibration happens, but the sound does not, because sound requires a hearer. That is an ontological position, a claim about what exists. Another answer: it makes a sound, because physics does not need an audience. A third: it depends what you mean by "sound."

That third answer is the point. "Sound" has two definitions here, the vibration in the air and the heard experience. So the disagreement may be an argument about a word, not an argument about the world. Ask which definition is doing more work, and how you would tell the two apart.

### Plato's cave

In [[entities/plato]]'s **Allegory of the Cave** from *Republic* VII, prisoners see shadows on a wall and mistake them for real things. Ask whether our situation is the same as theirs or different. Knowing you might be in a cave may change your feelings about it, but ask whether it changes your relationship to it.

Consider the perfect circle. You have never seen a perfect circle, only roughly circular things, yet you know what a perfect circle is. Where does that knowledge come from? An empiricist answer says you idealize, you average the imperfect ones. The problem: how do you average toward a perfection you have never encountered?

The prisoner who leaves the cave cannot go back. He may be worse off, not better. This is Plato's own worry, so take it seriously.

### Linear perspective

**Linear perspective** [[concepts/linear-perspective]] is a Renaissance method that does not show the world, it shows the world from a point. When a perspective becomes invisible as a perspective, you think you are looking at the world itself, not at one view of it. Ask whether perspective is a discovery about vision or an invention that trained vision. (As an aside, this links to Steyerl's argument from Week 2.)

### Reality behind appearances

The central question: is there a reality behind appearances, and if there is, what would count as evidence of it? The second half is the trap. Any evidence arrives as an appearance.

## Review

Check you can:

- State Plato's Allegory of the Cave precisely enough to argue against it.
- Distinguish an epistemological question about how well we know things from an ontological question about what kinds of things there are.
- Explain what the ontological turn is.
- Explain how linear perspective shows the world from a point, not the world itself.
- Bring a case, not a position, to Week 5.

# Oxbridge W07: Argument Workshop

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3: Frameworks and History]] · Week 7 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|← W06]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Purpose | The midpoint. No new material — six weeks of discussion put under interview pressure |
| Duration | 45 minutes, **template bent**: the three movements become *what an argument is* / *live pressure* / *build the spine* |
| Reading | none |
| Carried out | Every framework so far turned out to hide its edges. Is there anything that does not? |

## Overview

This lesson is the midpoint of the course. It brings no new material. Instead, you put six weeks of discussion under interview pressure. You learn what an argument is, hold a position under live questioning, and build the spine of an argument. You produce four lines on paper: a scaffold for speaking that stays with you and is not collected. Nothing here is written for submission ([[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]). The skills feed your [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]].

## The ideas

### What an argument is

**Argument.** An argument is not a survey of views. It is a committed act of reasoning. A claim narrow enough to be wrong is worth more than a claim broad enough to be safe. Compare two paragraphs on the same topic. One surveys three views and concludes that the truth lies somewhere in between. The other takes a narrow position and names the case that would defeat it. The narrow one could be wrong, and that is exactly why it is worth defending and worth listening to.

### Three moves of pressure

When you push a position, use only three moves:

- **The consequence.** If that is true, then what follows?
- **The hard case.** An example the claim does not cover.
- **The definition.** A word is doing all the work, so define it.

Afterward, ask yourself one question: at which push did you stop thinking and start defending? This is the same question the mock interview debrief asks. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]].

### The spine of an argument

The **spine** is four lines: your claim in one sentence, the reason, the strongest objection, and why the claim survives or how it must narrow. This is also the shape of a good interview answer under pressure: claim, reason, the objection you volunteer before it is put to you, and what you concede. If you can produce it on paper in ten minutes, you can produce it aloud in ninety seconds.

## Day by day

- **This session (45 minutes).** First, write the strongest objection to something you argued in the last six weeks, objecting to yourself, not to a classmate. Then judge the two paragraphs on the board and decide which is worth defending. In pairs, push a partner's position three times using the consequence, the hard case, and the definition, then swap and debrief. Finally, build your four-line spine on paper and read some aloud for the group to attack. No reading is set and nothing is collected.

## Assessment

None. This lesson is discussion only. See [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|Assessment — none]].

## Review

Check you can:

- Say what an argument is, and how it differs from an opinion or a reaction.
- Explain why a claim narrow enough to be wrong beats a claim broad enough to be safe.
- Push a position with the consequence, the hard case, and the definition.
- Hold a position under live pressure without collapsing or digging in.
- Build the spine of an argument in four lines: claim, reason, objection, and how it survives or narrows.

# Oxbridge W06: Does Reality Have a History?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3: Frameworks and History]] · Week 6 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|← W05]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Things considered real in the past are now considered false. Does this mean we were wrong then, or that reality itself changed? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | none |
| Bring | **Three artifacts** — Mercator beside Gall-Peters; an early modern map showing Taprobana; a one-paragraph account of Barry Marshall, 1984 |
| Carried out | The Merleau-Ponty quotation: the body is our general medium for having a world. If that is true, what happens when the medium is wrong? |

## Overview

This lesson asks whether reality can have a history. You look at beliefs people once held as real and now call false, and you decide whether we were simply wrong then or whether the framework itself changed. You use maps and one medical case to test the difference. You leave with one claim of your own: a framework you use every day that claims not to be one. That claim is what you defend in W07.

## The ideas

### Superseded beliefs

People used to be certain about things we now consider false. These beliefs split into two kinds. Some were **factually wrong**: the belief got the world wrong. In others the **category or definition** itself has shifted, so the belief was never quite a fact. The line between the two is hard to draw. The people who held these beliefs were not stupid; they reasoned well from a different starting point.

**Barry Marshall**, 1984, is the test case. The claim "they just did not have the data" does not hold here: the data was available, but the framework rejected it. A framework does something to data it cannot accept.

### Maps as frameworks

**Mercator** beside **Gall-Peters** shows two map projections of the same world. Mercator is not a lie; it is useful for navigation. That is the point: a **framework** is a set of chosen sacrifices. Some of those sacrifices are visible to the user, and some are not. Every map distorts, but distortions do not all carry the same consequences.

**Taprobana** is an island that appeared on maps for centuries. Its name referred unstably to Sri Lanka, to Sumatra, and to nowhere. Sailors still sailed toward it. Ask what it would take to answer whether Taprobana was real.

In a **video game map**, the edge of the map is disguised as a feature of the world. The mountain is too high. The road is closed. The edge is disguised instead of shown as a plain wall because a visible wall reminds you that you are inside something.

### Frameworks that hide themselves

**Naturalization** is the move by which a framework hides its limits by making them look like the world. A biased history book is not the real problem. The problem is the history that claims not to be biased.

[[entities/roland-barthes|Barthes]] puts it this way: the author who disappears behind the text is the most ideological author of all. The same holds for any framework that presents itself as no framework at all.

The closing image is from Merleau-Ponty: the body is our general medium for having a world. If that is true, what happens when the medium is wrong?

## Day by day

- **This week.** One 45-minute session, no reading. You sort superseded beliefs into factually wrong versus category shifted, test frameworks against the two map projections, Taprobana, and the Barry Marshall case, and name one framework you use every day that claims not to be one. That claim is the one you defend in W07.

## Review

Check you can:

- Say whether a superseded belief means we were wrong then or that reality itself changed.
- Tell a factually wrong belief apart from one where the category or definition has shifted.
- Use a historical example, such as Barry Marshall or Taprobana, precisely rather than as illustration.
- Explain how a framework works as a set of chosen sacrifices, using Mercator and Gall-Peters.
- Explain naturalization: how a framework hides its limits by making them look like the world.
- Hold a position on whether reality is the kind of thing that can have a history.

## Links

[[entities/roland-barthes]] · [[concepts/naturalization]] · [[concepts/framework]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]]

# Oxbridge W11: Whose Agreement Makes a Thing Real?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6: Collective Reality]] · Week 11 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|← W10]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Some things are real whether or not anyone agrees. Some things are real only because everyone agrees. Where is the line, and who draws it? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | none |
| Bring | The ten-item list, on the board |
| Carried out | Can we still share one world, or only private ones? |

## Overview

This lesson asks where the line falls between what is real no matter what anyone thinks and what is real only because people agree. You sort ten items into those two kinds, defend a hard case on one side of the line, and then name one thing you hold to be real that most people around you do not. Your job is to say who does the agreeing and what would make a thing count. This sets up whether we can still share one world (W12) and the idea that realness may rest on power (W13).

## The ideas

### Two kinds of real

Take ten items: gravity, money, a nation, Tuesday, a species, a debt, a disease, a genre, a race, a language. Some are real **regardless of agreement**. Gravity holds whether or not anyone agrees. Some are real **only because of agreement**. Tuesday is one: it exists because we all keep the same week.

A quick objection is that if a thing depends on agreement it is not really real. Test it: try to spend a currency nobody agrees on. Then ask which has more effect on your life this week, gravity or money. Money depends on agreement and still runs your week. So agreement-dependent things are real too, just in a different way. The task is to name that difference precisely, using the [[concepts/framework]].

### The hard cases

- **A species.** Is the boundary in nature, or in the way we classify?
- **A disease.** Was it there before it was named? Was addiction a disease in 1850?
- **A race.** This is the hardest item, because the sorting starts to break down.

### Who does the agreeing

Agreement raises a political question: does it need **everyone**, or **enough people**, or **the right people**? Some things are real by agreement and then stop being real; it is worth naming one and describing what its ending looked like.

If a hundred people agree and one refuses, is the one **wrong**, or simply **outside**? Whose disagreement counts as disagreement, and whose counts as error? Two easy answers do not hold. "Majority rules" fails when a persecuted minority is outnumbered but not wrong about its own status. "Experts decide" only pushes the question back: who certifies the experts, and by what agreement?

### From agreement to power

One answer is that this is not really agreement at all, it is **power**: the thing counts as real because those with power make it count. This is the entry to the idea that reality can be made, not only found, which the [[concepts/the-ontological-turn]] names. W13 takes it up.

### The mechanism of realness

The final move is to name one thing you believe is real that most people around you do not, and to say what would make it count. This forces you to describe the **mechanism of realness**, how a thing comes to be real, rather than just asserting that some instance is real.

## Day by day

- **This week (45 minutes).** You sort the ten items into two columns, then work through the hard cases (species, disease, race). You take the political turn (everyone, enough people, or the right people; the lone refuser; whose disagreement counts), reach the idea that realness may rest on power, and close by naming one thing you hold real that others do not and what would make it count. No reading is set.

## Review

Check you can:

- Draw the line between what is real regardless of agreement and what is real only because of agreement.
- Say who does the agreeing in a case like money, borders, or weekends.
- Defend where you place a hard case, such as a species, a disease, or a race.
- Name the difference between agreement-dependent reality and agreement-independent reality precisely.
- Explain why "majority rules" and "experts decide" do not settle whose disagreement counts.
- State what **power** adds to the account of realness.
- Describe the mechanism of realness for one thing you hold real that others do not.

# Oxbridge W08: Can the Body Be Trusted?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4: The Body and the Machine]] · Week 8 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|← W07]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | You know you are cold because you feel it. Is feeling more reliable than any system, or is the body just another framework? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | **None.** One quotation sent in advance |
| Sent ahead | "The body is our general medium for having a world" — [[entities/maurice-merleau-ponty\|Merleau-Ponty]] |
| Carried out | What can you do that a machine cannot? |

## Overview

This lesson asks whether feeling is more reliable than any system, or whether the body is just another framework. You start from a simple case: you feel cold, a thermometer reads a number, and you ask which one can be wrong. You then test the claim against four harder cases and against one quotation from Merleau-Ponty. You do not hand in written work. What you produce is a stated position of your own, and one question you carry into Week 9: what can you do that a machine cannot?

## The ideas

### Is feeling more reliable than a system?

Start with the cold case. A thermometer says 22 degrees and you are shivering. Which one is wrong? One strong answer is that neither is wrong: the thermometer measures the room and your body measures you. That answer forces a further question: what is the body an instrument of? You cannot escape into the thermometer either, because you only reach its reading through a body that reads it.

A classical position holds that you cannot be wrong about a feeling, only about its cause. You can feel cold and be mistaken about why, but the feeling itself is not an error.

### The body as window or medium

**Merleau-Ponty** says the body is our general medium for having a world. On this view the body is not a clear window onto things. It is the medium that shapes what can appear at all. This changes the meaning of a wrong reading. If the medium shifts, you may not be wrong about the world so much as have a different world. A blind person, on this view, is not perceiving less of the world but a different world.

### Four cases that complicate trust

Each case closes off one easy answer.

- **Phantom limb.** A person feels pain in a leg that is not there. The pain is felt, so is it real, and is it accurate?
- **Chronic pain without injury.** The pain signal fires with nothing to report. The question is whether the body is lying or reporting honestly about its own state.
- **Synaesthesia.** Someone hears color. This asks whether they perceive more of the world or simply differently.
- **Adaptation.** Move from a cold room to a warm one and the same water feels hot, then neutral. So which reading was correct?

Two distinctions do the work here. First, calling one body **normal** and another a malfunction assumes an answer: ask what makes a configuration normal rather than simply common. Second, "trusted" only means something once you say trusted **to do what**. A hammer that is bad at cutting is not untrustworthy, because cutting is not its job.

### What can a body do?

**Spinoza** offers a reframe: we do not yet know what a body can do. Instead of asking what a body **is**, ask what a body **can do**. The open question is whether this dissolves the problem or dodges it. At the end you state one of two positions: the body is an instrument to be corrected, or the body is the condition of there being anything to correct.

## Day by day

- **This session.** Read the Merleau-Ponty quotation sent in advance. In class you describe being cold without the word "cold" and without a number, work through the cold case, the four complicating cases, and the Spinoza reframe, then state your position. Carry one question out of the room: what can you do that a machine cannot?

## Review

Check you can:

- Argue whether feeling is more reliable than any system, or whether the body is just another framework.
- Explain what **Merleau-Ponty** means by the body as the general medium for having a world.
- Use the phantom limb, chronic pain without injury, synaesthesia, and adaptation cases to test whether the body can be trusted.
- Distinguish a **normal** configuration from a merely common one.
- Explain the **Spinoza** reframe: asking what a body can do rather than what it is.
- Answer what you can do that a machine cannot.

## Links

[[entities/maurice-merleau-ponty]] · [[entities/friedrich-nietzsche]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]]

# Oxbridge W13: Who Gets to Show Us the World?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7: Power and Visibility]] · Week 13 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|← W12]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is being seen a form of recognition or a form of capture? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | Two short extracts: [[entities/michel-foucault\|Foucault]] on the panopticon (*Discipline and Punish*); [[entities/frantz-fanon\|Fanon]], the look passage (*Black Skin, White Masks*) |
| Carried out | Is a view from nowhere possible? |

## Overview

This lesson asks whether being seen is a form of recognition or a form of capture. You read two short extracts, [[entities/michel-foucault|Foucault]] on the panopticon and [[entities/frantz-fanon|Fanon]] on the look, and set them against each other. You leave with one question carried forward into W14: is a view from nowhere possible?

## The ideas

### Watched versus seen

There is a difference between being **watched** and being **seen**. Watching observes what you do. The look, in Fanon's sense, decides in advance what you are. There is also a difference between changing because you *were* watched and changing because you *might be* watched. If a camera changes the behavior of people who were never going to steal, the force at work is not the camera but the possibility of being watched.

### Foucault: the panopticon

The **panopticon** is a design in which the prisoner cannot tell when he is being watched, so he watches himself. Power becomes automatic. It no longer needs an operator. This raises a question about where power is located: if power works best when nobody has to exercise it, it is no longer held by a person. Visibility becomes a trap, and someone set that trap. A framework that makes you police yourself may be more powerful than one that punishes you.

### Fanon: the look

The **look** does not merely observe. It fixes. It arrives before you speak and decides in advance what you are. So invisibility is a trap too. Foucault says visibility is a trap; Fanon says invisibility is also one, and both can be true at once. This raises who can afford invisibility and who is punished by it, and who has the option of being unmarked, seen as simply a person rather than as a type. Demanding to be seen may be a demand for power, or it may be a request for permission.

### The maker of the frame

One line holds the course together: every framework has a maker, and the maker is not in the picture. Being represented, having more people on screen, puts you in the position of the one shown, not the one who shows. This leads to the **awareness versus action question**: does knowing who made the frame change anything, or only how you feel about it? If you say awareness is enough, you must say enough for what.

## Day by day

- The session opens with a silent prompt: describe a time being watched changed what you did, though nobody said anything. You then work through Foucault's panopticon and Fanon's look, set the two against each other, and commit to the line that every framework has a maker who is not in the picture. It closes on the question carried into W14: is a view from nowhere possible?

## Review

Check you can:

- Argue whether being seen is recognition or capture.
- Explain the **panopticon** and how it makes a person watch himself.
- Explain Fanon's **look** and how it fixes a person before they speak.
- Set the panopticon against the look and say what each one catches that the other misses.
- Name who holds the position of showing and who is required to be seen.
- State the **awareness versus action question** and answer "enough for what".

# Oxbridge W12: Is a Common World Still Possible?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6: Collective Reality]] · Week 12 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|← W11]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | If each of us is served a different version of the world, is a shared world still available, and would it have to be built without representation? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, **Movement 2 is student-led** |
| Reading | [[entities/irmgard-emmelhainz\|Emmelhainz]], "Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", e-flux |
| Prepared | The **angle sheet**: one central question, eight angle questions. Each student picks one and brings a position |
| Carried out | Who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen? |

## Overview

This lesson asks whether a shared world is still possible when each person is served a different version of it. Before class you read Emmelhainz and use the **angle sheet**: pick one of the eight angle questions and bring a position you are willing to defend and have challenged. In class you present that angle and take one question before the next speaker. By the end you argue for or against a common world and name the cost of your answer. This feeds W13, which asks who gets to show us the world and who has to be seen.

## The ideas

### A shared world, or many worlds

When two feeds barely overlap, ask what kind of gap it is. A **difference of taste** is a gap in preference. A **difference of world** is a gap in the reality each person takes as given. Living in the same physical world does not close it: a shared physical world may not help you agree about anything you actually disagree about.

People have always held different information, so the real question is whether that gap has grown from a **difference of degree** into a **difference of kind**, a change not in how much people differ but in what kind of thing sharing has become, and how you would tell.

Ask also what a **shared world** even is: a shared set of facts, a shared set of images, or a shared set of problems.

### Sharing beyond representation

**Irmgard Emmelhainz**, in "Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", asks whether we can share a world **beyond representation**, that is, without images or accounts standing in for it. Test this by naming one thing that is shared but not represented. Shared experience is one answer: eating together, working together, rather than shared images. The open question is whether that scales beyond a single room.

Two framings pull against each other: the problem may be too many representations, or it may be that representation was always the wrong medium for sharing a world at all.

If a common world has to be **made rather than found**, built by people rather than discovered, then ask who is making it now. Saying "fix the algorithms" only pushes the question back: fix them toward what target, and who chooses it. That returns you to W11.

Ask, finally, whether **agreeing to disagree** is itself a shared world or the end of one.

## Day by day

- **In class.** Compare your feed with a neighbor and decide whether the gap is a difference of taste or a difference of world. Present your chosen angle and answer one question from the room before the next speaker; the angles get clustered on the board as they arrive. Then commit: is a common world still possible? If yes, name the ground it stands on. If no, say what replaces it. Close on the question you carry into W13: who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen?

## Review

Check you can:

- Say what follows if each person is served a different version of the world.
- Tell a difference of taste from a difference of world.
- Distinguish a difference of degree from a difference of kind, and say how you would tell.
- Use Emmelhainz to ask whether a shared world would have to be built beyond representation, and give one example of something shared that is not represented.
- Argue for or against the possibility of a common world, and name the cost of your answer.

## Links

[[entities/irmgard-emmelhainz]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|W11]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13]]

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-prep.body:
# Oxbridge Interview Preparation

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · course apparatus

## What the interview actually tests

**Not knowledge.** This course is built on one claim:

> The Oxbridge interview tests whether a candidate can think while being watched, revise a position without collapsing, and stay with a difficult question rather than resolving it prematurely.

The whole seminar prepares you for that. Three moves are practiced explicitly.

## The three moves

**1. Take a position quickly.** If you hedge, you lose the interview in the first minute. State a claim, then qualify it. **Never qualify first.**

**2. Absorb the push without abandoning the claim.** When the interviewer objects, do not surrender and do not just repeat yourself. Use one of two sentences:

> "That case is harder for my position, and here is why I think it still holds"
>
> "That case actually defeats my position, so let me narrow it."

**3. Follow the consequence.** The interviewer is usually asking where your claim leads, not whether it is true. **Volunteer the consequence before being asked.**

## The push line format

Every question in [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank|the question bank]] has two parts: a plain opening question, and a **push line** that replicates the interviewer's follow-up move. Practice them in pairs, with one student as interviewer.

> **Opening.** Is a photograph evidence?
>
> **Push.** You said it depends on whether it was edited. Every photograph involves choices about framing, exposure, and moment. So is every photograph edited, and does your distinction survive that?

## Mock interview format

**Twelve minutes per student. One question, no preparation time.**

The interviewer's job is to **push three times, not to be fair.**

Debrief for three minutes afterward on one thing only:

> At which push did the candidate stop thinking and start defending?

## Where the moves get drilled inside the course

The three moves are not confined to mock interviews. Each has a home session:

- **Take a position quickly:** Movement 3 of every session. One sentence, one reason, no abstentions. [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template|The template]] bans neutrality precisely to train this.
- **Absorb the push:** [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]] runs it as a paired drill with the three named pushes (the consequence, the hard case, the definition), and debriefs on the same question the mock does. With no essays in the course, W07 is entirely this drill, which makes it the most direct interview rehearsal in the fourteen weeks.
- **Follow the consequence:** [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|principle 5]]. All term the teacher asks about the consequence inside your own claim, so you hear the move roughly forty times before you have to perform it.
- **Movement under argument is praised, not penalized.** [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] makes changing position under pressure an explicit skill: anyone who moves columns must name the quotation that moved them.

## Scheduling

Mock interviews run in the week following [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]], if the timetable allows. This week is not one of the fourteen.

A full round is about 15 minutes per student: twelve minutes plus a three-minute debrief. One 45-minute session covers three students, so a larger cohort needs several sessions or a block outside the timetable. The number of sessions depends on cohort size and will be confirmed in class.

## The connection to the closing session

W14 aims at the same capacity the interview is testing:

> The best outcome is a room that can hold the paradox without either collapsing into relativism or fleeing back to naive realism. That capacity, holding a genuinely open question without needing to close it, is precisely what an Oxbridge interviewer is testing for.

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-.body:
# Oxbridge Course Design Principles

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · course apparatus

Six rules. They govern the shape of each session, the wording of each question, and what counts as a session going well. They are written for this course, and several apply to any ESL seminar room.

## 1. The question does the work

The teacher does not deliver a position. The question draws one out.

> A session is well designed when the students argue and the teacher mostly redirects. If the teacher talks for more than a third of the session, the question was too closed.

That last sentence is the test. It is about question design. A teacher talking too much is a symptom.

## 2. Scaffold from what students already own

**Never open with a philosopher.** Open with something you can already answer from experience: a map, a thermometer, a feeling of cold, a video game boundary, a photo on a phone. The philosopher arrives later, and only to **name** what you have already been arguing.

This is the most important sequencing rule in the course, and every session shows it:

- Berger goes on the board in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]] only after students have generated the idea themselves.
- Barthes arrives at the *end* of [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]], to name what students built out of maps and video-game boundaries.
- Spinoza's reframe closes [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]] rather than opening it.

## 3. Questions should be plain on the surface and catalytic underneath

The register to aim for:

- "What does the world look like?"
- "Where does the body end?"
- "Who agreed that this is real?"

Avoid academic scaffolding **in the question itself**. No sub-questions, no anticipated responses, no explanation attached. The complication belongs in the follow-up, spoken live, not printed on the slide.

This is why [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank|the question bank]] is written as single lines.

## 4. Close with a defensible position, not a summary

Every session ends by asking each student to state a position they will defend under pressure. The closing question is **carried out of the room, not resolved in it**.

## 5. Complicate from inside the student's own commitment

The Socratic move is not to bring in a counterexample from outside. It is to find the consequence you have not yet noticed inside your own claim, and to ask about that.

A worked example:

> "You said the body cannot lie. What about phantom limb pain?" is weaker than "You said the body cannot lie. Does that mean a person who feels pain in a missing leg is feeling something true?"

Both use the same case. The second makes your own claim do the work.

## 6. Register

Students here read English as a second language. Sentences should be short. Vocabulary should be plain. **Difficulty should live in the idea, never in the syntax.**

> A hard concept in easy words is the target. An easy concept in hard words is failure.

This rule is why the course can run Foucault, Bergson, and Emmelhainz with Grade 11 ESL students without dilution: the concepts are not simplified, the sentences are.

## How the principles show up elsewhere

- The five-part session shape in [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template|the template]] is principle 1 and 4 made structural: two minutes of silent writing so every student enters with something of their own, and a commit movement where **neutrality is the one banned position**.
- [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]] is principle 5 turned into a drill. The push line is the same move, performed by a student instead of the teacher.
- The four qualities the course names, commitment, pressure, precision, movement, are principle 4 stated as feedback. Nothing is graded ([[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|Assessment — none]]), so they are said aloud in the commit movement rather than written on anything: "that is a survey, not a position" is a sentence you can act on right away.

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list.m.body:
# Oxbridge Reading List

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · course apparatus

Everything the fourteen sessions read, quote, show, or cite. This doubles as the course's resource library.

## Set texts, assigned

| Week | Text |
|---|---|
| W01 | John Berger, *Ways of Seeing*, ch. 1 — first six pages |
| W02 | Hito Steyerl, "In Defense of the Poor Image", e-flux journal |
| W04 | Plato, Allegory of the Cave, *Republic* VII — a clean modern translation, roughly two pages |
| W09 | Tobias Rees, on AI and the concepts of the modern period, Noema |
| W12 | Irmgard Emmelhainz, "Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", e-flux journal |
| W13 | Michel Foucault, *Discipline and Punish* — panopticon extract |
| W13 | Frantz Fanon, *Black Skin, White Masks* — the look passage |

The BBC episode of *Ways of Seeing* works as a second way into W01 if you find the prose hard.

## Quotations used live

Five quotations are given in class rather than read in advance:

- **Merleau-Ponty**, *Phenomenology of Perception*, 1945: the body as general medium for having a world. (W08; sent in advance)
- **Sartre**: man is condemned to be free. (W05)
- **Camus**: the absurd as confrontation between human need and the silence of the world; we must imagine Sisyphus happy. (W05)
- **Barthes**: the author who disappears behind the text. (W06)
- **Spinoza**: we do not yet know what a body can do. (W08)

## Extension reading

Offered to groups that want to keep going; none is assigned.

- Susan Sontag, "In Plato's Cave", from *On Photography*
- Amelia Groom, "Permanent Collection"
- Donna Haraway, "Situated Knowledges"
- Benjamin Bratton, *The Terraforming*, or the shorter Noema pieces
- Rebecca Solnit, on maps and atlases
- Henri Bergson, *Matter and Memory*, on habit memory and pure memory
- Sigmund Freud, on repression and the return of the repressed
- Guy Debord, *The Society of the Spectacle* ([[entities/guy-debord]])
- Mark Fisher, *Capitalist Realism*
- Tim Ingold, *The Perception of the Environment*, introduction

## Visual and material references

- Mercator projection beside Gall-Peters (W06)
- Early modern maps showing Taprobana (W06)
- Renaissance perspective constructions (W04)
- Carsten Höller, the laboratory of doubt, for the body sessions (W08, optional visual anchor)
- One image no student will recognize: a minor painting, an unlabelled photograph, an object in an unfamiliar context (W01), plus one uncomfortable fact about it, withheld until Movement 2
- Two versions of one image, high resolution and badly compressed (W02)

## Cases used as examples

The course runs more on cases than on texts. The named ones:

- The thermometer, and the double slit experiment (W03)
- Barry Marshall and *H. pylori*, 1984 (W06)
- Taprobana, the island that appeared on maps for centuries, referring unstably to Sri Lanka, to Sumatra, to nowhere (W06)
- The video game map whose edge is disguised as a mountain (W06)
- Phantom limb, chronic pain, synesthesia, thermal adaptation (W08)
- The painted sheet, remembering as repainting (W10)
- The ten-item sorting list: gravity, money, a nation, Tuesday, a species, a debt, a disease, a genre, a race, a language (W11)

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-struct.body:
# Oxbridge Session Structure Template

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · course apparatus · **45 minutes**

Every session in the course follows this shape. All fourteen session plans use it, so once you know this page you can follow any of them.

## The five parts

| Part | Minutes | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Silent opening | 5 | One question on the board. Students write for two minutes. **No answers taken yet** |
| Movement 1 · elicit | 10 | Positions on the table. Concrete, experiential, no theory. The goal is disagreement, not accuracy |
| Movement 2 · complicate | 15 | The case, image or example that breaks the easy answer. The philosopher may arrive here |
| Movement 3 · commit | 10 | One sentence and one reason from every student. Others may challenge |
| Closing | 5 | One question on the board, unanswered, carried into next week |

### Silent opening

You write for two minutes before anything is said. The reason is explicit: it "guarantees every student enters the session with something of their own, which matters enormously for quieter and less confident speakers." In an ESL room this is not a warm-up. It is the mechanism that makes the rest of the session possible.

### Movement 1 · elicit

Get positions on the table. The disagreement is named out loud when it appears: "So we have two camps in the room." The goal is disagreement, not accuracy, so a wrong answer stated clearly is more useful here than a hedged correct one.

### Movement 2 · complicate

The case, image or example that breaks the easy answer. The pressure comes **from inside student positions rather than against them** (see [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|principle 5]]). This is where a thinker may arrive, "and only to give a name to the position a student has already taken."

### Movement 3 · commit

Each student states a position in one sentence and gives one reason. Others may challenge.

> [!important] One rule
> No student is allowed to remain neutral. Neutrality is the one banned position in this room.

### Closing

One question is written on the board, unanswered, and carried into the next week. It is posted to the group chat afterward with a quote attached.

## After the session

A short recap message goes to the group chat. The register is casual. It gives two or three sentences naming what emerged, one quote for the next session, and the closing question restated.

This is the only routine outside the room, and it does real work. It is how the closing question stays live across seven days, and it is where the next session's text or quotation is seeded.

## Where sessions deviate

Three of the fourteen bend the template, each for a stated reason:

- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]].** The movements become *what an argument is*, *live pressure in pairs*, and *build the spine*. Consolidation, no new material.
- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12]].** Movement 2 is student-led. Each student presents a chosen angle and answers one question from the room before the next speaks.
- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]].** The template is dropped entirely for four questions at roughly ten minutes each, and there is no closing question. "For the first time in fourteen weeks, students answer one instead."

classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-uni.body:
# Oxbridge Unit 1: The Image

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 1 of 8 · Weeks 1–2 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2 →]]

## Unit question

**Do images represent the world, or do they produce it?**

## Why this opens the course

You already live inside images. You have opinions about resolution, screenshots, compression, filters, and what counts as a real photograph. This unit starts there. It needs no prior reading to enter, and it stays rigorous without simplification.

[[entities/john-berger]] gives the first idea: seeing is not neutral. [[entities/hito-steyerl]] turns that idea into a political and economic argument.

The unit also installs the **method** you will use for the rest of the course: begin from an intuition you already hold, discover it does not survive a single hard case, then let a thinker arrive to name what you have been arguing. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|Course Design Principles]].

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01: Is perception ever neutral?]] — one unfamiliar image, seen twice: before and after you are told what it is. Berger arrives at the end.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02: Do images represent reality or produce it?]] — the same image at two resolutions. Steyerl turns the vocabulary of compression into an argument about access.

## Key texts

- [[entities/john-berger]], *Ways of Seeing*, chapter 1 (first six pages; the BBC episode is the alternative entry point)
- [[entities/hito-steyerl]], "In Defense of the Poor Image", e-flux journal

See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Concepts introduced

[[concepts/the-poor-image|The Poor Image]] · [[concepts/framework|Framework]]

## Preparation

Both sessions set a reading. This is the only consecutive pair in the course that does. Nothing is written or collected; the course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]. Come to W02 having read Steyerl, and having picked the single sentence you found most arguable, ready to say which and why.

## What you should leave with

> A defensible position on whether image quality is a technical property or a political one, and the start of a suspicion that how something is shown does more work than what is shown.

## Across the two weeks

- **The science vocabulary turns.** Steyerl uses vocabulary you may know well, resolution and compression, and then turns it into an argument about access. The same pattern returns in [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2]].
- **The real claim is strong.** This is not just that people interpret images differently. It is that seeing is already interpretive before any interpreting begins.

## Bridge to Unit 2

> If the image is not a neutral window, the next question is whether anything is. That moves the argument from pictures to measurement, where you expect to find safety.

W02's closing question does the handoff: a thermometer measures temperature; does it show you the temperature, or change it? You are meant to hear a change of subject. [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2]] removes the safety.

classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank..body:
# Oxbridge Question Bank

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · course apparatus

Single-line questions covering the full course arc: plain on the surface, catalytic underneath. Use them as openers, as closing questions, or as interview prompts. The single-line form is deliberate. [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|Principle 3]] keeps all scaffolding out of the printed question and puts the complication in the spoken follow-up.

## Image and perception

- Is perception ever neutral?
- What is a photograph evidence of?
- Is a low quality image worth less than a high quality one?
- Do images show us the world or make the world showable?
- Is a screenshot of a painting a painting?

## Measurement and the gap

- Can measurement reach the thing itself?
- Is the gap a problem with our instruments or a condition of observing?
- Which is wider, the gap between "cold" and the temperature, or between the reading and the temperature?
- What would it feel like to have no gap?

## Appearance and reality

- Is there a reality behind appearances?
- Where does your idea of a perfect circle come from?
- Does knowing you are in a cave change your relationship to it?
- Is the prisoner who leaves better off than the ones who stay?
- Is perspective a discovery or an invention?

## The gap as a way of living

- Is the gap a loss, a liberation, or just the condition?
- Can you lose something that never existed?
- Is revolt a position or a mood?
- Must we imagine Sisyphus happy?

## History and frameworks

- Does reality have a history?
- Were we wrong then, or did reality change?
- Is a map that distorts nothing possible?
- Was Taprobana real?
- Name a framework you use every day that claims not to be one.
- Why does a game disguise its edge as a mountain?

## The body

- Can the body be trusted?
- Can you be wrong about being cold?
- If the thermometer says 22 and you are shivering, which is wrong?
- Is a blind person perceiving less of the world, or a different world?
- What can a body do?

## Human and machine

- What can you do that a machine cannot?
- Is the human and machine line essential or contingent?
- Can there be understanding without life?
- What would a machine have to do for you to withdraw your answer?
- Could a machine have a past?

## Memory and forgetting

- What survives forgetting?
- Is forgetting a failure of memory or a function of it?
- Is a memory you revisit often more reliable or less?
- Are you responsible for what you forget?
- What is the difference between remembering and remembering remembering?

## Collective reality

- Whose agreement makes a thing real?
- Does agreement require everyone, enough people, or the right people?
- If a hundred agree and one refuses, is the one wrong or outside?
- Is a common world still possible?
- What is the last thing everyone in this room definitely saw?

## Power and visibility

- Who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen?
- Is being seen recognition or capture?
- Who can afford to be invisible?
- Is awareness of a framework enough, or does it change nothing?

## Synthesis

- Is a view from nowhere possible?
- What does the world look like?
- How does the world appear to us?
- Is "everything is a framework" itself a framework?
- What distinguishes a good frame from a bad one, if closeness to reality is unavailable?

## Interview format, with push lines

Practice in pairs. The push replicates the interviewer's follow-up move. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]] for the three moves being drilled.

**Is a photograph evidence?**
> Push: you said it depends on editing. Every photograph involves framing, exposure, and a chosen moment. So is every photograph edited, and does your distinction survive?

**Can a machine understand?**
> Push: you said understanding requires experience. Describe a test that would tell you whether another person has experience. If you cannot, is your criterion doing any work?

**Is a common world still possible?**
> Push: you said shared experience rather than shared images. Does that scale beyond a room, and if not, have you described a shared world or a small one?

**Were we wrong then, or did reality change?**
> Push: you said we were simply wrong. What counts as a disease has changed. Was addiction not a disease in 1850, or did we fail to notice that it was?

**Is being seen recognition or capture?**
> Push: you said the answer is to avoid visibility. Who has that option, and who is punished for taking it?

## How the bank maps onto the weeks

Each block belongs to a session, so you can use the bank for revision as well as for openers.

| Block | Session |
|---|---|
| Image and perception | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral\|W01]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it\|W02]] |
| Measurement and the gap | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself\|W03]] |
| Appearance and reality | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances\|W04]] |
| The gap as a way of living | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition\|W05]] |
| History and frameworks | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history\|W06]] |
| The body | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted\|W08]] |
| Human and machine | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent\|W09]] |
