classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-uni.body:
# Oxbridge Unit 3: Frameworks and History

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 3 of 8 · Weeks 6–7 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|← Unit 2]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4 →]]

## Unit question

**Does reality have a history?**

## The core provocation

Things considered real in the past are now considered false. Does that mean we were wrong then, or that reality itself changed?

> [!note] Start here
> You will probably answer that we were simply wrong. This unit works to make that answer harder to hold.

Three examples do the work:

- **The Mercator projection**, set beside Gall-Peters. Not a lie, a choice with consequences.
- **Taprobana**, an island that appeared on maps for centuries and referred to something, unstably. Sailors sailed toward it.
- **Barry Marshall**, who in 1984 had to infect himself because a framework in good standing could not accommodate the claim that ulcers were bacterial.

Marshall is the sharpest of the three. He blocks the easy escape. You may reach for "they just did not have the data," but here the data was available and the framework rejected it.

## The key insight

> [!important] The key insight
> A biased history book is not the problem. The problem is the one that claims not to be.

The image to remember is the video-game map: the edge is disguised as a feature of the world, the mountain is too high, the road is closed. The framework hides its own limits by **[[concepts/naturalization|naturalizing]]** them. A visible wall would remind you that you are inside something.

[[entities/roland-barthes]] names this: the author who disappears behind the text is the most ideological author of all.

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06: Does reality have a history?]] The three examples, the video-game map, and Barthes as the closing name.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07: Argument workshop]] The midpoint. No new material. Six weeks of discussion put under interview pressure, in pairs.

## Concepts introduced

[[concepts/naturalization|Naturalization]] · [[concepts/framework|Framework]] (introduced in Unit 1, given its defining property here)

## Preparation

Neither session sets a reading.

Nothing is written or collected ([[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]). In W07 you write four lines on paper, but they are a scaffold for speaking, not a submission.

## The argument workshop

W07 sits inside this unit for a reason. The framework question is one you can already argue, and W06 has just produced your own example. You leave W06 having named a framework you use every day that claims not to be one. W07 puts that sentence under pressure.

> [!important] Claim first
> Hedging feels safe and polite. In an Oxbridge interview it reads as having nothing to say. The drill: claim first, qualification second, never the reverse.

## Holding the question open

Both answers stay live. "We were wrong then" preserves a stable reality and makes knowledge historical. "Reality changed" makes reality itself historical, which is harder to hold but not absurd, since what counts as a disease, a species, or a nation genuinely does change. The useful move is to ask what each answer costs.

The opening examples sort into two columns: factually wrong in one, category shifted in the other. Noticing that criterion is already the argument.

## Bridge to Unit 4

> [!note] What comes next
> You will look for something that stands outside history. The body is the obvious candidate: cold is cold in any century.

W06 closes on the Merleau-Ponty quotation to set this up. [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4]] tests the candidate.

# Oxbridge Unit 2: The Gap

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 2 of 8 · Weeks 3–5 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|← Unit 1]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3 →]]

## Unit question

**Can any representation reach the thing itself?**

## The arc

Three sessions turn the same problem a quarter turn each. This is the longest unit and the one that introduces the course's central term.

**Week 3, epistemology.** This week is about how well any observation reaches its object. A thermometer changes the temperature of what it measures. In the double slit experiment, observation changes what is observed. Language calls something warm, and warm means different things to different speakers. The gap looks wider in language than in science, but it is present in both. This is the starting point, not the end.

**Week 4, ontology.** The question shifts from how well we can know things to what kind of things there are to know. [[entities/plato]] arrives here, with [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]], a technique for depicting the world from one point that came to look like the world itself.

**Week 5, the existential turn.** By now the gap cannot be closed. The question becomes how to live with it. [[entities/jean-paul-sartre]], [[entities/albert-camus]] and Heidegger appear as three positions you can adopt and defend, not as content to memorize.

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03: Can measurement reach the thing itself?]]: the thermometer, the double slit, then the same problem in language. No reading.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04: Is there a reality behind appearances?]]: the cave and the perspective construction. The ontological turn.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05: Is the gap a loss, a liberation, or a condition?]]: four quotations, three columns on the board, and permission to change columns.

## Concepts introduced

[[concepts/the-gap|The Gap]] · [[concepts/linear-perspective|Linear Perspective]] · [[concepts/the-ontological-turn|The Ontological Turn]]

## Preparation

Only W04 sets a reading: Plato, about two pages. W03 and W05 run on cases and quotations given live. The reading load is lightest exactly where the ideas are hardest.

What you carry between sessions is a position. W03 closes on the tree in the forest, and you are asked not to discuss it before W04. W04 asks you to **bring a case** to W05. Nothing is written or collected. The course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]].

## What to watch in this unit

If you come from a science background, you may treat science as the exception, the frame that reaches truth while others do not. Build that case as strongly as you can in week 3. Then, in week 4, ask what makes a good frame better than a bad one if "closer to an unframed reality" is not available as a test.

Two points to hold, one per session:

- **W03:** the claim is not that measurement is unreliable. It is that measurement is an *interaction*, and an interaction has two sides. "Precision and disturbance are not opposites; the more precisely you interact, the more you interact." Do not let this collapse into "everything is subjective."
- **W05:** the existentialists are positions, not biography. You do not need Sartre's life story. You need to say "I hold the Sartre position and here is why the Camus objection does not defeat it." That is the interview skill in miniature.

## Links between sessions

- **W02 → W03.** The thermometer question closes the image unit and opens this one.
- **W03 → W04.** W03 closes on the tree falling in the forest, and you are asked not to discuss it. W04 opens by polling it. If you answered "the gap is about reality" in W03, you have already stepped into ontology, and W04 uses that split.

## Bridge to Unit 3

> If frameworks cannot be escaped, the next question is whether they change. That is a historical question.

W04's closing question sets this up, and W05's closing question asks it directly: things once considered real are now considered false. Were we wrong then, or did reality change? This leads into [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3]].

# Oxbridge Unit 6: Collective Reality

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 6 of 8 · Weeks 11–12 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|← Unit 5]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7 →]]

## Unit question

**Whose agreement makes a thing real?**

## Week 11: agreement

Money is real, borders are real, weekends are real, and none of them would survive if everyone stopped agreeing.

The session runs on one exercise. You sort ten items into *real independently* and *real by agreement*: **gravity, money, a nation, Tuesday, a species, a debt, a disease, a genre, a race, a language.** Gravity and Tuesday sort themselves. The hard ones are the point.

> [!note]
> The sorting will break down, and that breakdown is the lesson.

Then comes the harder version, which is the unit's real subject: **agreement is never equally weighted. Whose agreement counts?**

## Week 12: Emmelhainz

[[entities/irmgard-emmelhainz]], "Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", argues that the shared world has fragmented into private, algorithmically shaped worlds. She asks whether a common ground can be found that does not depend on representation at all.

The session is built differently from every other. There is one central question with eight angle questions beneath it, printed on a sheet. You pick an angle, bring a position, and present it, answering one question from the room before the next speaker begins. **Movement 2 is student-led.**

The framing sent to the group chat:

> There is one central question the whole discussion builds toward, and eight smaller questions beneath it approaching the same problem from different directions. Pick one angle. You do not need a final answer, just a position you are willing to defend and have challenged.

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|W11: Whose agreement makes a thing real?]] — the sorting exercise, then the political turn.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12: Is a common world still possible?]] — Emmelhainz, and your own feeds as the opening evidence.

## Concepts introduced

None new. The unit applies [[concepts/the-ontological-turn|the ontological turn]] collectively: realness as a relation rather than a property, now with the question of who holds the relation.

## Preparation

This unit has the most student preparation in the course, and it is all spoken. W11 needs nothing in advance. For W12, read Emmelhainz, choose one of the eight angle questions, and arrive with a position on it. Movement 2 *is* the students, so the session depends on you coming ready.

Nothing is written or collected ([[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]).

## Teaching notes

- The lesson is not in either column of the sorting exercise. It is in watching items move between them, and in the moment when you move something and cannot say what moved it.
- W11's Movement 3 asks you to name one thing you believe is real that most people around you do not, and to say what would make it count. This forces you to describe the mechanism of realness rather than assert an instance of it.
- In W12, the question is not whether social media is bad. It is whether **sharing a world** requires representation at all.
- Watch for the answer "it is not agreement, it is power" in W11. That is the entry to Unit 7.

## Bridge to Unit 7

> [!note]
> If agreement is unequally weighted, the next question is who holds the weight.

[[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7]].

# Oxbridge Unit 7: Power and Visibility

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 7 of 8 · Week 13 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|← Unit 6]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8 →]]

## Unit question

**Who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen?**

## The two positions

**[[entities/michel-foucault]]:** visibility is a trap. The panopticon works because the prisoner does not know when he is watched, so he watches himself. Power does not need to look. It needs only to be *able* to look.

**[[entities/frantz-fanon]]:** being seen is not neutral either. The look can fix a person in place. It arrives before they speak and decides in advance what they are. Fanon adds what Foucault leaves out: **not everyone is seen the same way.**

## The move that makes this the penultimate unit

This unit collects everything. The framework that hides its edges is now revealed to have an owner. Perspective has a position, and someone occupies it. The map has a maker. The category has an author.

The line at the center of this unit is the course's whole argument in one sentence:

> **Every framework has a maker, and the maker is not in the picture.**

It re-reads every earlier unit: [[concepts/linear-perspective|perspective]] from W04, the Mercator projection from W06, [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]] itself. Nothing new is introduced. What changes is that the frameworks acquire owners.

## Session

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13: Who gets to show us the world, and who has to be seen?]]: two short extracts, and the awareness-versus-action question pressed hard.

## Concepts introduced

None new. The unit supplies the political reading of [[concepts/framework|framework]] and [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]] that the earlier weeks held back.

## Preparation

Read two short extracts, one from Foucault and one from Fanon. This is the densest reading in the course, so read closely.

Nothing is written or collected. The course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]. The session's central question is: who decides what is visible, and does knowing the answer change anything?

## The questions this unit asks

- **Foucault and Fanon are paired for their asymmetry, not to make Fanon an illustration of Foucault.** Foucault describes a general condition. Fanon describes a distributed one. Not everyone is seen the same way, and a theory of visibility that cannot register that difference is the kind of framework this course has been taking apart.

- **Does knowing who made the frame change anything, or only how you feel about it?** If you say awareness is enough, ask: enough for what. Unit 8 applies this same question to the course itself.

- **Two easy answers are closed.** "So the solution is not to be seen" meets the question: who can afford invisibility, and who is punished by it? "Representation fixes this, more people on screen" meets W12's question: does being represented give you the position of the one who shows, or only of the one shown?

- **Opening question:** describe a situation in which being watched changed what you did, even though nobody said anything.

## Bridge to Unit 8

The final move is to turn the critique back on the course.

W13 closes on the course's title question. [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8]].

concepts/framework.md.body:
# Framework

**The [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]]'s central term**, and the subject of its throughline:

> Frameworks conceal their own constructed edges, and they actively shape reality rather than merely representing it.

A framework is **any system that makes something knowable by excluding most of what could be known.**

## Three properties

1. **It is a set of chosen sacrifices.** The Mercator projection preserves angles and distorts area. **There is no projection that sacrifices nothing.**
2. **It is productive, not merely descriptive.** [[concepts/linear-perspective|Linear perspective]] did not record how vision works. It trained vision to work that way.
3. **It hides its own edges.** This is the property the whole course turns on. See [[concepts/naturalization]].

Property 3 is what makes the term non-trivial. Everyone accepts that frameworks exist. The claim that does real work is that they **systematically conceal that they are frameworks.**

## Test question

> Name a framework you use every day that claims not to be one.

You answer this in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]], and everyone answers. Common answers: exam grades, the calendar, the news feed, "common sense", the school timetable, the map app. Your answer becomes your essay topic in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop|W07]].

## Where the term gets its edges

The concept is built across the course rather than defined once:

| Session | What it adds |
|---|---|
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral\|W01]] | Seeing is already framed before any interpreting begins |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances\|W04]] | A framework can be a datable invention that comes to look like the world |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history\|W06]] | Property 1 (chosen sacrifices) and property 3 (hidden edges), via the map and the video-game boundary |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real\|W11]] | Frameworks are collectively held, and the holding is unequally weighted |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world\|W13]] | **Every framework has a maker, and the maker is not in the picture** |
| [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible\|W14]] | The term is turned on itself: is "everything is a framework" a framework? |

## The self-application problem

The course's final question is whether the concept survives being applied to itself. There are two live answers, both developed in [[concepts/view-from-nowhere]]. Either the demand for an unframed view is incoherent rather than merely unsatisfied, or frames can be compared by their consequences without any access to an unframed reality. The second is [[concepts/situated-knowledge|Haraway's route]].

## Related in other courses

Media Studies reaches the same territory through [[concepts/representation|representation]] and mediation. Media do not show the world. They go between us and it, selecting and shaping on the way. The vocabulary differs. The claim about selection is the same one.

concepts/linear-perspective.md.body:
# Linear Perspective

**A key example in the [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]]**, because it is a datable invention that came to look like the structure of vision itself.

> Perspective does not show the world. It shows the world **from a point.** It assumes a single, motionless, monocular viewer, and it converts that assumption into geometry so convincing that for centuries it read as simply how things look.

## The philosophical payoff

When a perspective becomes **invisible as a perspective**, we mistake it for the world.

That is [[concepts/naturalization|naturalization]] made visible. You can watch it happen rather than being told about it.

Every other case of naturalization the course uses (the map, the video-game boundary, the category) has to be argued for. This one can be shown: here is the construction, here is the date, here is the assumption it encodes.

## Good pressure question

> Is perspective a **discovery** about vision, or an **invention** that trained vision?

The follow-ups, from [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]]: *perspective does not show us the world, it shows us the world from a point, what is the difference?* and *if a perspective becomes invisible as a perspective, what do we think we are looking at?*

## Where it comes from in the course

Not from art history. It arrives via [[entities/hito-steyerl|Steyerl]] in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02]] and is developed in W04 alongside Plato. So you meet it as a claim about images and access before you meet it as a claim about vision.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] · [[entities/hito-steyerl]] · [[concepts/framework]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] (in the list of frameworks that hid their edges)

concepts/naturalization.md.body:
# Naturalization

**The process by which a constructed thing comes to look like a natural fact.**

## Three images students remember

- **The video game map.** The edge is disguised as a feature of the world. The mountain is too high. The road is closed. **A visible wall would remind you that you are inside something.**
- **The history book that claims no bias.** A biased book is not the problem. The book that claims not to be is.
- **[[entities/roland-barthes|Barthes]].** The author who disappears behind the text is the most ideological author of all.

## Why this concept and not just "framework"

> Naturalization is the mechanism that makes [[concepts/framework|framework]] the course's central term rather than a trivial one. **Everyone accepts that frameworks exist. The claim that matters is that they systematically conceal that they are frameworks.**

Without naturalization, "everything is a framework" is a shrug. With it, the claim has a testable consequence: you should expect the most powerful frameworks to be the ones that feel least like choices.

## The demonstrable case

[[concepts/linear-perspective|Linear perspective]] is naturalization you can watch rather than be told about: a technique, invented at a datable moment, that came to read as the structure of vision itself.

## Where it is developed

Barthes goes on the board at the end of [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]], not the start. You build the concept out of maps and video-game boundaries first. The sentence then arrives to name what you have made. This ordering follows [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|principle 2]].

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]

W13 completes it: the naturalized framework turns out to have a maker, and **the maker is not in the picture.**

concepts/situated-knowledge.md.body:
# Situated Knowledge

**[[entities/donna-haraway|Donna Haraway]]'s answer to the choice between objectivity and relativism**, and a useful counter-move in the final weeks of the [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]].

## The argument

The view from nowhere and the view from everywhere are **the same evasion**. Both refuse responsibility for a position.

Knowledge is always from somewhere. Admitting where does not weaken the claim. **It makes the claim accountable.**

## Why it matters

By week 13 you can be stuck between two positions you can both see are bad: "science is neutral" and "everything is subjective." **Situated knowledge** is a third option, and one you can actually defend:

> A partial view that names its own location is better than a total view that does not. And **better is a real word here rather than a rhetorical one.**

That last point is what makes the concept do work in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]. The session's first question asks what tells a good frame from a bad one if closeness to an unframed reality is unavailable. Situated knowledge gives you a test, accountability of position, that does not need the unframed reality the course has spent fourteen weeks removing.

## The pressure it still faces

It does not dissolve W14's fourth question. If every position is situated, then the claim that every position is situated is also situated, and the regress is the same one. What it changes is the consequence. On Haraway's account the regress is not a problem to escape but the reason for naming your location. That is a livable answer rather than a resolution. Whether it is enough stays an open question.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] (as an extension) · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] · [[concepts/view-from-nowhere]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4]]

## Reading

Haraway's "Situated Knowledges" is on the course's extension list, not assigned. The concept is taught from the argument rather than the text.

concepts/the-ontological-turn.md.body:
# The Ontological Turn

**The pivot from asking *how well can we know things* to asking *what kind of things are there to know*.**

The **epistemological question** assumes a stable reality and asks how reliable our access to it is. The **ontological question** suspends that assumption.

## The classroom version

Think of the tree falling in the forest.

> Those who say no sound are not claiming that our hearing is unreliable. They are claiming that **sound is a relation rather than a property.**

That distinction is the whole idea. It is why [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]] closes on the question without discussing it and [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] opens by polling it. You arrive having taken a side without knowing which question you answered.

## Why the course needs it

This is the move that makes the second half of the course possible. Once reality is allowed to be relational, questions about history, the body, machines, and collective agreement all become live in the same way.

Each later unit is the same turn applied to a new domain:

| Unit | The relational claim |
|---|---|
| [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history\|U3]] | What counts as a disease or a species is historical, not fixed |
| [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine\|U4]] | Agency and understanding may be separable from being alive |
| [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality\|U6]] | Money, nations and debts are real by a relation, not a property |

## Telling the two apart

W04 follows up with a test of whether the turn has actually happened:

> Is this an argument about the world or an argument about a word? **How would you tell the difference?**

If you cannot separate the two, you have made a **semantic point** and mistaken it for an ontological one. That is the most common failure mode of this concept, so name it when you see it.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|W11]] · [[entities/plato]]

concepts/the-gap.md.body:
# The Gap

**The distance between a representation and the thing represented, which can be narrowed but not closed.**

The organizing term of [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2]] of the [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]], and the concept the rest of the course argues from.

## Established in three moves

- **Measurement.** The thermometer changes the water. Observation changes the double slit result. **Measuring is an interaction, and interactions have two sides.**
- **Language.** Cold means different things to different speakers. Some words do not translate.
- **Perception.** Nothing reaches you except through a body that processes it.

## The conclusion, and why it is only half the point

The usual conclusion is that science narrows the gap and language widens it. That is correct but not enough. The real question comes next:

> Is narrowing progress **toward** something, given that the target cannot be inspected?

That question turns an observation about knowledge into [[concepts/the-ontological-turn|one about being]], and it is why [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]] does not resolve.

## Three positions on it

These are not three answers to be graded. They are three stances you can adopt and defend. This is the form the course wants every position to take.

| Position | The claim | The pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **Loss** | There is a real world and we are locked out of it | Locked out implies you know what is on the other side. How? |
| **Liberation** | If there is no fixed reality, we get to make one | Make one out of what? |
| **Condition** | It is just what having a mind is like | If it is simply the condition, why does it feel like a loss to so many people? |

You work these in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] against Sartre, Camus and Heidegger. Heidegger's contribution threatens the term itself: if the framework is what makes understanding **possible** rather than what blocks it, does the word "gap" still fit? **Is a lens an obstacle to sight?**

## The block to hold

> The claim is not that measurement is unreliable. It is that measurement is an interaction, and an interaction has two sides. **Precision and disturbance are not opposites; the more precisely you interact, the more you interact.**

Do not collapse this into "everything is subjective." That reading makes the concept useless. It removes the difference between narrowing the gap and ignoring it.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2]]

Applied to your own past in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10]]: the painted sheet is the gap between a memory and its event.

entities/benjamin-bratton.md.body:
# Benjamin Bratton

**Born 1968.**

## The claim in one line

Computation is **planetary infrastructure** rather than a set of tools, and AI may be the only way to know systems too large for any single mind to perceive.

## Quote to put on the board

> The Copernican trauma was not that we were displaced, but that we could only know it through an instrument.

## How the Oxbridge course uses him

He is the natural next step after [[entities/tobias-rees|Rees]] if you want to keep going.

Bratton reframes AI as **an instrument of perception rather than a rival to human thought**. This loops back to the thermometer in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself|W03]]. If knowing through an instrument is the normal condition and not a compromise, the week-9 question changes shape: the interesting thing about a machine is not whether it thinks like us, but what it lets us see.

The board quote puts [[concepts/the-gap|the gap]] and the AI question in one line.

## Reading

*The Terraforming*, or the shorter Noema pieces. This is extension reading, not assigned.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[entities/tobias-rees]]

concepts/the-poor-image.md.body:
# The Poor Image

**[[entities/hito-steyerl|Hito Steyerl]]'s term for the low-resolution, heavily compressed, repeatedly re-uploaded image.**

## The argument in one move

Resolution looks like a technical property. It actually works as a **marker of value, access, and institutional ownership.**

> An image degrades because it circulates. A pristine image is pristine because it was **kept** rather than shared.

The poor image is therefore both **evidence of exclusion and of defiance**: what remains when something travels far enough to reach people who were never the intended audience.

## Questions to consider

> Is a poor image democratic, or only cheaper to distribute? **Are those the same thing?**

A pairing to go with it: if an image loses quality every time it is shared, what does high quality tell us about how much it was shared?

## A claim to test

It is tempting to say the low-resolution version and the pristine version are "the same image." But if the two versions produce different feelings, different levels of trust, and different audiences, **in what sense are they the same?** To hold this line, you have to argue that an image is its file rather than its effects. That is a defensible position, and a harder one than it first looks.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1]]

Steyerl's account of [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]] carries forward into [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]], so the two concepts arrive from the same source a fortnight apart.

## Also taught in Art Appreciation

The same Steyerl essay is an assigned text in Art Appreciation's [[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-11-aura-and-the-poor-image|L11]], paired with Benjamin on aura. The Oxbridge course does not hold it: see [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]]. The two courses treat it differently. Art Appreciation runs a degradation lab: you degrade an image on purpose, then describe exactly what changed. Oxbridge runs it as an argument about who could afford a neutral image.

concepts/view-from-nowhere.md.body:
# View from Nowhere

**Thomas Nagel's phrase for the aspiration to a perspective that belongs to no particular position: complete, unlocated, unframed.**

The [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge Discussion Group]] uses it as its closing question. It "names the course throughline in five words."

## Two live answers

**No, and the demand is a category error.** Asking for an unframed view is asking to see without being anywhere. That is not a failure we suffer. It is an incoherent request.

**No, but the aspiration still does work.** You can compare frames even without access to an unframed reality: by their consequences, by what they let you do, by whose costs they hide. See [[concepts/situated-knowledge]].

The question is genuinely open, and the course does not pick a side.

## The final trap

> Is "everything is a framework" itself a framework? If yes, why accept it. If no, you have just produced the view from nowhere.

This is the fourth question in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]], and the reason the session exists. The course does not resolve it.

The aim is a room that can hold the paradox without either collapsing into relativism or fleeing back to naive realism. Holding a genuinely open question without needing to close it is precisely what an Oxbridge interviewer tests for.

## What the phrase collects

By W14 the term is doing retrospective work. Every framework the course examined is an instance of a view **from somewhere** that presented itself as a view from nowhere:

the map · [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]] · the body as medium · machine cognition · the categories that decide who counts · and, if the fourth question lands, the course itself.

## Appears in

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8]] · [[entities/friedrich-nietzsche]] (perspectivism as the counterweight when you try to rescue an unframed view) · [[entities/donna-haraway]]

## A note on the source

Nagel is named here for the phrase only. No Nagel text is assigned or read in this course. The concept as taught is the course's own, with the phrase borrowed. If you go looking for his book *The View from Nowhere* (1986), you will find an argument with a different shape.

entities/donna-haraway.md.body:
# Donna Haraway

**Born 1944.**

## The claim in one line

The view from nowhere and the view from everywhere are **the same evasion**. Knowledge is always situated. Naming its position makes it **accountable** rather than weaker.

## Quote

> I am arguing for politics and epistemologies of location, positioning, and situating.

## How the Oxbridge course uses her

She gives you a way out in the final weeks. When you get stuck between neutral science and total relativism, Haraway offers a third option you can defend.

Both stuck positions are dead ends. The course spends six weeks removing the neutral view, and it rules out the relativist shrug in every commit movement. [[concepts/situated-knowledge|Situated knowledge]] is the way out that does not require taking either back.

She also extends naturally from [[entities/tobias-rees|Rees]] in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]], if you want to keep going.

## Concept

[[concepts/situated-knowledge|Situated Knowledge]]: the argument in full, and the pressure it still faces in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]'s fourth question.

## Reading

"Situated Knowledges" is on the extension list. It is not assigned. The concept is taught from the argument rather than the text. The essay is considerably harder than anything else the course assigns.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[concepts/situated-knowledge]] · [[concepts/view-from-nowhere]]

entities/frantz-fanon.md.body:
# Frantz Fanon

**1925 to 1961.**

## The claim in one line

The look does not merely observe. **It fixes** a person in place. It arrives before they speak and decides in advance what they are.

## Key quote

> I was given not one but two, three places.

## How the course uses him

He is paired with [[entities/michel-foucault|Foucault]] to introduce **asymmetry**. Foucault describes a general condition of visibility. Fanon describes a **distributed** one: visibility that falls on different people in different ways. A theory of visibility that cannot register who is seen how is exactly the kind of framework this course takes apart.

The questions that follow from him are the hardest in the course:

- Foucault says visibility is a trap. Fanon says invisibility is also one. **Can both be true?**
- Is demanding to be seen a demand for power, or a request for permission?
- **Who in this room has the option of being unmarked**, of being seen as simply a person rather than as a type?

Both easy exits are closed. One exit says "the solution is not to be seen." That meets a question: who can afford invisibility, and who is punished by it? The other exit says "more representation fixes it." That meets another question: does being represented give you the position of the one who shows, or only of the one shown?

## Set text

The passage from *Black Skin, White Masks* in which he is fixed by a look and a phrase before he has spoken. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13]] · [[entities/michel-foucault]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7]]

entities/friedrich-nietzsche.md.body:
# Friedrich Nietzsche

**1844 to 1900.**

## The claim in one line

There are no facts, only interpretations. **The demand for a disinterested view is itself an interested move.**

## A key quote

> There is only a perspective seeing, only a perspective knowing.

## Where he appears in the course

Nietzsche gives the strongest statement of **perspectivism**: the view that there is no neutral, unframed knowledge, and that all seeing and knowing happens from a perspective. This is the position [[concepts/view-from-nowhere|the closing question]] tests.

He shows up in two places:

- As a counterweight when you try to defend an unframed view.
- In [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]], as the suspicion that the body, not the mind, is doing the reasoning.

He has no session of his own and no set text.

## The risk

Nietzsche is the thinker most likely to be used as a conversation-ender: "there are no facts, so nothing you say counts." Watch for that move and name it. Perspectivism is a claim, and a claim still has to be argued for. If it is true of itself, then it is one perspective among others. That is the fourth question of [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] arriving early, which is fine, as long as you name it.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]] · [[concepts/view-from-nowhere]]

entities/henri-bergson.md.body:
# Henri Bergson

**1859 to 1941.**

## The claim in one line

Lived time is **duration**: accumulated and indivisible, not a sequence of separable states. Memory divides into **habit** performed by the body and **pure memory** that survives whole.

## Key quote

> The past survives under two distinct forms: in motor mechanisms, and in independent recollections.

## How the course uses him

Bergson does double duty, which is unusual in this course:

- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|Week 9]]**: he supplies the strongest objection to machine minds. A system that can be reset to a previous state has no duration.
- **[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|Week 10]]**: he reframes forgetting as a failure of *attention* rather than of *storage*. On this account we forget nothing. We simply cannot attend to most of it.

The two uses are connected by one question: if a machine forgot the way a body forgets, by accumulating distortion rather than deleting files, would the week-9 objection survive?

## Paired with Freud

Week 10 runs Bergson and [[entities/sigmund-freud]] as two incompatible accounts that reach one conclusion: **forgetting is a function of memory, not a failure of it.** They disagree about almost everything else. That is the point worth making explicit. It is the course's cleanest example of an argument that does not depend on picking a winner.

## Reading

*Matter and Memory*, on habit memory and pure memory, is on the extension list. It is not assigned.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10]] · [[entities/sigmund-freud]]

entities/irmgard-emmelhainz.md.body:
# Irmgard Emmelhainz

**Contemporary.**

## The claim in one line

The shared world has fragmented into **private, algorithmically shaped worlds**. This raises the question of whether a common ground can be found that does not depend on representation at all.

## Quote to put on the board

> Can we share a world beyond representation?

Her essay title, and the session's central question.

## How the course uses her

Her essay is the set text for week 12, and the most personally implicating reading in the course.

Keep the question philosophical rather than letting it become a complaint about social media. The question is not whether the feed is bad. It is whether **sharing a world requires representation at all.**

If you answer "shared experience, not shared images: eating together, working together," you have given the strongest available answer. The question back is: **does that scale beyond a room?** If it does not, you have described a shared world or a small one, and saying which is the whole argument.

## Session format

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12]] is the only student-led session: one central question with eight angle questions beneath it. Each student takes an angle and presents a position.

## Set text

"Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", e-flux journal. Freely available. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible|W12]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6]]

entities/hito-steyerl.md.body:
# Hito Steyerl

**Born 1966.**

## The claim in one line

Image quality is not only a technical property. It is **a marker of value, access, and circulation**. Perspective shows the world from a point rather than showing the world.

## Key quote

> The poor image is a copy in motion.

## How the Oxbridge course uses her

Steyerl is **the hinge of the first unit.** She lets you use your own vocabulary of resolution and compression, then turns that vocabulary into a political argument. Her account of [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]] carries forward into [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]], so she is the only thinker whose argument spans two units.

## Set text

"In Defense of the Poor Image", e-flux journal. Before [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02]], write one paragraph on **the single sentence you found most arguable**. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Concept

[[concepts/the-poor-image|The Poor Image]]: the term and its argument in full.

## Also taught in Art Appreciation

[[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-11-aura-and-the-poor-image|L11]] pairs her with Benjamin on aura and runs a degradation lab. Oxbridge runs the same essay as an argument about who can afford a neutral image. Art Appreciation runs it as an argument about what reproduction does to a work.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it|W02]] · [[concepts/the-poor-image]] · [[concepts/linear-perspective]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1]]

entities/jean-paul-sartre.md.body:
# Jean-Paul Sartre

**1905 to 1980.**

## The claim in one line

There is no given human essence. So you are wholly responsible for what you make of yourself. This is **a burden rather than a gift.**

## Quote to put on the board

> Man is condemned to be free.

## How the Oxbridge course uses him

Sartre is offered as **one of three available positions on [[concepts/the-gap|the gap]]**, not as content to memorize.

Sartre answers the *loss* camp directly: **you cannot lose an original that never existed.** If you arrive at [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] saying "there is a real world and we are locked out of it", meet the question: can you lose something that never existed?

**The word "condemned" is the pressure point worth pushing on.** Why the harsh word, if freedom is good?

## What you actually need

You do not need Sartre's biography. You need to be able to say "I hold the Sartre position, and here is why the Camus objection does not defeat it." **That is the interview skill in miniature.**

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] · [[entities/albert-camus]] · [[concepts/the-gap]]

entities/maurice-merleau-ponty.md.body:
# Maurice Merleau-Ponty

**1908 to 1961.**

## The claim in one line

Perception is not a mental picture assembled from data. **The body is the medium through which there is a world for us at all.**

## Quote to put on the board

> The body is our general medium for having a world.

*Phenomenology of Perception*, 1945. You get this quotation before [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]], a session with no reading that still arrives with something prepared.

## How the Oxbridge course uses him

**The anchor of week 8.** The follow-up question is the one you generate yourself:

> If the body is the medium, **what happens when the medium is wrong?**

Phantom limb and chronic pain are the test cases. Synaesthesia and thermal adaptation extend them. The sharpest form of the question, once the cases are on the table: if the medium is wrong, are you wrong about the world, or do you have a different world?

The quotation is also [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06]]'s closing question, so it sits on the board for a week before the session that uses it.

## Where the session goes next

Merleau-Ponty establishes the body as medium rather than window. Spinoza's reframe closes the session by changing the question from what a body **is** to what a body **can do**. That shift is what makes [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] continuous with W08 rather than a new subject. Both map capacities instead of testing essences.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4]]

entities/michel-foucault.md.body:
# Michel Foucault

**1926 to 1984.**

## The claim in one line

Power works through **visibility and classification**, not only through force. The panopticon works because the watched person, unsure when they are seen, **watches themselves.**

## Quote to put on the board

> Visibility is a trap.

## How the Oxbridge course uses him

**Week 13.** The point is not to treat the panopticon as a metaphor for surveillance cameras. The harder claim is this: **power that makes you police yourself needs no operator at all.**

Questions to hold onto: if power works best when nobody has to exercise it, where is it located? Is visibility a trap, and who set it? Is a framework that makes you police yourself more or less powerful than one that punishes you?

An opening prompt sets this up without naming him: describe a situation in which being watched changed what you did, even though nobody said anything. You supply the panopticon before you read it.

## Paired with Fanon

**Fanon is not just an illustration of Foucault.** Foucault describes a general condition. [[entities/frantz-fanon|Fanon]] describes a distributed one. Not everyone is seen the same way, and a theory of visibility that cannot register that difference is exactly the kind of framework this course has been taking apart.

## Set text

The panopticon extract from *Discipline and Punish*. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|W13]] · [[entities/frantz-fanon]] · [[concepts/naturalization]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7]]

entities/plato.md.body:
# Plato

**c. 428 to 348 BCE.**

## The claim in one line

What we take for reality may be appearances, and there may be a level of reality that appearances imperfectly reflect.

## Quote to put on the board

> They would believe that the shadows of the objects were the truth.

## How the Oxbridge course uses him

The cave forces **[[concepts/the-ontological-turn|the ontological turn]]**.

The productive question is not whether Plato is right. It is whether our situation is the same as the prisoners' or different, and what would count as evidence either way.

Three questions carry the session. The third is the one to take most seriously:

- Is our situation the same as theirs, or different?
- You have never seen a perfect circle, only approximately circular things. Where does the knowledge of a perfect circle come from?
- **Is the prisoner who leaves better off than the ones who stay?** One answer: the prisoner who leaves is worse off, because he cannot go back. Take this seriously. It is Plato's own worry.

## Where he returns

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] and [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]] both name the W04 question as the structural template: **is the difference essential, or is it just where we currently stand?** Naming the repetition is what turns a sequence of topics into one argument.

## Set text

The Allegory of the Cave, *Republic* VII, in a clean modern translation, roughly two pages. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|W04]] · [[concepts/the-ontological-turn]] · [[concepts/the-gap]]

entities/john-berger.md.body:
# John Berger

**1926 to 2017.**

## The claim in one line

The way we see things is affected by what we know or what we believe. So **seeing is never a neutral reception of what is there.**

## Quote

> We never look at just one thing; we are always looking at the relation between things and ourselves.

## How the course uses him

Berger **opens the course**. His prose is plain enough to enter right away, and his claim is strong enough to hold up under a whole semester of pressure.

His sentence goes on the board in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]]. It is the clearest example of [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|principle 2]] in the course.

One question to test the claim: Berger says we never look at one thing, we look at the relation between things and ourselves. Is that true of a photograph of a stranger?

## Set text

*Ways of Seeing*, chapter 1, first six pages. The BBC episode of the same name is offered as a second entry point if you find the prose hard. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Also taught in Art Appreciation

Berger anchors [[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-10-berger-and-the-reproduction|Art Appreciation L10]] ("a reproduction is not a neutral copy") and heads its theorist spine.

The two courses take different chapters of the same argument: Art Appreciation runs Berger on **reproduction**, Oxbridge runs him on **perception**.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral|W01]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1]] · [[concepts/framework]]

entities/sigmund-freud.md.body:
# Sigmund Freud

**1856 to 1939.**

## The claim in one line

Forgetting is **active work rather than decay**: what is pushed down returns in distorted forms, and part of what shapes you is inaccessible to you.

## Quote to put on the board

> The repressed does not disappear; it returns.

## How the course uses him

Freud is paired with [[entities/henri-bergson]] in week 10. Two incompatible accounts reach the same conclusion: **forgetting is a function of memory, not a failure of it.**

His account raises a hard question:

> If forgetting is something you **do** rather than something that happens to you, **are you responsible for what you forget?**

In [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|week 9]] he supplies the second objection to machine minds: **a system whose weights can be inspected has no unconscious** in this sense. Like Bergson's duration objection, you then test it for whether it names a difference in kind or a difference in current engineering.

## Reading

Freud on repression and the return of the repressed is on the extension list. It is not assigned.

## Note on scope

The course uses one Freudian claim and does not teach psychoanalysis. Nothing here asks you to accept the wider framework. The session is not about memory techniques, and it is not about therapy.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10]] · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[entities/henri-bergson]]

entities/tobias-rees.md.body:
# Tobias Rees

**Contemporary.**

## The claim in one line

AI breaks concepts that defined the modern period, because **agency, creativity, knowledge, language, and understanding turn out to be separable from being alive or being human.**

## Key quote

> AI can have agency, creativity, knowledge, language and understanding without either being alive or being human.

Two further lines:

> AI defies many of the most fundamental, most taken-for-granted concepts that have defined the modern period.

> Deep learning systems have qualities that, up until recently, were considered possible only for living organisms in general and for humans in particular.

## How the course uses him

**The set text for week 9.**

Rees is useful because his claim is strong enough that you may want to resist it. That forces you to say what the human property actually is.

The question his lines aim at: if agency and understanding can come apart from being alive, were they ever properties of life, or properties we assigned to life because we had no other examples?

## The counterweight, built in

The session does not leave Rees unopposed. [[entities/henri-bergson]] supplies duration: a system that can be reset has no duration. [[entities/sigmund-freud]] supplies the unconscious: a system whose weights can be inspected has none. Both objections face the same test: **are these differences in kind, or in current engineering?**

## The Snell move

Rees points toward the claim that the interior self was not available to Homeric Greeks and was constituted over centuries partly by writing. If something that fundamental can be produced by a technology, **what might AI be producing right now that we cannot yet see?**

## Preparation

Three guiding questions come with the text. The third does the real work:

1. What concept does Rees think AI breaks?
2. Is his claim about machines or about us?
3. **Where does his argument go too far?**

## Set text

The Noema essay on AI and the concepts of the modern period. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|the reading list]].

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09]] · [[entities/benjamin-bratton]] · [[entities/donna-haraway]]

classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w.body:
# Oxbridge W05: Is the Gap a Loss, a Liberation, or a Condition?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2: The Gap]] · Week 5 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances|← W04]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history|W06 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Given that no representation reaches the thing itself, how should we live? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | **None.** Four quotations, delivered live |
| Prepared | Students arrive with a position and a case, from W04's closing question |
| Carried out | Things considered real in the past are now considered false. Were we wrong then, or did reality change? |

## Overview

This lesson asks how to live once you accept that no representation reaches the thing itself. You start with a position on **the gap**: is it a loss, a liberation, or a condition? There is no reading. Instead, four quotations arrive live, one at a time, each one pressing on the position you hold. You produce a defended stance and, if the argument moves you, a clear account of what moved you and why. The closing question, whether we were wrong in the past or reality itself changed, carries into W06.

## The ideas

### Three readings of the gap

**The gap** is the distance between any representation and the thing itself. You can read that distance in three ways, and each carries its own problem.

- **Loss.** "There is a real world and we are locked out of it." But being locked out implies you already know what is on the other side. How could you know that?
- **Liberation.** "If there is no fixed reality, we get to make one." But you have to make it out of something. Out of what?
- **Condition.** "It is just what having a mind is like." But if it is simply the condition, why does it feel like a loss to so many people?

### From knowing to living

There are two different moves here. One is an **epistemological claim**, a claim about what we can know. The other is a claim about how to live. Saying "we cannot reach the thing itself" does not by itself tell you how to act. Watch for the point where you cross from one to the other.

### Sartre

[[entities/jean-paul-sartre|Sartre]] wrote, "Man is condemned to be free." If there is no essence, no given nature, and no original to return to, then the gap may not be a loss at all: you cannot lose something that never existed. Note the word Sartre chooses. He calls freedom a condemnation, not a gift. That is a harsh word for something usually treated as good.

### Camus and the absurd

[[entities/albert-camus|Camus]] wrote, "The absurd is born of the confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world." The **absurd** is not in us and not in the world. It lives in the meeting between the two. This raises a further question: is revolt against the absurd a position you can actually hold, or only a passing mood?

Camus also wrote, "We must imagine Sisyphus happy." Ask whether that convinces you or works as a rhetorical trick. Is happiness inside the condition the same thing as accepting a loss?

### Heidegger and thrownness

Heidegger's idea is **thrownness**: we are always already thrown into a world we did not choose, with tools and frameworks that were there before us. If a framework is what makes understanding possible, rather than what blocks it, the word "gap" may no longer fit. A lens is not an obstacle to sight.

### Movement

**Movement** is the fourth quality the course names: changing your position under argument, while saying which quotation moved you and why. This is the one session that treats changing your mind as an achievement, not a lapse. It rehearses the second interview move: absorb the push without abandoning the claim.

## Day by day

- **This session.** Write your position on the gap and one reason. The room sorts into three columns: loss, liberation, condition. The four quotations arrive one at a time, each pressing on a position you hold. At the end you return to your column, and if you move, you say which quotation moved you and why. Close with the carried-forward question: were we wrong in the past, or did reality change?

## Review

Check you can:

- State the three readings of **the gap**: loss, liberation, and condition, and give the problem with each.
- Defend one reading against the other two.
- Explain why Sartre calls freedom a condemnation, not a gift.
- Define the **absurd** in Camus and say where he locates it.
- Explain Heidegger's **thrownness** and why it questions the word "gap".
- Separate an **epistemological claim** from a claim about how to live.
- Describe **movement** and say why changing your position under argument counts as a skill.

# Oxbridge W10: What Survives Forgetting?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|Unit 5: Memory and Forgetting]] · Week 10 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|← W09]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real|W11 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | Is forgetting a failure of memory, or a function of it? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | none |
| Prepared | Students bring **one memory from before they were ten**, willing to describe it out loud |
| Carried out | Money is real. Borders are real. Weekends are real. Who agreed? |

## Overview

This lesson asks whether forgetting is a failure of memory or a function of it. You bring one memory from before you were ten and use it as evidence about how memory actually works. You produce a one-sentence answer to the core question by the end of the session. The closing question about money, borders, and weekends carries forward into W11.

## The ideas

### Is the memory the event?

When you recall something, you may not be describing the event at all. You may be describing **a photograph, a story you were told, or a previous time you remembered it**. Clarity is not proof: your clearest dreams are not your truest ones, so clarity does not track accuracy. A memory retold many times can blur until you cannot tell which part is yours.

### The painted sheet

**The painted sheet** is a model of memory as repainting, not retrieval. Remembering is not pulling a file from storage. It is painting over a surface, and the new paint covers the old. After twenty years of remembering, what you hold is the last painting, made from the previous painting, not the event. On this model, a memory you revisit often may be less reliable, because each recall repaints it. This raises a further distinction: remembering something is not the same as **remembering remembering it**.

### Bergson

[[entities/henri-bergson|Bergson]] splits memory in two. **Habit memory** is performed by the body: you do not recall how to ride a bicycle, you do it. **Pure memory** survives whole, and attention filters it rather than losing it. On this account we forget nothing. We simply cannot attend to most of it. If nothing is lost and only access fails, you can ask whether that makes forgetting less serious or more.

### Freud

[[entities/sigmund-freud|Freud]] treats forgetting as work, not accident. Things are pushed down, and they return in distorted forms: slips, dreams, repetitions. If forgetting is something you do rather than something that happens to you, you can ask whether you are responsible for what you forget.

### The machine version

Linking back to W09: if a machine forgot the way a body forgets, by accumulating distortion rather than deleting files, would the human and machine line still hold?

## Day by day

- The lesson runs in one 45-minute session. You bring and describe a memory from before you were ten, then note how you know it happened. The class works through the painted sheet, Bergson, and Freud, and you commit to a one-sentence answer to the core question. The closing question is: money is real, borders are real, weekends are real, who agreed?

## Review

Check you can:

- Argue whether forgetting is a failure of memory or a function of it.
- Use your own memory as evidence without turning it into anecdote.
- Explain the painted sheet model and why a revisited memory may be less reliable.
- Distinguish remembering something from remembering remembering it.
- Distinguish Bergson's habit memory from pure memory, and explain the claim that we forget nothing.
- Explain Freud's view that forgetting is work that returns as slips, dreams, and repetitions.
- Say what survives when the record does not.

# Oxbridge W09: Is the Human and Machine Line Essential or Contingent?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4: The Body and the Machine]] · Week 9 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|← W08]] | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10 →]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | When you say a machine cannot do something, are you describing what a mind necessarily is, or what technology currently happens to be? |
| Duration | 45 minutes, [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-session-structure-template\|standard template]] |
| Reading | [[entities/tobias-rees\|Rees]], Noema — with three guiding questions sent in advance |
| Carried out | Human memory is repainted every time it is used. Machine memory is a record that can be loaded or deleted. Is that a difference in kind? |

## Overview

This lesson asks whether the line between human and machine is essential or contingent. You start from a list of things you can do that a machine cannot, then test each item against what machines already do. You read Rees, weigh Bergson and Freud against him, and end by committing to one sentence: is the human and machine distinction essential or contingent. That commitment, and the question of whether human and machine memory differ in kind, feeds directly into [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10]].

## The ideas

### Essential or contingent

A property is **essential** if it is part of what a mind necessarily is. A property is **contingent** if it is only what technology currently happens to be. When you name something a machine cannot do, ask which kind of claim you are making. For each item, two tests help: what exactly would a machine have to do for you to withdraw the item, and has any item like it already been withdrawn in the last ten years. Common answers stretch under pressure. "Feel" needs a test for evidence of feeling in anything, including another person. "Understand rather than predict" needs a test that separates the two; if none exists, the distinction may do no work. "Have a body" points to being alive rather than to bodies, since robots have bodies. "Create something new" needs a definition of new, since much human creation is recombination.

### Rees

**[[entities/tobias-rees|Tobias Rees]]** argues that AI breaks concepts we take for granted. Three of his lines:

> AI defies many of the most fundamental, most taken-for-granted concepts that have defined the modern period.

> Deep learning systems have qualities that, up until recently, were considered possible only for living organisms in general and for humans in particular.

> AI can have agency, creativity, knowledge, language and understanding without either being alive or being human.

The pointed question: if agency and understanding can come apart from being alive, were they ever properties of life, or properties we assigned to life because we had no other examples?

### Bergson and Freud as counterweight

**[[entities/henri-bergson|Henri Bergson]]** holds that lived time is **duration**: time accumulated and indivisible, not a sequence of separate states. A system that can be reset to a previous state has no duration.

**[[entities/sigmund-freud|Sigmund Freud]]** holds that there is a part of you that you did not author and cannot access, which shapes what you do: the unconscious. A system whose weights can be inspected has no unconscious in that sense.

Ask whether these are differences in kind or only in current engineering. If a system accumulated distortion instead of storing records, would either objection survive? That question opens W10.

### The Snell move

The interior self, the sense of having an inner life, may not have been available to Homeric Greeks. It was constituted over centuries, partly by writing. If something that fundamental can be produced by a technology, AI may be producing something now that we cannot yet see.

## Day by day

- **This session.** Read Rees in Noema before class and answer three questions: what concept does Rees think AI breaks; is his claim about machines or about us; and where does his argument go too far. In class you list what a machine cannot do, test each item, weigh Rees against Bergson and Freud, and commit to one sentence on whether the human and machine distinction is essential or contingent. Essentialists must name the property. Contingentists must say whether any distinction could ever be essential on their view.

## Review

Check you can:

- Distinguish an **essential** property from a **contingent** one.
- Use **Rees** to say where the human and machine line has already moved.
- Explain **Bergson's** duration and why a system that can be reset has none.
- Explain **Freud's** unconscious and why inspectable weights differ from it.
- Explain the Snell move: how writing helped constitute the interior self.
- Argue whether repainted human memory and loadable machine memory differ in kind or in degree.

# Oxbridge W14: Is a View from Nowhere Possible?

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8: Synthesis]] · Week 14 of 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world|← W13]]

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Core question | The title carries a deliberate echo of Nagel and names the course throughline in five words |
| Duration | 45 minutes, **template dropped**: four questions at ≈ 10 minutes each |
| Reading | **None.** Students think back over the term — their notes, and the group-chat thread |
| Prepared | The position they have changed their mind about |
| Carried out | Nothing. For the first time in fourteen weeks, students answer a question instead |

## Overview

This is the final session of the course. You look back over the whole term and answer four large questions directly, instead of carrying out a task. There is no reading and nothing to hand in. Come ready to name one position you have changed your mind about this term and to say what changed it. The session pulls the course's throughline into one line: is a **view from nowhere** possible, a view of reality that no particular framework shapes? The phrase echoes the philosopher **Thomas Nagel**.

## The ideas

### Is an unframed view of anything even possible?

Every framework you studied this term hid the edges that made it a framework rather than reality itself. The examples run through the whole course: the map, [[concepts/linear-perspective|linear perspective]], the body, machine cognition, and the categories that decide who counts. If even science is a chosen set of exclusions, what marks a good frame from a bad one, if not closeness to an unframed reality that no one can reach? This is the week 4 question returning. [[concepts/situated-knowledge|Situated knowledge]] is the third option if you are stuck between neutral science and total relativism: knowledge is always tied to a position, but that does not make all positions equal.

### Does the human and machine line survive its own test?

The course drew the line between human and machine at **memory**. Human memory is sedimented and repainted: it builds up and distorts over time. Machine memory is a clean record: it stores and returns. But if a system learned the way a body learns, through accumulation and distortion rather than storage, would the distinction hold, or were you only describing what AI happens to be right now? This has the same shape as the Plato question from week 4.

### Whose agreement made this real?

Take any object in the room and trace it back. Its reality rests on agreement. Push further and agreement becomes power. Then the real question: are power and agreement two different things, or the same thing described from two positions?

### Is "everything is a framework" itself a framework?

This is the hardest move and the reason the session exists. The course has trained a suspicion of frameworks. Now apply that suspicion to the course. If every position is framed, is that claim framed too? If it is, why accept it? If it is not, you have found your view from nowhere. Ask also whether the course gave you a better view or only a different one, and what would tell you which. Ask whether the suspicion is useful, or whether it ends in a place where nothing can be said.

## Day by day

- **The single session (45 minutes).** You open on the prompt "What does the world look like?" and sit with it silently for two minutes. Then you work through the four questions, about ten minutes each, with no scaffolding. You close by answering, not asking: say one thing you now believe that you did not believe at the start of the course, and say what changed it.

## Review

Check you can:

- Name a position you changed your mind about this term, and say what changed it.
- Explain what a **view from nowhere** would be and why the course doubts one is possible.
- Use **situated knowledge** as a third option between neutral science and total relativism.
- Say whether the human and machine line, drawn at **memory**, survives its own test.
- Apply the course's suspicion to the course itself and judge whether "everything is a framework" is itself a framework.
- State the throughline of the course in your own words.
