# Oxbridge Unit 4: The Body and the Machine

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 4 of 8 · Weeks 8–9 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|← Unit 3]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|Unit 5 →]]

## Unit question

**Where does the thinking thing end?**

## Why these two sessions belong together

Both sessions ask the same structural question: **is a boundary essential or contingent?** Week 8 asks whether the body is a reliable instrument or a framework like any other. Week 9 asks whether the line between human and machine is a real difference in kind or just a description of where technology currently stands.

One line holds the two weeks together:

> What a body can do and what a machine can do turn out to be the same kind of question. Both are about mapping capacities, not testing essences.

## Week 8: the body

[[entities/maurice-merleau-ponty]] gives the anchor: the body is our general medium for having a world. If that is true, what happens when the medium is wrong?

You work through four cases, one at a time: **phantom limb, chronic pain without injury, synaesthesia, thermal adaptation.** Each one breaks a different escape route. The session closes on Spinoza's reframe: stop asking what a body **is** and ask what a body **can do**.

## Week 9: the machine

[[entities/tobias-rees]] argues that AI defies concepts that have defined the modern period; that deep learning systems have qualities once thought possible only for living things; and that a system can have agency, creativity, knowledge, language and understanding without being alive or human.

[[entities/henri-bergson]] and [[entities/sigmund-freud]] supply the counterweight: **duration** and **the unconscious** as things a system without a history cannot have. [[entities/donna-haraway]] and [[entities/benjamin-bratton]] extend the argument outward.

## Sessions

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted|W08: Can the body be trusted?]] — describe being cold without the word cold and without a number. Four cases, then Spinoza.
- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent|W09: Is the human and machine line essential or contingent?]] — the whole session is one list, which you write in the first two minutes.

## Concepts introduced

[[concepts/situated-knowledge|Situated Knowledge]]

## Preparation

W08 sends you one quotation in advance. It is the only session in the course with no reading that still arrives with something prepared. W09 sends the Rees essay with three guiding questions. The third question, "where does his argument go too far?", invites you to disagree before you open the text.

Nothing is written or collected. The course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]].

## Teaching notes

- **W09 repeats the shape of W04.** Both ask whether a difference is essential or just where we currently stand. The same pairing returns a third time in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14]]'s second question.
- **W08's opening prompt is the whole session in miniature:** describe being cold without using the word cold and without using a number. It is harder than it looks.
- In W09, both sides face a hard demand. The essentialists must name the property. The contingentists must say whether *any* distinction could ever be essential on their view, or whether they have made the word meaningless.
- **Carsten Höller's laboratory of doubt** is an optional visual anchor for W08.

## Bridge to Unit 5

> The strongest surviving distinction students usually offer is that human memory is sedimented and repainted while machine memory is a clean record. That claim deserves its own session.

W09 closes on exactly that question, which [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|Unit 5]] takes up.

# Oxbridge Unit 5: Memory and Forgetting

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 5 of 8 · Week 10 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|← Unit 4]] | [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6 →]]

## Unit question

**What survives forgetting?**

This is a one-session unit. It tests one claim: that human memory is repainted while machine memory is a clean record. This is the last distinction left standing after Week 9, so it gets a session of its own.

## The image to work from

> A painted sheet. Each time you remember something, you do not retrieve a stored file. You repaint the surface, and the new paint covers the old. What you have after twenty years of remembering is not the event. It is the last painting, made from the previous painting.

## The two philosophers

Two accounts that disagree with each other, yet reach the same conclusion from opposite directions:

- **[[entities/henri-bergson]]** separates **habit memory**, which the body performs, from **pure memory**, which survives whole and is filtered out by attention rather than lost. On this account you forget nothing. You simply cannot attend to most of it.
- **[[entities/sigmund-freud]]** proposes that forgetting is not decay but active work: things are pushed down, and they return in distorted form.

> Between them, the same conclusion arrives from two directions. **Forgetting is not the failure of memory. It is a function of it.**

The two accounts are incompatible and converge anyway. That is the point. It is the cleanest example in the course of an argument that does not depend on picking a winner.

## Session

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting|W10: What survives forgetting?]] — you bring a memory from before you were ten, and discover how many of you are describing a photograph or a story.

## Concepts introduced

None new. The unit works the concepts you already have: [[concepts/the-gap|the gap]] applied to your own past, and [[concepts/framework|framework]] applied to attention.

## Preparation

No reading. Bring **one memory from before you were ten**, and be willing to describe it out loud. This is the only session whose preparation is personal rather than textual.

Nothing is written or collected. The course is [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]. One question to hold: is forgetting a failure of memory or a function of it?

## Focus

This is not about how to remember better or how to revise for exams. The question is what memory is for.

The session returns to Week 9. It asks the harder version: if a machine forgot the way a body forgets, by accumulating distortion rather than deleting files, would the human/machine line still hold? Bergson's objection from Week 9 is on trial here.

## Bridge to Unit 6

> If each person's past is repainted privately, the question becomes how any two people share anything at all.

W10 closes on the question that opens the next unit: money is real, borders are real, weekends are real, who agreed? [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6]].

# Oxbridge Seminar Plan

> [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · fourteen weekly sessions · **Spring 2027, dates unassigned**

This page shows the whole course: what happens each week, what it feeds, and where the order matters.

## Status

The course runs for fourteen weekly sessions in Spring 2027. It has no fixed dates yet. Teaching would resume after the winter vacation, around **Mon 2027-02-22** ([[calendar|school academic calendar]]). Fourteen unbroken weeks reach about the week of **2027-05-24**. Qingming (around 2027-04-05) and May Day (around 05-01 to 05-05) push the close to about **2027-06-07**. These dates are provisional. They may shift when the school publishes the spring calendar. Sessions are numbered by week.

## The arc

The units are not a list of topics. Each unit closes by producing the question the next one opens with. The sessions hand off the same way. W02 ends on the thermometer, which is W03's opening prompt. W03 ends on the tree in the forest, which W04 polls in its first five minutes. **The handoffs are the course.** The order carries more than it looks like it would.

| Week | Session | Unit | The move |
|---|---|---|---|
| W01 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w01-is-perception-ever-neutral\|Is perception ever neutral?]] | U1 | Seeing is already interpretive. Berger arrives only after students have said it |
| W02 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w02-do-images-represent-reality-or-produce-it\|Do images represent reality or produce it?]] | U1 | Resolution turns from a technical property into a political one |
| W03 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w03-can-measurement-reach-the-thing-itself\|Can measurement reach the thing itself?]] | U2 | The gap, in measurement and then in language. Science narrows it; nothing closes it |
| W04 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w04-is-there-a-reality-behind-appearances\|Is there a reality behind appearances?]] | U2 | The ontological turn. Plato, and perspective as a datable invention |
| W05 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition\|Is the gap a loss, a liberation, or a condition?]] | U2 | Three livable positions on the gap, adopted and defended |
| W06 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w06-does-reality-have-a-history\|Does reality have a history?]] | U3 | Maps, Taprobana, H. pylori. Frameworks hide their edges |
| W07 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w07-argument-workshop\|Argument workshop]] | U3 | Midpoint consolidation. Claim first, qualification second |
| W08 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w08-can-the-body-be-trusted\|Can the body be trusted?]] | U4 | The body as medium, not window. Spinoza's reframe |
| W09 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w09-is-the-human-and-machine-line-essential-or-contingent\|Is the human/machine line essential or contingent?]] | U4 | Rees against Bergson and Freud. The same question as W04 |
| W10 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w10-what-survives-forgetting\|What survives forgetting?]] | U5 | The painted sheet. Forgetting as a function, not a failure |
| W11 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w11-whose-agreement-makes-a-thing-real\|Whose agreement makes a thing real?]] | U6 | The sorting exercise breaks, and the breaking is the lesson |
| W12 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w12-is-a-common-world-still-possible\|Is a common world still possible?]] | U6 | Emmelhainz. Student-led angles |
| W13 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w13-who-gets-to-show-us-the-world\|Who gets to show us the world?]] | U7 | Foucault and Fanon. Every framework has a maker |
| W14 | [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible\|Is a view from nowhere possible?]] | U8 | The suspicion applied to the course that trained it |

## Units

- [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-1-the-image|Unit 1: The Image]]: W1–2. Berger and Steyerl. You already live inside images, so the course can start rigorous without starting hard.
- [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-2-the-gap|Unit 2: The Gap]]: W3–5. Epistemology, then ontology, then the existential turn. The same problem turned a quarter turn each week.
- [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-3-frameworks-and-history|Unit 3: Frameworks and History]]: W6–7. Does reality have a history, then the midpoint pressure workshop.
- [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-4-the-body-and-the-machine|Unit 4: The Body and the Machine]]: W8–9. Two sessions asking one structural question: is a boundary essential or contingent?
- [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-5-memory-and-forgetting|Unit 5: Memory and Forgetting]]: W10. The single-session unit, and the most personal one.
- [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-6-collective-reality|Unit 6: Collective Reality]]: W11–12. Agreement, then the fragmentation of the shared world.
- [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|Unit 7: Power and Visibility]]: W13. The unit that collects everything. The framework turns out to have an owner.
- [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-8-synthesis|Unit 8: Synthesis]]: W14. Four questions, no reading, no new material.

## Nothing is set, collected, or graded

**The course is discussion only.** There is no written work, no assessment, and no attainment codes. See [[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|Assessment — none]].

Each week asks the same of you: **read the text if there is one, and arrive with a position.** Seven of the fourteen sessions set a reading. The rest run on cases you already have. The only thing that travels between sessions is the closing question, posted to the group chat with a quote attached.

Six of these questions began as essay prompts. All six now run as **discussion questions** in [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-question-bank|the question bank]]. Four criteria describe a strong contribution: **commitment**, **pressure**, **precision**, and **movement**. Name them aloud when you commit and move.

The course produces no artifact. Nothing outlives the room except the group chat.

## Readings, by week

Only seven sessions have a set text. The rest run on cases you already have. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-course-design-principles|the design principles]].

| Week | Text |
|---|---|
| W01 | Berger, *Ways of Seeing*, ch. 1 (first six pages) |
| W02 | Steyerl, "In Defense of the Poor Image", e-flux |
| W04 | Plato, Allegory of the Cave, *Republic* VII (≈ two pages, modern translation) |
| W09 | Rees, on AI and the concepts of the modern period, Noema |
| W12 | Emmelhainz, "Can We Share a World Beyond Representation", e-flux |
| W13 | Foucault, *Discipline and Punish*, panopticon extract; Fanon, *Black Skin, White Masks*, the look passage |

W03, W05, W07, W08, W10, W11 and W14 set no reading. W08 sends one quotation in advance. W09 sends three guiding questions with the text. For full holdings, see [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-reading-list|Reading List]].

## Where the sequence is load-bearing

Four points where the order carries weight:

1. **W01 → W02.** W02 calls back your W01 commitments by name. If you said perception can be trained toward neutrality, you "must now say what a neutral image would look like and who would be able to afford it."
2. **W02 → W03 → W04.** Two handoffs are disguised as topic changes: the thermometer, then the tree in the forest. You are meant to meet W03 as a new subject and find that it is not.
3. **W08 → W09.** W08 ends on one line: what a body can do and what a machine can do are the same kind of question. Without it, W09 reads as a change of subject.
4. **W04 → W09 → W14.** The same structural question comes three times: is the difference essential, or is it where we currently stand? W14's second question depends on your having met it twice already.

# Oxbridge Unit 8: Synthesis

[[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge|Oxbridge]] · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-seminar-plan|Seminar Plan]] · Unit 8 of 8 · Week 14 · [[classes/oxbridge/unit-plans/oxbridge-unit-7-power-and-visibility|← Unit 7]]

## Unit question

**Is a view from nowhere possible?**

The phrase echoes the philosopher **Nagel**, and it names the throughline of the whole course.

## What the session does

Four questions. No reading, no new material.

You hold the whole semester in one hand and turn its critique back on itself. If every framework hides its edges, what about the framework this course has been building? Is "everything is a framework" itself a framework that hides its edges? The strongest move in this room is to notice that the course has trained you in a suspicion that cannot be applied to itself without collapsing.

## Session

- [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w14-is-a-view-from-nowhere-possible|W14: Is a view from nowhere possible?]] — four questions at roughly ten minutes each, and the only session in the course with no closing question.

## Concepts

[[concepts/view-from-nowhere|View from Nowhere]] is the unit's own concept. [[concepts/situated-knowledge|Situated Knowledge]] is the escape route you need in question 1: the third option when you are stuck between "science is neutral" and "everything is subjective."

## Preparation

No reading. Bring **the position you have changed your mind about**. This is the only preparation in the course that asks you to look back rather than forward, and the closing question depends on it. Think back over the term, using your notes and the group chat.

Nothing is written or collected ([[classes/oxbridge/assessments/oxbridge-writing-and-assessment|discussion only]]). The course ends on its title question, spoken.

## The three retrospective moves

Each of the four questions reaches back into a different part of the course, which makes the session a synthesis rather than a review:

1. **Is an unframed view of anything even possible?** The map, perspective, the body, machine cognition, the categories that decide who counts. Every framework in the term, in one list.
2. **Does the human/machine line survive its own test?** The W09 question, re-asked after W10 supplied the memory objection. It is structurally identical to the Plato question from week 4.
3. **Whose agreement made this real?** W11 and W13 in one: push until someone says *power* rather than *agreement*, then ask whether they are different things or the same thing described from two positions.
4. **Is "everything is a framework" itself a framework?** The hardest move, and the reason the session exists.

## Notes

- Question 4 is not meant to resolve. The aim is a room that can hold the paradox without collapsing into relativism or fleeing back to naive realism. Holding a genuinely open question without needing to close it is precisely what an Oxbridge interviewer tests for.
- The closing is inverted. For the first time in fourteen weeks you carry no question out of the room. You answer one instead: say one thing you now believe that you did not believe when the course began, and say what changed it.
- Because the preparation asks you to look back, the last session is built on **movement**, the fourth of the four qualities the course names.

## After the unit

Mock interviews may run in the following week if the timetable allows: twelve minutes per student, one question, no preparation. That week sits outside the fourteen. See [[classes/oxbridge/oxbridge-interview-preparation|Interview Preparation]] for the format.

# Albert Camus

**1913 to 1960.**

## The claim in one line

The absurd is not in us and not in the world but **in the meeting** between the human demand for clarity and the world's silence. The honest response is neither despair nor false hope.

## Key quotes

> The absurd is born of the confrontation between the human need and the unreasonable silence of the world.

> We must imagine Sisyphus happy.

You meet both in [[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]], and not together. The first opens the position. The second tests whether it is livable.

## How the Oxbridge course uses him

Camus is used to test whether the **condition** position is livable. Two questions to work through:

- Camus locates the absurd in the meeting, not in us and not in the world. Does that change anything?
- Is *We must imagine Sisyphus happy* convincing, or is it a rhetorical trick? Is happiness inside the condition the same as accepting a loss?

> [!important] The sharpest question
> Is **revolt** a defensible philosophical position, or a mood dressed as one?

This is the question you will most want to answer with feeling rather than argument. Answer it with argument.

## Links

[[classes/oxbridge/lesson-plans/oxbridge-w05-is-the-gap-a-loss-a-liberation-or-a-condition|W05]] · [[entities/jean-paul-sartre]] · [[concepts/the-gap]]

# 9479 S1 A1: Recording Milestone

[[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design|A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/assessments/9479-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/9479-s1-lesson-05-recording-pages-and-a1|Lesson 05]] · Attainment 1 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Fri 2026-10-09, in session |
| Category | Attainment, the first of four in the 50% category |
| Format | Portfolio review of your recording work, in class, with nothing added during the review |
| Assesses | **AO1 Record**, 15 marks of Component 1 |
| What is reviewed | Your intention, your Stage 1 pages, your sustained study, and the supporting studies behind it |
| Feeds | Component 1 Portfolio, and the mid-term grades due Thu 2026-10-29 |
| Returned | Sat 2026-10-10, banded, one-to-one |
| Unit | [[classes/a-level-art-design/unit-plans/9479-s1-unit-2-recording-and-sustained-study\|U2 Recording and Sustained Study]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Present recording pages an examiner could read in order, without you standing next to them explaining.
2. Record from **primary** sources as well as secondary ones, and show it.
3. Record the same subject in more than one way: different angles, viewpoints, close-up study, surface quality, tone, form.
4. Make your intention legible from what you chose to record, not only from what you wrote about it.
5. Reflect critically in writing on what the recording gave you and what it did not.
6. Band your own work against the AO1 criteria and land within one band of your teacher.

## The task

You make nothing new for A1. It reviews the recording work Unit 2 has been building since Week 1, in the state it is in on the day.

What is on the table:

- **Your intention.** The written statement, plus the mind map behind it.
- **Stage 1 pages.** Your recording pages, built and sequenced.
- **The sustained study.** The single extended piece, finished to the standard the rest of the work sits at.
- **Supporting studies.** Everything that fed the above, including the holiday sketchbook recording, dated.

This is a **Component 1 milestone**, so it is marked with the real Cambridge criteria rather than a classroom substitute. Component 1 is eventually marked by Cambridge as one whole portfolio out of 60. A1 samples the AO1 column of that grid, 15 marks, while there is still a semester left to act on it.

## Instructions

**Before the review.** On Thu 10-08 you mark your own recording against the AO1 criteria below, in writing and honestly. That self-check is part of the assessment protocol, not a warm-up. Then you get a fixes list only. Nothing new starts the day before a review.

**On the day.**

1. Lay out the intention, the Stage 1 pages, the sustained study and the supporting studies, in the order you want them read.
2. The review happens in session, with you present.
3. **Nothing is added during the review.** Work that is not on the table at the start is not assessed.

**After.** A1 comes back banded on Sat 2026-10-10. You convert the feedback into **three specific written actions**, one to one. Those three actions are retrieved at A2.

**If you are absent.** Contact your teacher at least 24 hours before the review. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8). Request extensions 24 hours ahead too.

## Rubric

**AO1 Record**, 15 marks, from Cambridge's Component 1 grid. Full grid and all four AOs: [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessment-criteria|9479 Assessment Criteria]].

AO1 asks you to *record ideas, observations and insights relevant to intentions, reflecting critically on work and progress.* Three things are judged: **selection of subject matter**, **methods of recording**, and **communication of intention through critical reflection**.

| Level | Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|
| **5** | 13–15 | Perceptive selection of relevant subject matter from a variety of sources · highly effective methods of recording ideas, insights and observations · clear intention communicated **consistently** through critical reflection |
| **4** | 10–12 | Confident selection of relevant subject matter from a variety of sources · effective methods of recording · clear intention communicated through critical reflection |
| **3** | 7–9 | Competent selection of relevant subject matter from different sources · competent methods of recording · competent communication of intention through critical reflection |
| **2** | 4–6 | Sufficient selection from different sources · adequate methods of recording · some communication of intention through critical reflection |
| **1** | 1–3 | Limited selection from sources · limited methods of recording · basic ability to communicate intention through critical reflection |
| **0** | 0 | No creditable response |

Two distinctions decide most of the marks:

- **"A variety of sources" against "different sources."** Levels 4 and 5 need variety. In practice that means primary recording (places, people, objects, gallery or studio visits) alongside secondary material, not a folder of images off a screen.
- **"Consistently" against once.** Level 5 needs critical reflection running through the work, not one strong statement at the front.

Your mark is then curved under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] rather than reported raw, because it is a Forecast Grade signal partway through a two-year course, not a Cambridge score.

## After the sit

- Returned Sat 2026-10-10, banded, with feedback given one to one on a rota.
- You write **three specific actions** from that feedback. Not three feelings about it.
- The self-check target: your own banding lands within one band of your teacher's. This is the calibration habit the whole course leans on, and the gap is tracked across all four attainments.
- A1 feeds the mid-term grades due Thu 2026-10-29.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **CS1**, formal elements study set + Recording Page 1 | The first version of what A1 reviews. Reread its feedback |
| **CS2**, intention statement + mind map | Your intention, already written and marked once |
| **CS3**, the sustained-study progress check | Whether the sustained study is actually on track |
| **CS4**, recording pages build check (Wed 09-30) | The dress rehearsal. What CS4 flagged is what A1 will find |
| The break sketchbook homework | Primary-source recording, dated. This is where "a variety of sources" is won |
| [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessment-criteria\|The AO1 criteria]] | The Thu 10-08 self-check. Use Cambridge's words, not your own summary of them |

# 9479 S1 A3: Development Milestone

[[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design|A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/assessments/9479-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/9479-s1-lesson-13-final-plan-and-a3|Lesson 13]] · Attainment 3 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Thu 2026-12-10, in session |
| Category | Attainment, the third of four in the 50% category |
| Format | Portfolio review of the whole development run, in class, with nothing added during the review |
| Assesses | **AO3 Develop**, 20 marks of Component 1 |
| What is reviewed | Compositions 1 and 2, the targeted tests, your written evaluation, and the final composition plan |
| Feeds | Component 1 Portfolio, and the build run that makes the final outcome |
| Returned | Fri 2026-12-11, banded |
| Unit | [[classes/a-level-art-design/unit-plans/9479-s1-unit-4-development\|U4 Development]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Produce two genuinely different compositions rather than one composition twice.
2. Run targeted tests that answer a question you actually had, and record the answer.
3. Push one real alternative, reject it on paper, and annotate why you rejected it.
4. Argue your palette and materials from **meaning**, not from preference or availability.
5. Evaluate your own development in writing, naming weaknesses as precisely as strengths.
6. Produce a final composition plan **complete enough that a capable stranger could begin the piece from it.**

## The task

A3 reviews the whole development run. You make nothing new for it.

What is on the table:

- **Composition 1 and Composition 2**, photographed and laid out side by side.
- **The targeted tests**, with the critique response written up.
- **Your written evaluation** of the development.
- **The final composition plan**: full-size or scaled, with structure, values and the sequence of work marked, plus the thumbnails that tested it and the annotated rejection.
- **Palette and materials**, swatched and tested on the actual support you will use.

This is the last review before the final outcome is built. Everything it asks for exists so that the build run is execution, not invention.

## Instructions

**Before the review.** On Wed 12-09 you self-check against the AO3 criteria below, **in writing.** Settle your palette and materials, swatch them, test them on the real support, and name them for what they carry, before the review, not during the build.

**On the day.**

1. Lay out both compositions side by side, the tests, the evaluation and the plan.
2. The review happens in session, with you present.
3. **Nothing is added during the review.**

**After.** A3 comes back banded on Fri 12-11. You then **physically amend the plan** from the feedback and initial the changes. This is the one attainment whose feedback you can still spend, because the outcome has not been built yet.

**If Friday is lost.** Foreign Culture Day may take Fri 12-11. If it does, the feedback lesson moves to the next available session. The assessment itself does not move.

**If you are absent.** Contact your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8).

## Rubric

**AO3 Develop**, 20 marks, from Cambridge's Component 1 grid. Full grid: [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessment-criteria|9479 Assessment Criteria]].

*Develop ideas through investigations informed by contextual and other sources, making purposeful connections and demonstrating analytical and critical understanding.*

Four things are judged: **purposeful connections**, **an investigation showing analytical and critical understanding**, **exploration of visual elements**, and **critical reflection on your own strengths and weaknesses**.

| Level | Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|
| **5** | 17–20 | Perceptive and mature connections between contextual and other sources · focused investigation demonstrating highly effective analytical and critical understanding · accomplished exploration of visual elements to communicate ideas · **insightful** reflection on own strengths and weaknesses |
| **4** | 13–16 | Confident connections · **focused** investigation demonstrating confident analytical and critical understanding · effective exploration of visual elements · effective reflection on own strengths and weaknesses |
| **3** | 9–12 | Competent connections · **thorough** investigation demonstrating competent analytical and critical understanding · competent exploration of visual elements · competent reflection |
| **2** | 5–8 | Some evidence of connections · adequate investigation demonstrating some analytical and critical understanding · adequate exploration · adequate reflection |
| **1** | 1–4 | Limited evidence of connections · limited investigation demonstrating basic analytical and critical understanding · limited exploration · basic reflection |
| **0** | 0 | No creditable response |

Two things separate the top two levels here:

- **"Focused" against "thorough."** Level 3 covers the ground. Levels 4 and 5 make the development *converge*: each composition, test and decision narrows toward one outcome instead of adding options.
- **Exploring visual elements means alternatives.** Cambridge asks for alternative compositions, angles, viewpoints, perspectives, forms and designs, visible in your own imagery. The rejected alternative, annotated, is worth more than a third variation you kept.

AO3 carries the most marks of any AO in Component 1, 20 of 60, because this specification weights Develop above Present. Your mark is then curved under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] rather than reported raw.

## After the sit

- Returned Fri 2026-12-11 (or the next available session if Foreign Culture Day takes it), banded.
- You amend the composition plan physically and initial the changes.
- Your actions from A2 are retrieved and checked.
- The homework after this is the written plan adjustment: what changed and why.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **CS8**, both compositions photographed side by side | The comparison A3 will make. Make it yourself first |
| **CS9**, targeted tests + critique response | Already marked once. The critique response is AO3 reflection evidence |
| The direction sentence you defended at A2 | The development should visibly serve it |
| Mon to Wed of Lesson 13 | The plan, the thumbnails, the palette. All three are assessed |
| [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessment-criteria\|The AO3 criteria]] | The Wed 12-09 self-check, in writing |

# 9479 S1 A2: Exploration and Artist Study

[[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design|A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/assessments/9479-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/9479-s1-lesson-09-artist-2-bridge-piece-and-a2|Lesson 09]] · Attainment 2 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Mon 2026-11-09, in session |
| Category | Attainment, the second of four in the 50% category |
| Format | Portfolio review of the whole of Unit 3, in class, with nothing added during the review |
| Assesses | **AO2 Explore** and **AO3 Develop**, 35 marks of Component 1 |
| What is reviewed | Twelve media experiments, your media selection, the scale trial, both artist pages, and the bridge piece |
| Feeds | Component 1 Portfolio, and the direction you take into Unit 4 |
| Returned | Tue 2026-11-10, banded |
| Unit | [[classes/a-level-art-design/unit-plans/9479-s1-unit-3-exploration-and-artist-study\|U3 Exploration and Artist Study]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Experiment widely enough that the media choice you make is a decision, not a default.
2. Say **why** you selected the media you did, in terms of what you are trying to communicate.
3. Set two artists against each other and name the **tension** between them, not their similarities.
4. Make a bridge piece that visibly carries something from the artist study into your own work.
5. Reflect critically on which experiments failed, and what the failure told you.
6. Leave the review with **one direction you can defend in two minutes.**

## The task

A2 reviews everything Unit 3 produced. You make nothing new for it.

What is on the table:

- **Twelve media experiments**, documented in the sketchbook.
- **Your media selection**, with the written note saying what you are taking forward and why.
- **The scale trial.**
- **Artist pages for both artists**, with your analysis.
- **The bridge piece**, made in one sustained session and finished across the Juniors Days gap.

The bridge piece is the load-bearing item. It is the object that proves the artist study changed your work rather than sitting beside it.

A2 is marked on **two** AO columns, which is why it carries the most marks of any milestone this semester: AO2 Explore (15) and AO3 Develop (20).

## Instructions

**Before the review.** Plan and sign off the bridge piece on Mon 11-02. Make it on Tue 11-03. Finish it during the six-day Juniors Days gap, on the schedule you dated in your sketchbook. The gap is the finishing window, not a break from it.

**On the day.**

1. Lay out all five items in the order you want them read.
2. The review happens in session, with you present.
3. **Nothing is added during the review.**

**After.** A2 comes back banded on Tue 11-10. You write **one sentence** naming the direction you are taking into Unit 4, and defend it in a two-minute stand-up to the room. A direction you cannot defend out loud is not yet a direction.

**If you are absent.** Contact your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8).

## Rubric

**AO2 Explore (15) + AO3 Develop (20) = 35 marks**, from Cambridge's Component 1 grid. Full grid: [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessment-criteria|9479 Assessment Criteria]].

### AO2 Explore, 15 marks

*Explore and select appropriate resources, media, techniques and processes, reviewing and refining ideas as work develops.*

| Level | Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|
| **5** | 13–15 | Perceptive selection of media, techniques and processes · highly effective and **consistent** understanding of appropriate skills to explore visual elements · highly effective experimentation to review and refine ideas as work develops |
| **4** | 10–12 | Confident selection of appropriate media, techniques and processes · effective and consistent understanding of appropriate skills · effective experimentation to review and refine |
| **3** | 7–9 | Competent selection of media · competent understanding of appropriate skills · **relevant** experimentation to review and refine |
| **2** | 4–6 | Sufficient selection of media · adequate understanding of appropriate skills · adequate experimentation |
| **1** | 1–3 | Limited selection of media · basic understanding of appropriate skills · limited experimentation |
| **0** | 0 | No creditable response |

Cambridge states clearly that AO2 does **not** mean technical skill alone. Twelve beautiful experiments that were never reviewed or refined sit lower than eight rougher ones that visibly learned from each other.

### AO3 Develop, 20 marks

*Develop ideas through investigations informed by contextual and other sources, making purposeful connections and demonstrating analytical and critical understanding.*

| Level | Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|
| **5** | 17–20 | **Perceptive and mature** connections between contextual and other sources · focused investigation demonstrating highly effective analytical and critical understanding · accomplished exploration of visual elements to communicate ideas · insightful reflection on own strengths and weaknesses |
| **4** | 13–16 | Confident connections · focused investigation demonstrating confident analytical and critical understanding · effective exploration of visual elements · effective reflection on own strengths and weaknesses |
| **3** | 9–12 | Competent connections · **thorough** investigation demonstrating competent analytical and critical understanding · competent exploration of visual elements · competent reflection |
| **2** | 5–8 | **Some evidence** of connections · adequate investigation demonstrating some analytical and critical understanding · adequate exploration · adequate reflection |
| **1** | 1–4 | Limited evidence of connections · limited investigation demonstrating basic analytical and critical understanding · limited exploration · basic reflection |
| **0** | 0 | No creditable response |

At this milestone AO3 is judged on the **connections**: research to recording to experiment to your own work. The bridge piece is where a marker looks for them. An artist page that describes an artist without changing anything downstream shows AO3 at level 1 or 2, however well written it is.

Both marks are then curved under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] rather than reported raw.

## After the sit

- Returned Tue 2026-11-10, banded on both AOs separately.
- You write and defend the one-sentence direction.
- Your three written actions from A1 are retrieved and checked here. That is the point of writing them down.
- Self-check target unchanged: your own banding within one band of your teacher's.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **CS5**, twelve media experiments documented | The AO2 evidence base. If it is not documented it does not count |
| **CS6**, Stage 3 page + media selection note | The written "why this medium" that AO2 level 4 and 5 need |
| **CS7**, artist analysis pages | Already marked once. The A2 version should be visibly better |
| The bridge piece finishing schedule | Dated in your sketchbook. Keep to it: the gap is the only finishing time there is |
| Your **three actions** from A1 | They are checked at this review |
| [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessment-criteria\|The AO2 and AO3 criteria]] | Self-check before the review, in writing |

classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessme.body:
# 9479 Assessment Criteria

Cambridge's assessment objectives and marking grid for **9479 for examination in 2028, 2029 and 2030**, the specification you sit.

## The four assessment objectives

Cambridge's wording, syllabus p.12:

| AO | Name | Definition |
|---|---|---|
| **AO1** | Record | Record ideas, observations and insights relevant to intentions, reflecting critically on work and progress. |
| **AO2** | Explore | Explore and select appropriate resources, media, techniques and processes, reviewing and refining ideas as work develops. |
| **AO3** | Develop | Develop ideas through investigations informed by contextual and other sources, making purposeful connections and demonstrating analytical and critical understanding. |
| **AO4** | Present | Present a personal and coherent response that realises intentions and applies visual language to communicate ideas. |

The AO names are **Record, Explore, Develop, Present**.

## Weighting

**As a percentage of the qualification** (syllabus p.13):

| AO | AS Level % | A Level % |
|---|---|---|
| AO1 Record | 25 | 25 |
| AO2 Explore | 25 | 25 |
| AO3 Develop | 29 | 31 |
| AO4 Present | 21 | 19 |

**As a percentage of each component** (syllabus p.13):

| AO | Component 1 | Component 2 | Component 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| AO1 Record | 25 | 25 | 27 |
| AO2 Explore | 25 | 25 | 27 |
| AO3 Develop | 33 | 25 | 33 |
| AO4 Present | 17 | 25 | 13 |

## Marks per component

| Component | Name | Marks | Weighted to | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | Portfolio | 60 | 90 | 60% of AS, 30% of A Level |
| **2** | Externally Set Assignment (15-hour supervised test) | 60 | 60 | 40% of AS, 20% of A Level |
| **3** | Personal Investigation (practical + 2000 to 2500 words) | 75 | 150 | 50% of A Level |

All three components are **externally assessed by Cambridge**. Component 1 is internally set with no question paper, and Cambridge assesses the portfolio as a whole, awarding one mark out of 60 (syllabus p.26).

## Component 1: marks per AO

| AO | Marks |
|---|---|
| AO1 Record | 15 |
| AO2 Explore | 15 |
| AO3 Develop | **20** |
| AO4 Present | **10** |
| **Total** | **60** |

Component 1 puts a greater focus on AO3 Develop and a smaller focus on AO4 Present. This is a change from the previous specification, which weighted the AOs equally.

## Component 1: what you must evidence

Cambridge's elaboration of each AO for the portfolio (syllabus pp.14 to 16), given as the criterion and the evidence it asks for.

### AO1 Record

- **Selected relevant subject matter from a variety of sources.** Recording from a range of primary and secondary sources such as places, people and objects, to visually investigate a chosen theme, media or area of study. This should include research into relevant artists, designers and craftspeople, cultural investigation, and museum, gallery, workshop or studio visits.
- **Recorded ideas, insights and observations using different methods.** Observational study using the most effective processes available: drawing, sketching, painting, samples, prints, modeling, maquettes, photography. Cambridge asks specifically whether different angles, viewpoints, close-up study, surface quality, color, tone and form have been investigated.
- **Communicated intentions through critical reflection.** The selected sources and observational studies are relevant to intention, with clear personal engagement visible in the selections.

### AO2 Explore

- **Selected appropriate media, techniques and processes.** Evidence of reviewing and refining media use to select the most relevant to take forward, with the chosen media reflecting your intentions.
- **Developed an understanding of appropriate skills and visual elements.** Understanding of the inherent properties of media and the visual elements, developing technical skill and control. Cambridge states explicitly that this does **not** mean technical skill alone.
- **Experimented with media, techniques and processes, reviewing and refining as work develops.** Different ways of applying techniques, showing a willingness to take creative risks. Either a selection of media explored for their different properties, or one medium used in different ways to explore its full potential.

### AO3 Develop

- **Formed purposeful and personal connections.** Connections forged between research, recording and exploration to create your own developed ideas, concepts and work.
- **Crafted an investigation that demonstrates analytical and critical understanding.** Evidence of how ideas and imagery moved forward over the duration of the study, with effective decision making throughout.
- **Explored visual elements to communicate ideas.** Alternative compositions, angles, viewpoints, perspectives, forms and designs considered within your own developed imagery.
- **Reflected critically on own strengths and weaknesses.** Awareness of successes, strengths and weaknesses in techniques, ideas and imagery, sufficient to outline modifications.

### AO4 Present

- **Realises intentions.** Evidence across the portfolio that intentions were realised, and that work was thoughtfully and appropriately selected and presented so ideas and progress read clearly.
- **Considers application of visual language to communicate ideas.** Understanding of visual elements such as color, tone, line, form, texture and composition to create a personal visual language, explored throughout the portfolio and used thoughtfully.

## Component 1: the marking grid

Cambridge's five levels, syllabus pp.31 to 33. Each AO is marked on its own level, so a portfolio can sit at different levels on different objectives.

| Level | AO1 Record (15) | AO2 Explore (15) | AO3 Develop (20) | AO4 Present (10) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **5** | **13–15.** Perceptive selection of relevant subject matter from a variety of sources · highly effective methods of recording ideas, insights and observations · clear intention communicated consistently through critical reflection | **13–15.** Perceptive selection of media, techniques and processes · highly effective and consistent understanding of appropriate skills to explore visual elements · highly effective experimentation to review and refine ideas as work develops | **17–20.** Perceptive and mature connections between contextual and other sources · focused investigation demonstrating highly effective analytical and critical understanding · accomplished exploration of visual elements · insightful reflection on own strengths and weaknesses | **9–10.** Accomplished portfolio that fully realises intentions · perceptive application of visual language to communicate ideas |
| **4** | **10–12.** Confident selection from a variety of sources · effective methods of recording · clear intention communicated through critical reflection | **10–12.** Confident selection of appropriate media, techniques and processes · effective and consistent understanding of appropriate skills · effective experimentation to review and refine | **13–16.** Confident connections · focused investigation demonstrating confident analytical and critical understanding · effective exploration of visual elements · effective reflection on own strengths and weaknesses | **7–8.** Confident portfolio that effectively realises intentions · confident application of visual language |
| **3** | **7–9.** Competent selection from different sources · competent methods of recording · competent communication of intention through critical reflection | **7–9.** Competent selection of media · competent understanding of appropriate skills · relevant experimentation to review and refine | **9–12.** Competent connections · thorough investigation demonstrating competent analytical and critical understanding · competent exploration of visual elements · competent reflection on own strengths and weaknesses | **5–6.** Competent portfolio that realises intentions · relevant application of visual language |
| **2** | **4–6.** Sufficient selection from different sources · adequate methods of recording · some communication of intention through critical reflection | **4–6.** Sufficient selection of media · adequate understanding of appropriate skills · adequate experimentation to review and refine | **5–8.** Some evidence of connections · adequate investigation demonstrating some analytical and critical understanding · adequate exploration of visual elements · adequate reflection on own strengths and weaknesses | **3–4.** Adequate portfolio that partly realises intentions · some application of visual language |
| **1** | **1–3.** Limited selection from sources · limited methods of recording · basic ability to communicate intention through critical reflection | **1–3.** Limited selection of media · basic understanding of appropriate skills · limited experimentation to review and refine | **1–4.** Limited evidence of connections · limited investigation demonstrating basic analytical and critical understanding · limited exploration of visual elements · basic reflection on own strengths and weaknesses | **1–2.** Basic portfolio that does not fully realise intentions · limited application of visual language |
| **0** | 0. No creditable response | 0. No creditable response | 0. No creditable response | 0. No creditable response |

Reading down any column, the level words run: **perceptive, confident, competent, sufficient or adequate, limited or basic.** The same ladder runs through all three components.

## How this maps onto the semester

Component 1 is marked **as a whole portfolio, once, by Cambridge**. The attainments in [[classes/a-level-art-design/assessments/9479-s1-assessments|the register]] are BNDS milestones that sample the portfolio as you build it, so each one is marked against the AO columns it draws on rather than against all four:

| Attainment | AO columns used | Marks available |
|---|---|---|
| A1 Recording | AO1 | 15 |
| A2 Exploration and artist study | AO2 + AO3 | 35 |
| A3 Development | AO3 | 20 |
| A4 Final portfolio | AO1 to AO4 | 60 |

Under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] these marks are curved rather than reported raw, so a milestone mark is a Forecast Grade signal, not a Cambridge score.

classes/a-level-art-design/assessments/9.body:
# 9479 S1 The Final

[[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design|A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/assessments/9479-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · End of Term Exam category, 20%

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Date not yet fixed. It falls in or around the exam window, Mon 2027-01-11 to Mon 2027-01-18 |
| Category | End of Term Exam, 20% of the semester grade |
| Format | A teacher assessment of your portfolio so far against the Cambridge criteria. **No exam paper and no invigilated sitting** |
| Assesses | AO1 to AO4, the whole of Component 1 |
| What you do for it | Nothing new. The evidence is the portfolio you submitted at A4 |
| This class | Sits **no department finals**, so the exam window carries no other Art and Design commitment |

## Objectives

The Final is not a task you prepare separately for. It asks one question: **taken as a whole, where is this portfolio against the Cambridge criteria at the end of Semester 1?**

What it establishes for you:

1. A single reading of your portfolio as one body of work rather than four milestones.
2. A defensible Forecast Grade to carry into Semester 2 and the Personal Investigation.
3. A clear statement of which AO is currently your weakest. Semester 2 planning acts on that.

## The task

There is no task. This is the important thing to understand about it.

A studio course has no exam paper to sit. Cambridge assesses Component 1 as one whole portfolio, once, at the end of the course. The school's End of Term Exam category asks for a summative 20% grade covering previously taught content. Those two facts are satisfied by **assessing the portfolio you have already made**, against the same criteria Cambridge will use, at the semester boundary.

So there is nothing to revise for, nothing to bring, and nothing to hand in that you have not already handed in.

## Instructions

**For you:** submit A4 properly on Thu 2027-01-07 and the Final takes care of itself. It reads the same portfolio.

**What happens:**

1. Your A4 submission is marked against all four AOs. That is A4's own mark.
2. Your portfolio is then assessed **as a whole** against the Component 1 criteria. This is a different judgment: not the sum of four milestones but one reading of the body of work.
3. That whole-portfolio judgment is the End of Term grade, 20% of the semester.
4. It is reported with your other grades on Wed 2027-01-20.

**During the exam window (Mon 01-11 to Mon 01-18)** there are no Art and Design classes. You do not sit anything for this course that week.

## Rubric

The **same Cambridge Component 1 grid** used for A4, applied to the portfolio as a whole: [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessment-criteria|9479 Assessment Criteria]].

| AO | Marks |
|---|---|
| AO1 Record | 15 |
| AO2 Explore | 15 |
| AO3 Develop | 20 |
| AO4 Present | 10 |
| **Total** | **60**, weighted to 90 by Cambridge |

The difference between this and A4 is the unit of judgment, not the criteria:

- **A4** asks whether each AO is evidenced in the portfolio, milestone by milestone.
- **The Final** asks what level the portfolio sits at when read once, end to end, the way Cambridge will read it. A portfolio can pass every milestone and still read as level 3 overall if the parts do not add up to one coherent body of work.

Under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] this grade is curved against CIE past-paper data, allowing for where the class is in its learning trajectory, and it should make a reliable Forecast Grade. It is not a raw Cambridge score, and it is not a prediction of the mark Cambridge will award in 2028.

## After it

- Reported with grades and comments on **Wed 2027-01-20**.
- Read alongside your A4 feedback in the W21 one-to-ones, Tuesday to Thursday.
- The weakest-AO finding is what Semester 2 planning uses. Semester 2 is Component 3, the Personal Investigation, where AO1 and AO2 both carry more weight (27% each) than they do in Component 1.

# 9479 S1 A4: Final Portfolio

[[classes/a-level-art-design/a-level-art-design|A Level Art & Design]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/assessments/9479-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/a-level-art-design/lesson-plans/9479-s1-lesson-15-submission-week-and-a4|Lesson 15]] · Attainment 4 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Due | Thu 2027-01-07, submitted in session |
| Category | Attainment, the fourth of four in the 50% category |
| Format | The complete Component 1 portfolio, submitted digitally. **No edits after submission** |
| Assesses | **AO1 to AO4**, all 60 marks of Component 1 |
| What is submitted | The resolved final outcome plus the complete supporting portfolio, sequenced and edited |
| Marking window | Thu 2027-01-07 to Wed 2027-01-20, nine working days |
| Returned | W21, one to one, Tue to Thu. Grades and comments due Wed 2027-01-20 |
| Unit | [[classes/a-level-art-design/unit-plans/9479-s1-unit-5-final-outcome-and-portfolio\|U5 Final Outcome and Portfolio]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Photograph your outcome as the version an examiner will actually see. The photograph **is** the work as far as submission is concerned.
2. Sequence the whole journey so it reads in order without you narrating it: theme, recording, exploration, artists, development, outcome.
3. Cut what does not earn its place, and say what you cut.
4. Check your own portfolio against all four AO descriptors, in writing, before it goes.
5. Submit a portfolio that realizes the intention you set in Week 1, or that shows honestly where the intention changed and why.

## The task

A4 is the semester's submission. It is the only attainment marked on all four AOs, because it is the whole portfolio rather than a slice of it.

What you submit:

- **The resolved final outcome**, photographed properly: rig, light, full shot, detail passes, cropped, corrected, named and filed to the template.
- **The complete supporting portfolio**: intention, recording pages, sustained study, media experiments, media selection, scale trial, both artist studies, the bridge piece, both compositions, targeted tests, evaluations, and the final composition plan.
- **In sequence**, laid out as a run order that a stranger can follow.

You submit all work digitally. Cambridge takes no hyperlinks and no QR codes. Annotation is assessed within AO3 and must be **typed**.

## Instructions

**Submission week runs Mon 01-04 to Fri 01-08, and every day has a job.**

1. **Mon 01-04.** Photograph the outcome, then prepare the images: crop, correct, name, file to the template.
2. **Tue 01-05.** Sequence the portfolio. Lay the full run order out and walk it once. Then a peer walks it and tells you where a stranger stumbles.
3. **Wed 01-06.** Edit and clean. Cut what does not earn its place and **log every cut.** Then do the final AO check: all four descriptors, in writing, signed.
4. **Thu 01-07.** Submit, in session. **Nothing is edited after.**
5. **Fri 01-08.** Submission is acknowledged, you write your semester reflection, and the winter homework is set.

**The rule that matters most: no edits after submission.** Work not in the portfolio on Thursday is not in the portfolio.

**If you are absent.** Contact your teacher **at least 24 hours before** the deadline. Request extensions 24 hours ahead. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8). The school's usual late-work cutoff, roughly three weeks before the last school day of the semester, falls inside the winter break for S1, so do not rely on it.

## Rubric

**All four AOs, 60 marks**, from Cambridge's Component 1 grid. Full descriptors for every level: [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessment-criteria|9479 Assessment Criteria]].

| AO | What it judges here | Marks |
|---|---|---|
| **AO1 Record** | Selection of subject matter from a variety of sources, methods of recording, intention communicated through critical reflection | 15 |
| **AO2 Explore** | Selection of media and processes, understanding of skills and visual elements, experimentation that reviews and refines | 15 |
| **AO3 Develop** | Purposeful connections, a focused investigation with analytical and critical understanding, exploration of visual elements, reflection on strengths and weaknesses | **20** |
| **AO4 Present** | Realizing intentions, and applying visual language to communicate ideas | 10 |

### AO4 Present, the one A4 adds

The other three AOs have been sampled at A1, A2 and A3. AO4 is assessed for the first time here, because it is a property of the portfolio as a whole.

| Level | Marks | Descriptor |
|---|---|---|
| **5** | 9–10 | **Accomplished** portfolio that **fully** realises intentions · perceptive application of visual language to communicate ideas |
| **4** | 7–8 | Confident portfolio that effectively realises intentions · confident application of visual language |
| **3** | 5–6 | Competent portfolio that realises intentions · relevant application of visual language |
| **2** | 3–4 | Adequate portfolio that **partly** realises intentions · some application of visual language |
| **1** | 1–2 | Basic portfolio that does **not fully** realise intentions · limited application of visual language |
| **0** | 0 | No creditable response |

AO4 is where sequencing and editing are paid for. Cambridge asks that the work be "thoughtfully and appropriately selected and presented" so that ideas and progress read clearly. A portfolio holding strong work in a confusing order loses marks here that the work itself had earned.

AO4 is 10 marks of 60 in this specification, **down** from the old equal split. Do not spend more time on presentation than on development, which is worth double.

Marks are curved under [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|the BNDS framework]] rather than reported raw. Cambridge itself will mark this portfolio as a whole out of 60 at the end of the course. A4's mark is the school's forecast of that.

## After the sit

- **Marking window Thu 2027-01-07 to Wed 2027-01-20**, nine working days. Grades and comments are due Wed 2027-01-20.
- W20 (from Mon 01-11) is the school exam window. There are **no Art and Design classes** that week.
- Portfolios come back in **W21**, one to one, Tuesday to Thursday.
- Winter vacation runs 2027-01-24 to 2027-02-21. Your winter homework is three candidate Personal Investigation themes with annotated references, due Mon 2027-02-22: the [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-c3-winter-brief|C3 Winter Brief]].

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **CS10**, mid-production review reflection | The last checkpoint before the outcome was finished |
| The amended composition plan from A3 | What the outcome was supposed to be. AO4 asks whether it was realized |
| Your cut log from Wed 01-06 | Evidence of editing judgment, and useful to you in Semester 2 |
| All three earlier self-checks | The AO check on Wed 01-06 is the fourth and the only one covering all four AOs |
| [[classes/a-level-art-design/9479-assessment-criteria\|The full criteria grid]] | Sign the final check against Cambridge's words |

# Art Appreciation S1 A1: The Unit 1 Board

[[classes/art-appreciation/art-appreciation|Art Appreciation]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/assessments/art-appreciation-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-03-the-first-board|Lesson 03]] · Attainment 1 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Fri 2026-09-18, one 45-minute session |
| Category | Attainment, the first of four in the 50% category |
| Format | **A group board built on the wall, plus your own individual written justification** |
| Marked on | Adjacency reasoning · Legibility of the argument in the layout · Description · Your written justification |
| Grade | **Half collective, half individual.** The board is the group's; the justification is yours |
| Criteria issued | Two weeks ahead, not on the day |
| Materials | Wall space, pins. **No glue** |
| Unit | [[classes/art-appreciation/unit-plans/art-appreciation-s1-unit-1-origins-and-ancestral-memory\|U1 Origins and Ancestral Memory]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Put two images next to each other **for a reason that belongs to that pair** and to no other pair.
2. Make an argument that is **legible from the layout before a word is read**.
3. Describe an object by **what it does**, not by what it reminds you of.
4. Write a justification that gives the reasons the wall cannot say out loud.

## The task

Your group builds a board on the wall from the print pool: images spanning Chauvet, Lascaux, Neolithic figures and ritual objects. The pool is over-supplied on purpose, so selection is a real decision rather than a scramble.

Then each of you writes your own justification of it.

The standard, stated once and worth memorizing:

**A board without reasons is a mood board.**

Every adjacency has to carry a reason. If the reason you give for putting A next to B would work just as well for A next to C, it is not yet a reason.

## Instructions

1. **Select** from the print pool. You cannot use everything, and what you leave out is part of the argument.
2. **Arrange** on the wall with pins. No glue: the arrangement has to stay changeable until you are satisfied.
3. **Test each adjacency.** For every pair, ask: could this reason be moved to a different pair? If yes, the pair is decorative.
4. **Step back and read your own wall.** Somebody who arrives knowing nothing should be able to see what you are claiming before you explain it.
5. **Write your justification individually.** What the board argues, what each adjacency does, and what the arrangement leaves out.

**The grade is half collective.** The board earns a shared mark; your justification earns your own. Understand how that works before you start, or you will spend the last session arguing about it instead of hanging.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8).

## Rubric

Four criteria. The first three are the board (shared); the fourth is yours.

| | **Adjacency reasoning** | **Layout legibility** | **Description** | **Written justification** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | Every pairing carries a reason that could not be transferred to a different pair. At least one adjacency is genuinely surprising and survives scrutiny | The argument is visible on arrival. Distance, grouping and gaps all doing work | Objects are described by what they do: what they are for, what they make happen, who used them | Gives the reasons the wall cannot state, names what was excluded and why, and does not simply narrate the board |
| **Convincing** | Reasons are specific to their pairs, with one or two that could be moved | The argument reads clearly with a moment's looking | Mostly functional description, with occasional drift into association | Clear reasons throughout, including at least one exclusion |
| **Competent** | Pairings are related, and the reasons are true but general | An order is visible; the argument needs a sentence of help | Description mixes what objects do with what they look like | States what the board argues and gives reasons for most of it |
| **Partial** | Images are grouped by subject or by looking similar | The board reads as a collection | Description is mostly visual resemblance | Narrates the board rather than justifying it |
| **Undeveloped** | No reasoning offered for the arrangement | No argument discernible | Objects named, not described | Little or no justification |

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a curved grade rather than a raw score.

## After the sit

The course's review protocol, used on every assessment:

1. **The criteria**, in front of you.
2. **Ten minutes of silence** with your own work and the criteria before anything is discussed.
3. **One named strength.**
4. **One move**: the single next thing.

Marking is back within five working days.

**Leave the boards up.** Unit 2 opens against them, and the December and January comparisons work much better if the first board is still on the wall.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **CS1**, the darkroom reflection (Fri 2026-09-04) | Written in the room, on the image as physical trace. It rehearses the description habit |
| **L01 and L02**, opening the atlas and what survives | The method itself: why adjacency is an argument |
| The criteria sheet | You have two weeks with it. Use it while you are hanging, not after |

# Art Appreciation S1 A2: The Titian and Manet Comparison

[[classes/art-appreciation/art-appreciation|Art Appreciation]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/assessments/art-appreciation-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-05-titian-to-manet|Lesson 05]] · Attainment 2 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Tue 2026-10-13, the Tuesday double |
| Category | Attainment, the second of four in the 50% category |
| Format | **In-class essay, closed.** No notes, no phones, no reading brought in |
| The task | One claim about Titian against Manet, evidenced from the pictures |
| Marked on | The claim · Evidence from the pictures · Comparison as argument · Precision of language |
| Feeds | The mid-term grades due Thu 2026-10-29 |
| Returned | Inside a week, because mid-terms need it |
| Unit | [[classes/art-appreciation/unit-plans/art-appreciation-s1-unit-2-narrative-myth-and-allegory\|U2 Narrative, Myth and Allegory]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Locate a **specific refusal** Manet makes of Titian, and say what that refusal costs.
2. Build a comparison from differences that **carry meaning**, not from an inventory of what is different.
3. Argue **one claim**, evidenced from the pictures rather than from their reception.
4. Write about paintings without decorating the sentences.

## The task

You write an in-class essay on two paintings, closed book.

You make **one claim** about Titian against Manet and you argue it from what is in the pictures.

The trap, and it is the whole reason this assessment exists:

**A list is not a comparison.**

Anyone can produce a list of differences: the gaze, the maid, the cat, the shoes, the flowers, the hand. A list is inventory. A comparison identifies which difference matters and argues what it does. One difference, followed properly, beats six differences noted.

The second trap is arguing from **reception**. What critics said in 1865 is interesting, and it is not evidence about the picture. You read on *Olympia*'s reception as homework so you know the difference between the painting and the noise around it.

## Instructions

1. **Choose your difference before you start writing.** Not the most obvious one, the most productive one.
2. **State your claim in your first paragraph.** A claim is arguable: somebody could disagree with it. "Manet's Olympia is different from Titian's Venus" is not a claim.
3. **Evidence every step from the picture.** Point at what is actually there: where the eyes go, what the hand does, how the space is built, what the paint itself does.
4. **Say what the refusal costs.** Manet gives something up by refusing Titian. Naming the cost is what separates a good essay from a competent one.
5. **Do not narrate the paintings.** Assume your reader can see them.

**Closed conditions.** No notes and no reading brought into the room. What you know is what you carry.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher **at least 24 hours before**. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8). This one also carries mid-term grades, so an absence has knock-on consequences.

## Rubric

Four criteria, equally weighted.

| | **The claim** | **Evidence from the pictures** | **Comparison as argument** | **Precision of language** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | One arguable claim, stated early, held throughout, and worth making. It identifies a refusal and names what the refusal costs | Every step evidenced from what is in the picture, at the level of where the eye goes and what the paint does | One difference followed all the way. The comparison produces something neither picture would have shown alone | Every adjective is earned. Nothing decorative. The prose does the analysis rather than dressing it |
| **Convincing** | A clear arguable claim, held, with the cost of the refusal implied rather than named | Consistently evidenced from the pictures, with one or two assertions unsupported | A dominant difference is followed, with minor detours into inventory | Controlled and mostly precise |
| **Competent** | A claim is present but broad, or drifts by the end | Some evidence from the pictures, some from what was taught | Two or three differences noted, one developed | Clear, with some vague or ornamental phrasing |
| **Partial** | A topic rather than a claim | Assertion with occasional gestures at the pictures | A list of differences, undeveloped | Loose, with unearned adjectives doing the work of argument |
| **Undeveloped** | No identifiable claim | Argues from reception or from memory of the lesson, not from the pictures | Description of two paintings in sequence | Imprecise throughout |

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a curved grade rather than a raw score.

## After the sit

The course's review protocol: **the criteria** in front of you, **ten minutes of silence** with your own work, **one named strength**, **one move.**

Marking is inside a week rather than the usual five working days, because **A2 carries the mid-term grades due Thu 2026-10-29** along with participation.

## How to prepare

| Where it came from | What to use it for |
|---|---|
| **CS2**, the ten-frame storyboard, no captions or dialogue | Reading what a picture decided. It is the direct rehearsal for this |
| **CS3**, the storyboard debrief (Fri 2026-10-09) | Where a sequence stopped being legible. The same diagnostic you apply to a painting |
| The *Olympia* reception reading | So you know what reception is, and therefore what it is not evidence of |
| Your **A1 justification** and its feedback | The same skill in a different form: reasons that belong to their pair |
| The criteria sheet | You have it two weeks in advance. Use it to plan the essay, not to check it afterwards |

# Art Appreciation S1 A3: The Food and Ethics Essay

[[classes/art-appreciation/art-appreciation|Art Appreciation]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/assessments/art-appreciation-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-09-food-the-table-and-ethics|Lesson 09]] · Attainment 3 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Tue 2026-11-17, the Tuesday double |
| Category | Attainment, the third of four in the 50% category |
| Format | In-class essay |
| The task | One claim about food, the table and ethics, argued from the pictures |
| Marked on | The claim · Evidence from the pictures · Argument from the pictures rather than from ethics · Precision of language |
| Returned | Within five working days |
| Unit | [[classes/art-appreciation/unit-plans/art-appreciation-s1-unit-3-food-the-table-and-ethics\|U3 Food, the Table and Ethics]] |

## Objectives

This assessment asks you to show that you can:

1. Look at **domestic labor as labor**.
2. Say what a table does when it is **the same table every time**.
3. Argue one claim about food and ethics **from the pictures themselves, not from the ethics**.
4. Say who is not in the picture, and what their absence is doing.

## The task

An in-class essay on the unit's material: the table as a moral space, Heda and the image of work, Rosler, and the artists who do something the paintings could not.

You make **one claim** and argue it from the pictures.

Here is the specific difficulty of this essay, and the reason it comes third rather than first: the subject invites you to argue from ethics. Food, class, labor and who is absent from the table are all questions with moral answers available before you have looked at anything. An essay that arrives at the right ethical position without going through the pictures has not done the work this course teaches.

So the ethics has to be found in the picture, in what it selected, arranged, lit and left out. Not brought to it.

## Instructions

1. **Choose your pictures first, then your claim.** If the claim came first, check whether the pictures actually support it or whether you are illustrating an opinion.
2. **State the claim early** and keep it.
3. **Argue from what is there**: the arrangement of the table, what the light does, what state the food is in, whose hands are visible, what work is implied and what work is hidden.
4. **Treat absence as evidence.** Who is not in the picture is a decision the picture made, and it is arguable.
5. **Earn every adjective.** This is the criterion CS4 rehearsed on Heda.

**If you are absent.** Tell your teacher at least 24 hours before. Illness needs a doctor's note. Without advance contact the mark may be 0, even for genuine illness (AL Student Guide p.8).

## Rubric

Four criteria, equally weighted. The third is the one that distinguishes this essay from A2.

| | **The claim** | **Evidence from the pictures** | **From the pictures, not the ethics** | **Precision of language** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Perceptive** | One arguable claim about food, the table and ethics, worth making and held throughout | Every step evidenced from arrangement, light, state, hands, absence. Absence is used as evidence rather than mentioned | The ethical reading is **produced by** looking: it could not have been written without these pictures | Every adjective earned. Domestic labor described as labor, without sentiment |
| **Convincing** | A clear arguable claim, held | Consistently evidenced from the pictures, with one or two unsupported steps | The ethics is grounded in the pictures, with occasional appeals to general position | Controlled and mostly precise |
| **Competent** | A claim is present but broad | Some evidence from the pictures, some from the readings | The ethical position and the visual analysis run in parallel rather than one producing the other | Clear, with some vague phrasing |
| **Partial** | A topic rather than a claim | Assertion with occasional reference to the pictures | The position is asserted first and the pictures are recruited to illustrate it | Loose, sentimental about labor or food |
| **Undeveloped** | No identifiable claim | No evidence from the pictures | An essay about ethics that happens to mention paintings | Imprecise throughout |

Under the [[shared/bnds-assessment-framework|BNDS framework]] this becomes a curved grade rather than a raw score.

## After the sit

The course's review protocol: the criteria, ten minutes of silence, one named strength, one move.

Marking back within five working days. This unit hands directly to Unit 4, which takes the same question into mediation, so what this essay reveals is immediately usable.

| **L06**, the table as a moral space | What a table does when it is the same table every time |
| **L08**, Heda and the image of work | Domestic labor as labor, which is objective 1 |
| **L09**, Cassatt then Rosler in the period before the sit | Your comparative material; Weems follows the essay and hands forward to Unit 4 |
| Your **A2 feedback** | The same essay skills. The one move you were given is checked here |

# Art Appreciation S1 A4: The Unit 4 Synthesis

[[classes/art-appreciation/art-appreciation|Art Appreciation]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/assessments/art-appreciation-s1-assessments|S1 Assessment Register]] · [[classes/art-appreciation/lesson-plans/art-appreciation-s1-lesson-12-photography-and-after|Lesson 12]] · Attainment 4 of 4

## At a glance

| | |
|---|---|
| Sits | Tue 2026-12-15, the Tuesday double |
| Category | Attainment, the last of four in the 50% category |
| Format | **In-class constellation build plus a written argument** |
